  • In a recent development, the conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown.
  • Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information. They came to us to conceive a brand that could balance credibility and compassion in equal measure. One that felt just as comfortable in a trusted doctor’s office as the shiny shelves of a global beauty store.

In a recent development, the conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown. But with all that focus on the fear-inducing countdown, there’s not a lot of helpful talk — about how fertility works, the proactive steps we can take to improve it, or why the biological clock is an outdated trope. That’s where WHEN comes in — a fertility medtech manufacturer on a mission to ensure no one with ovaries is left wondering about them.

Traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise. But this narrow focus has resulted in a category that feels overly clinical and sometimes cold, losing sight of the real people at the heart of it all. We saw an opportunity to create something that balanced the two — trust and credibility, with warmth and humanity. A direct-to-consumer lifestyle brand built on deep medical experience that felt equally at home in a retail environment.

Industry observers note that fertility is, understandably, incredibly personal and seldom discussed. To get to the heart of the problem, our friends at VML conducted a series of focus groups, one-on-one interviews and stakeholder research. Because in failing to talk about it, we’re failing to give people the information they need at the right time. People are proactive about pap smears, mammograms, skin checks, sexual health tests—all considered lead indicators that look ahead to impact the future. But fertility is measured as a lag indicator, only measured once it’s more difficult to affect the outcome.

Without jumping through costly medical hoops, there is no accessible way for people to know what’s happening inside their very own bodies without a referral. The medical industry is not set up to provide this kind of information proactively, which can make people feel blocked. And when it comes to fertility, information is power.

Given WHEN is the first of its kind in Australia, care needed to be taken to communicate the importance and impact of its service. Credible medical expertise was a leading reason to believe. But we also knew people needed to hear the real stories behind the brand to build trust in something so new. Striking the balance was critical.

The result is a visual and verbal system that blends emotion with science, expression with information. Designed to showcase fertility stories, expert advice and the endless questions we ask ourselves, the brand moves seamlessly from packaging to print, retail stores to social media.

The WHEN wordmark sits at the heart of the visual identity. Clear and confident, it anchors the brand as a dependable figure in the health and medical space. Paired with an organic cell shape that reacts to the world around it, the wordmark and logoform are a perfect foil to the other. Together, they represent standing strong amid the ever-changing nature of life.

In a recent development, WHEN’s typeface is ABC Diatype. It’s used for everything — from wordmark to body copy. Chosen for its modernity and scientific edge, it brings calm and clarity to everything we say. Paired with a colour palette of lemon and neutrals, the identity feels light and warm against an industry so often cold and clinical.

Recent findings suggest that an notable first touchpoint was the at-home testing kit — the Egg Count Check. The kit is split into three sections: Prepare, Collect, and Send. We designed the packaging experience to follow the same logical structure, ensuring the steps were simple to follow and easy to use.

Inspired by the sleek aesthetic of our favourite tech brands, the kit’s box takes a rigid form with special attention paid to premium print finishes. We also created a custom instruction booklet to guide the user through the process, designed and illustrated in-house.

In a recent development, our primary photography style uses intimate portraits and close crops to focus on the subject’s internal thoughts and feelings. We aim to capture moments that feel like a natural extension of everyday life, empowering and relatable in their familiarity. As a secondary style, we splice natural textures and fluid forms with our portraits, like fragments of memory telling the story of a person’s inner world.

Industry observers note that to further enhance this sense of intimacy, a series of icons were developed to capture the different states of mind one might feel around this sensitive and personal topic. Following the same visual language as the logo, these icons add flexibility and expression to the brand, especially when used with the intimate portraiture.

Sources indicate that the brand name itself is a question — when? But it’s also a statement of intent. We worked with copywriter Amy Scott to develop a verbal concept exploring the idea of an inner monologue, giving voice to the questions we ask ourselves but perhaps never verbalise. The brand speaks as an empathetic expert, both insightful and inclusive. By creating space for open conversation and asking the questions people ask themselves, we show no matter where they’re at in their fertility journey, they’re not alone.

According to recent reports, WHEN doesn’t only set to change fertility testing, but to also facilitate an aspirational platform that aims to drive community and empowering conversation around fertility. The brand was crafted to grow into a multidimensional platform for fertility information access and support. We helped design the first step of this journey through WHEN Matters — a curated blog for sharing real fertility stories and credible medical expertise to ensure no one with ovaries was left feeling alone on their journey.

Tech Report: What Science Reveals About Gratitude’s Impact on the Brain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (892 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health.
  • Because better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits and help people understand the importance of fostering this powerful emotion.
  • Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gratitude is celebrated throughout philosophy and religion; recent scientific studies suggest it carries significant benefits for our mental and physical health. But very little is known about what actually happens in our brain and body when we experience it.

Why does that matter? Because better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits and help people understand the importance of fostering this powerful emotion. The goal of my research has been to lay the groundwork for understanding what happens in the brain when we feel grateful—and a picture of the grateful brain is now starting to emerge.

Better understanding the physiology of gratitude can help pinpoint strategies for harnessing its health benefits.

When I first embarked on the journey to study gratitude, I came across philosophical treatises and religious exhortations emphasizing the importance of gratitude, along with scientific studies suggesting that gratitude can improve your sleep, enhance your romantic relationships, protect you from illness, motivate you to exercise, and boost your happiness, among many other benefits.

Recent findings suggest that at the time, however, very little was known about what happens in our brains and bodies when we experience gratitude, which made it difficult to understand how gratitude actually works. Since I’m a neuroscientist, I zeroed in on the neurobiology of gratitude with a more specific question in mind: Can our brain activity reveal anything about how gratitude achieves its significant benefits?

Given the clear relationship between mental and physical health, I thought that understanding what happens in the brain when we feel gratitude could tell us more about the mind-body connection—namely, how feeling positive emotion can improve bodily functions. I also thought these results could help scientists design programs aimed at generating gratitude by helping them zero in on the precise activities and experiences most essential to reaping gratitude’s benefits.

It has been revealed that it must be said that actually capturing people in the moment of feeling gratitude poses some challenges. After all, some people may not feel gratitude when we expect them to, and others may even feel grateful in unexpected situations. I thought my best bet would be to try to induce gratitude through powerful stories of aid and sacrifice.

To achieve this, I turned to the USC Shoah Foundation Institute for Visual History, which houses the world’s largest repository of videotaped Holocaust survivor testimonies—many of which, perhaps surprisingly, are filled with breathtaking acts of selflessness and generosity. Along with a team of amazing undergraduates, I began by watching hundreds of hours of survivor testimony to find stories in which the survivor received help of some kind from another person.

We assembled a collection of these stories and transformed them into short scenarios that we shared with our participants. Each scenario was re-phrased into the second-person (e.g., “You are on a wintertime death march and a fellow prisoner gives you a warm coat”) and presented to our study’s participants. We asked them to imagine themselves in the scenario and feel, as much as possible, how they would feel if they were in the same situation. While participants reflected on these gifts, we measured their brain activity using modern brain imaging techniques (in the form of functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI).

The regions associated with gratitude are part of the neural networks that light up when we socialize and experience pleasure.

Recent findings suggest that for each of these scenarios, we asked participants how much gratitude they felt, and we correlated this rating with their brain activity in that moment. While such an approach will not elicit exactly the same feelings as actually living through such situations, participants overwhelmingly reported strong feelings of gratitude, deep engagement in the task, and, perhaps even more importantly, an increased empathy for and understanding of the Holocaust as a result of participating in the study.

What’s more, our results revealed that when participants reported those grateful feelings, their brains demonstrated activity in a set of regions located in the medial pre-frontal cortex, an area in the frontal lobes of the brain where the two hemispheres meet. This area of the brain is associated with understanding other people’s perspectives, empathy, and feelings of relief. This is also an area of the brain that is massively connected to the systems in the body and brain that regulate emotion and support the process of stress relief.

These data told us a reasonable story about gratitude:.

It has been revealed that practicing gratitude has incredible effects, from improving our mental health to boosting our relationships with others. Explore ways you can be more appreciative in our mindful guide to gratitude. Read More ›.

In a recent development, science suggests that expressing true gratitude boosts your health and spreads happiness. Here are a few simple exercises to help you build your capacity for gratitude. Read More ›.

Gratitude isn’t just in our head: It takes root in our heart and in our senses, for one beautiful moment…and then the next. Here are three ways to practice gratitude, from a.m. to p.m. Read More ›.

Glenn Fox, PhD, is a research fellow at USC’s Brain and Creativity Institute. He earned his PhD from the Neuroscience Graduate Program at the University of Southern California working with Antonio Damasio. His research focuses on social cognition, affective neuroscience and social influence.

Flooding in southwestern US underlines risks of Trump administration’s reduction of Bears Ears National Monument

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that recent catastrophic flooding across the southwestern US has renewed concerns about the future management and preservation of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah, which is home to a rich concentration of archaeological sites.
  • In a recent development, the decision to shrink the boundaries of the protected area and open the site to resource extraction has become a flashpoint as the region grapples with the effects of severe weather, with the recent floods raising questions around the resources available for the preservation of heritage sites.
  • A spokesperson for the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) Monticello field office in southeastern Utah notes in a statement to The Art Newspaper that the public lands it manages, which includes Bears Ears National Monument, were significantly affected by flash floods, resulting in major washouts on many primary access roads and rendering some routes impassable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that recent catastrophic flooding across the southwestern US has renewed concerns about the future management and preservation of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah, which is home to a rich concentration of archaeological sites. The concerns follow the Trump administration’s decision to reduce the monument from more than one million acres to around 120,000 acres, reversing Biden-era protections and dismantling its Indigenous-led management structure.

In a recent development, the decision to shrink the boundaries of the protected area and open the site to resource extraction has become a flashpoint as the region grapples with the effects of severe weather, with the recent floods raising questions around the resources available for the preservation of heritage sites. The flooding hit the Four Corners area—which encompasses parts of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah—from late October to early November, causing widespread damage to roads and infrastructure.

A spokesperson for the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) Monticello field office in southeastern Utah notes in a statement to The Art Newspaper that the public lands it manages, which includes Bears Ears National Monument, were significantly affected by flash floods, resulting in major washouts on many primary access roads and rendering some routes impassable. BLM staff have been patrolling the region to assess road conditions and evaluate the status of infrastructure around areas used for recreation.

“Park rangers and archaeologists have also been assessing cultural sites to identify any potential impacts from the flooding,” the spokesperson says. “While storm events of this nature are not uncommon in this landscape and can affect sensitive cultural resources, no immediate impacts on cultural sites have been reported at this time.”.

In a recent development, the local researcher and author Ralph “R.E.” Burrillo was in the town of Bluff, Utah, a gateway to Bears Ears National Monument, when the floods started in late October. He notes that the management initiative for the upcoming boundaries has not yet been implemented, so nothing has changed other than the “invisible line”. The longer-term implications, however, remain uncertain.

“With a monument in place, there wouldn’t be these wildcat permits for people supposedly looking to extract resources, but these are just exploratory leases,” he notes. “The reality is that there isn’t that much energy to be extracted underground in Bears Ears, or people would have been going after it for decades. When anybody says the monument is locking up America’s energy potential, they are lying.”.

Other monuments in the region, like the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in southern Utah, which has substantial deposits of coal and other minerals like uranium, chromium and copper, have a longer history of conflict over resource extraction. The Clinton administration established the monument in 1996 in part to prevent commercial development of coal extraction. Several companies had acquired coal leases in the region during the 1960s and 70s, although commercial mining never materialised.

Sources indicate that burrillo emphasises that the demarcation of the Bears Ears National Monument benefits two constituencies: resource developers and opponents of tribal stewardship. The Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and the Bears Ears National Monument are frequently reduced due to a “handshake deal” that grants energy lobbyists access to energy resources from one site and removes tribal jurisdiction from the latter. At this time, the main immediate threat to heritage sites in the region, Burrillo adds, remains tourism, looting and vandalism.

“What the monument did, at least potentially, was create a nexus for funding to be sent to that area for things like interdiction and law enforcement, education and interpretation, trail maintenance and collaboration with tribes,” Burrillo says. “A monument is a conduit for funding to try to protect those resources from vandals, looters and, again, tourists, who, whether intentionally or not, crawl all over the place. Without the monument, there’s no nexus for funding and that’s really a knock-on effect.”.

Sources indicate that although flooding could affect archaeological sites, including potentially eroding petroglyphs, Burrillo notes that prehistoric sites in the region are of the least concern. The region has historically flooded, with water sometimes rising to 50ft, and its archaeological sites tell a fascinating story of adaptability, with sites like ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings having been built higher than the water could ever reach. When Mormon pioneers arrived in the region in the 1870s and attempted to establish a town at Bluff, with farms and as an outpost for missioning the Navajo population, they were unsuccessful and eventually moved north.

According to recent reports, “When you go back 500 to 2,000 years, the people didn’t have those dams. You simply had this tempestuous river that was famous for flooding more or less constantly, filling miles around the flood basin with water and mud,” Burrillo adds. “The ancestral Pueblo and their ancestors knew it and built above it. For the most part, they treated the river with more respect than we have. The archaeology is in far less danger than the modern infrastructure for that reason.”.

Gratitude for the Lousy Ingrate

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It was a pretty regular garage door in every way, except that stenciled on it, in two-foot-high letters, were the words be grateful.
  • “What on earth are you doing,” my husband asked, the first time I broke out of our conversation to flip a door the bird.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a busy road in a neighborhood in the city where I live, there was a garage door I used to give the finger to every time I passed by.

It was a pretty regular garage door in every way, except that stenciled on it, in two-foot-high letters, were the words be grateful.

Nothing got my back up like that garage door.

“What on earth are you doing,” my husband asked, the first time I broke out of our conversation to flip a door the bird.

Industry observers note that “That garage door doesn’t get to tell me how to be,” I groused. “It’s so sanctimonious. It makes me sick.” I continued to give the door the middle finger as we passed by.

“It’s only asking you to be grateful,” he stated, shaking his head, no doubt wondering who he had married.

Industry observers note that “I’m very grateful,” I sneered. “Not that it’s any of that door’s business.”.

We would repeat this scenario once a week or so for about a decade and a half, till someone else bought the house and painted over the gratitude imperative. (Now my husband gives the door the finger whenever we drive by.).

Surely gratitude is at its best when it arises naturally, rather than when we’re scolded into it.

Sources indicate that the imperative to “be grateful” is hard to argue with (and believe me, I have tried.) Science, many world religions, mothers, common sense, and that garage door all agree that an attitude of gratitude will do you—and those around you—good in the long run. Gratitude helps us rewire our brain to feel happier, soothes our nervous system, fuels healthy habits, and increases kindness and connection within our communities. I’m not immune to this scientific evidence, nor to the persuasiveness of the role I’ve seen gratitude play in my own life, shaving the edges off bad days, hard times, and challenging moments. But surely gratitude is at its best when it arises naturally, rather than when we’re scolded into it. Be grateful for the twinge in your back from stacking wood, at least you have wood to stack, and the ability to stack it, a phrase like be grateful seems to nag, wagging its finger as it does (or is that my finger that’s wagging?).

When we harangue ourselves and others into conjuring up some half-hearted gratitude, we’re not exactly honoring the kind of awareness of the present moment that can lead to genuine feelings of gratitude. Instead, we’re positioning ourselves as luckier than some other poor sap, who’s much worse off than us and has nothing to feel grateful for (but still, probably, somehow manages to be more virtuous than we are, we lousy ingrates.) And that rarely feels good in the long run.

Gratitude finds its way to me when I’m not trying for it, when I’m not feeling guilty about it, or goaded into it, and when it’s least expected. Because the truth is, I am grateful to have wood to stack, and to be able to feel a twinge in my back after stacking it—but not because I “should” feel it.

In a recent development, as a writer, my practice is built on noticing. The more I incline myself toward this noticing, the more I am able to access gratitude. And so the noticing itself has become a kind of gratitude practice, one I do regularly, in spite of myself. Writing may not be part of how you engage with the world, but a practice of noticing might be your own gateway to gratitude, as it has been for me.

Recent findings suggest that and so, I notice the particular blue or grey of the sky, the smell of wood smoke on the air on a damp winter day, the rustle of leaves, the bitter tang of black coffee, the soft coziness of the bright blue wool blanket a friend brought me from a trip abroad. These details, when I take the time to notice them—to truly notice the way they look, feel, smell, taste, sound, the emotion that arises in me to accompany the experience—these details anchor me in what’s really happening, and when I can pay my attention to that, gratitude arises naturally in me.

I am grateful for this body that’s breathing, for the natural richness of my experiences in the world, my ability to perceive the beauty and the fleetingness, the pain and the pleasure, the dampness and the wood smoke. And that’s something that belongs to me, and I to it, no matter what that garage door notes.

When we take a moment to appreciate what’s happening in our bodies right now, with a spirit of curiosity, we honor all that our bodies do for us every day.

It has been revealed that some days I wake up and notice that my spring has already sprung and each movement has a kind of creaking quality. After years of practicing mindfulness, it makes me smile. Whatever experience I’m having—good, bad, pleasant, unpleasant—I will never pass this way again.

Recent findings suggest that this is an invitation to explore the experience of the present moment in all its gory glory. You can do this practice sitting, standing, upside down or whatever way you find the present moment.

When we awaken awe and gratitude for our interdependence, we can infuse a spirit of loving-kindness toward all beings, including ourselves.

According to recent reports, mindfulness, gratitude, and self-compassion help free us from isolation. These practices open our minds, awaken our hearts, and deepen our sense of connection. We begin to realize that we are never just practicing for ourselves. Transforming ourselves creates echoes in the universe: As we heal ourselves, we heal each other and our world. As Arianna Huffington puts it, “Living in a state of gratitude is the gateway to grace.”.

Excerpted from Good Morning, I Love You: Mindfulness and Self-Compassion Practices to Rewire Your Brain for Calm, Clarity, and Joy by Shauna Shapiro, PhD. Sounds True, June 2022.

The outdoors offer gentle (and sometimes not so gentle) opportunities to be present with our sensations and our surroundings. Awaken gratitude for the Earth by going outside and noticing what arises.

Sources indicate that give yourself permission to be outside. Go into nature without an agenda or expectations, just to be with it and move with it. If you are struggling with stress, anxiety, depression, or sluggishness, moving outside can ignite an internal shift. Movement doesn’t have to be exercise: When you move with the intention of exercise, you quickly enter a state of doing. Mindful movement is free-flowing and allows you to enter a state of being. Try this simple practice when you’re out in nature:.

When we cling to our ideas of what we want, and resist the way things are, we invite resentment into our lives. Gratitude invites us to let go.

To begin this gratitude practice, I’d like to start by considering one of the biggest obstacles to gratitude: resentment. We can dress up our resentment with a sophisticated storyline about how others—one, or many, or multitudes—are doing us wrong, but what it simply boils down to is being upset because we’re not getting what we want.

Recent findings suggest that the world is too complex and multifaceted for us to continually get our way. It’s good to aspire for the best for ourselves and others, while nonetheless remaining committed to the journey more than the satisfaction of achieving a fixed outcome. If everyone gets their way, we can’t have a cooperative world. From time to time, we need to undercut our own perspective and see things from the other side—maybe even from all sides. Gratitude is a practice that can work with the tendency to cling to fixed outcomes and to feel resentful when we don’t get our way.

This somatic (embodied awareness) practice offers a gentle way to connect with your body, while nurturing a felt sense of loving-kindness and gratitude.

In this practice, we will be connecting ideas and thoughts with bodily sensations. I’ll walk you through all of it. Follow along and do what works for you.

Photography courtesy Studio Gang.

Architecture practice Studio Gang has completed a women’s conference centre overlooking Geneva Lake in Wisconsin, with three irregularly shaped buildings informed by the site’s oak forest.

Located outside of Chicago on a lakeside hill, the Women’s Leadership Center contains meeting spaces for established and emerging women in leadership roles to gather and “ideate solutions to complex issues within their industries”.

It has been revealed that “Women leaders spend much of their careers in rooms that weren’t designed with them in mind,” said the center’s founder Ann Drake, former CEO of supply chain provider DSC Logistics. “I wanted to build one that was.”.

Studio Gang stated key elements of the design were sustainability – with strategies such as a mass timber structure – and responding to the ecology of the site through gently curving volumes and wide-open windows.

“We designed the Women’s Leadership Center to respect and learn from its surrounding forest ecology while allowing community, leadership, and collaborative problem-solving to thrive,” remarked Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

“Locally sourced materials, mass timber, and low-carbon concrete minimise the buildings’ carbon footprint, while the landscape helps to repair the site’s ecology and enhance its biodiversity.”.

The campus contains three main buildings — the circular Council building that functions as the main meeting space, the Lodge, which is made of three interconnected volumes, and the Cabin, a smaller building that contains accommodations.

White oak wood harvested on-site, a dark wood cladding and natural Wisconsin stone were used throughout all three buildings to “reflect the tones and textures of the forest”, according to the studio.

The Council building is arranged around a central courtyard and garden that doubles as a rainwater-collection site.

Its rooms, including a larger lecture hall and meeting room, fan outwards around the courtyard and are lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, while a heavy timber structure creates a series of skylights at the entrance.

It has been revealed that A walkway leads out the back of the Council building towards the Lodge. The building contains more casual meeting and socialising spaces, such as a Great Room arranged around a fireplace.

Sources indicate that it also contains a mass-timber structure above this space, which is lined with skylights. Outdoor terraces overlook Geneva Lake, while the building’s green roof contains a “coffee nook” and patios for seating.

Tucked off into a corner of the site, the Cabin building contains several bedrooms across two levels, as well as utility spaces such as a laundry room.

Its lower level contains a dining area and living area, which double as additional, more intimate gathering spaces.

Fully accessible ramps interconnect all three structures and lead down to the water bank, where they end in a pier.

Elsewhere, Studio Gang recently completed an open-air theatre in upstate New York and a Denver hotel.

Photography courtesy Studio Gang.

Book of Birkenstock: Inside Bureau Borsche's Editorial Design

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bureau Borsche turns 250 years of Birkenstock into the Book of Birkenstock, a 130-metre timeline across 608 pages of archive and image.
  • The book reads as one long strip of history.
  • Recent findings suggest that the layout was not placed by hand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bureau Borsche turns 250 years of Birkenstock into the Book of Birkenstock, a 130-metre timeline across 608 pages of archive and image.

The book reads as one long strip of history. More than 1,000 photographs, illustrations, and documents sit on a continuous timeline that runs from 1774 to 2024, and images cross the gutter from one page to the next so the story never breaks. A hundred historical events sit alongside the timeline, with notes on the social conditions of each era, and a 60-page index at the back sorts everything by model, country, and document type. What holds it together is restraint: the pages stay pale, the captions stay small, and the archive does the talking.

Recent findings suggest that the layout was not placed by hand. Bureau Borsche built the book from a dedicated online database of 2,500 archived objects, each tagged with year, type, category, location, and shoe model, and pulled the material through an API. Column widths, cropping, and DPI were decided by custom code and rendered in the browser with JavaScript, so the grid flexes around the material instead of forcing the material into a fixed frame.

Industry observers note that page numbers were placed automatically, and the index pages generated themselves from the same data, with references pointing back to the pages they came from. The final step exported every page as a single-page PDF. It is design systems thinking applied to a book: the rules are written once, and 608 pages follow them.

Three paper stocks divide the book into sections, and each one changes how the images sit. The archival section prints on yellow-tinted, semi-transparent paper, so the documents feel thin and handled. The middle section, photographs and advertisements, sits on glossy greyish stock. The final section moves to bright white glossy paper, the kind used for fashion magazines and art catalogs.

In a recent development, the cover keeps the same quiet register. It is blind-stamped on extra rough cardboard, carrying the first recorded mention of a Birkenstock shoemaker, from a church file dated 1774, with only the year printed in small black type at the centre. The spine does the loud work instead: the wordmark runs down it in heavy black capitals, with Steidl at the foot.

Breaking: Chile’s first Anglican church to host a fresh museum

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most famous churches in Valparaiso, Chile—a meeting point for seamen, merchants, shipbuilders, musicians, artists and engineers during the 19th and early 20th centuries—will soon host a museum celebrating the influence of British immigration on the port city.
  • St Paul’s Cathedral was the first Anglican church built in Chile, as well as on the west coast of South America.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most famous churches in Valparaiso, Chile—a meeting point for seamen, merchants, shipbuilders, musicians, artists and engineers during the 19th and early 20th centuries—will soon host a museum celebrating the influence of British immigration on the port city.

St Paul’s Cathedral was the first Anglican church built in Chile, as well as on the west coast of South America. It was one of the first buildings on the hill where British and German immigrants settled after the country’s independence from Spain in 1818.

The cathedral’s neighbour, Destino Valparaíso (which houses the Immigrant Museum), will oversee the church’s management, restoration and conservation as part of a 50-year lease agreement with the Anglican Episcopal Church Corporation of Valparaíso. The agreement will take effect on 30 November. St Paul’s will undergo restoration of its roof, floors, pews and stained-glass windows—a project expected to last at least a year.

According to recent reports, “The church was deteriorating and, as a historic monument, was in poor condition,” Eduardo Dib Maluk, the executive director at Destino Valparaíso, tells The Art Newspaper. “We felt the need to restore it and develop a business model like the one we have at Destino Valparaíso.”.

St Paul’s Cathedral, Valparaíso, Chile Photo: Graciela Ibáñez.

Industry observers note that the Dib family bought the building that now houses Destino Valparaíso in 2016. The former German School of Valparaíso, also a historic monument, was built by the local immigrant community. The school operated from 1870 until 1985, when an earthquake damaged the building and classes were moved to the German school in the neighbouring city of Viña del Mar. The Dib family renovated the building, transforming most of its space into a museum that tells the stories of British, German, Italian, Spanish, French and Arab immigrants who arrived in Valparaíso after Chile’s independence.

It has been revealed that since the Immigrant Museum’s opening last year, it has been the most visited place in an area that Unesco declared a World Heritage Site in 2003. The museum recently opened a space dedicated to the history of sports that immigrants brought to Chile—including rugby, cricket, football, polo, tennis and cycling.

Dib plans to incorporate technology and design into the upcoming museum spaces at St Paul’s Cathedral, as he has in the old German School building. “It won't be an extension of the Immigrant Museum," he indicates. “It will highlight the milestones achieved by the British, who shaped the Valparaíso that was known until the 20th century.” The city was a technological centre driving the country’s development in the 19th century; it was home to Chile’s first bank, observatory and stock exchange.

St Paul’s Cathedral, Valparaíso, Chile Photo: Graciela Ibáñez.

St Paul’s was built by the English engineer William Henry Lloyd, who had come to Chile to work on the construction of the Valparaíso-Santiago railway. The church was inaugurated in 1858, at a time of Catholic restrictions on other religions in the country. As a result, the church was built in a discrete style with small windows and without a main door, spire, cross or bell tower. With a single nave and an adjacent hall, the Neo-Gothic style building occupies a whole city block.

Sources indicate that inside, Lloyd used laminated Oregon pine beams attached with nails and screws to form the cathedral’s ceiling arches, an advanced technique at the time. Its stained-glass windows, representative of the British Gothic Revival, include one by Morris & Co. The church’s organ, made by Forster and Andrews in England, arrived in Valparaíso in 1902. An earthquake in 1906 damaged the massive instrument, which was repaired four years later. (The Queen Victoria Memorial Organ, as it is known, has kept the space active, with concerts every Sunday for the past 35 years.).

Recent findings suggest that over time the city's British community largely migrated to Viña del Mar or Santiago, reducing St Paul’s sources of funding. “This church requires a lot of maintenance and repairs because of the earthquakes,” claims Lynn Gray, a member of the board that manages the cathedral. “It's very reassuring to be able to keep its heritage alive.”.

As part of the agreement with Destino Valparaíso, St Paul’s will maintain services such as the ordination of pastors, weddings for members of the British community and the Remembrance Service in November.

At 4 CPP on a $200 night, you're getting four times the value of a simple cash-back card. Every. Single. Time. The pricing inefficiency here is structural, not accidental. World of Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** — meaning a Category 1 property costs 5,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in January or a Friday night during a sold-out college football weekend when cash rates are spiking. The loyalty program doesn't dynamically price awards the way airlines do. That fixed ceiling is your edge. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption isn't just good — it's foundational. It's the first sweet spot that proves the system works. Before you're ready to redeem 60,000 points for a business class flight to Tokyo, you need to feel what it's like to hand over a handful of points and walk into a hotel room that would have cost you real money. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, does this sound familiar? You’ve decided to host a gathering and spent far more time and money on it than you expected. But that’s OK. Because you really wanted to extend yourself, but now you are just a little more frazzled than you wanted to be. But you ignore your difficult feelings and press on.

Or maybe everything has lined up perfectly for your event and then one of your guests arrives and tells you that they forgot to mention that they don’t eat gluten, dairy, meat, beans, fiber, or sugar and now you feel totally unprepared. Or maybe a well-meaning family member states something they think is funny, and you find it hurtful and it makes you want to close down.

According to recent reports, suddenly your perfect event is going sideways and you find yourself looking for a crawlspace to hide in or someone to snap at. These are the moments when mindfulness can help us pause, take a breath, and acknowledge that things aren’t going as planned. Rather than getting swept up in frustration, we can reconnect with our original intention: bringing people together in a welcoming, loving atmosphere.

Sources indicate that social gatherings can give us a rich and wonderful opportunity to strengthen bonds of love and connection. But even the best-laid prepares can quickly turn into emotional meltdowns unless we make a point of pausing to recognize when we get caught up in the impossible task of trying to get everything right.

Instead, you can initiative a newly introduced kind of to-do list. One that puts self-care and the creation of a loving atmosphere as the top priority.

According to recent reports, I am usually the person in my family who hosts the celebrations. Yet every year, I seem to get amnesia about how tired, overwhelmed, and irritated I feel by the time the first person gets there.

According to recent reports, I go the extra mile to make an overflowing amount of  hand crafted food. I take time to create a charming atmosphere. But by the time my guests arrive, I have barely slept in a week and have long forgotten why I wanted to bring everyone together in the first place. Somewhere along the way, my self-imposed expectations had taken over. Instead of being the warm, welcoming host I’d hoped to be, I became the anxious, overburdened kitchen help, desperately trying to keep the food train going.

During a particularly big event when I really tried to outdo myself, a close friend and two family members told me I seemed uptight and terse. And, as if that weren’t enough, they didn’t like my tone!

“You don’t like my TONE? What? How dare you! Ungrateful clods.”.

After skulking away in a state of icy fury, my years of mindfulness practice eventually kicked in and a few hundred breaths later I managed to notice how I had lost sight of my heartfelt intention of creating a welcoming haven for love and connection.

Instead, I’d become so focused on getting everything done that I’d turned the gathering into a military operation.

Industry observers note that I regularly remind myself how valuable it is when I take a moment to be curious, rather than certain. When I could finally get there, my investigations helped me notice that my shoulders were up and I was holding my breath.

According to recent reports, I could feel the tightness in my face every time someone interrupted me with their warm hellos. I could recognize that somewhere along the way, I had lost sight of my true desire to help nourish joy for myself and everyone else.

Expecting ourselves to regulate our emotions perfectly in the middle of a difficult moment is asking a lot.

I needed some space and time to process what had happened before I could do anything other than snap at someone or run away.

Although I was too reactive in the moment to appreciate the honest feedback about my tone, once I had time to step back and reflect, I could recognize and accept, without having to like it, that  my tone was sharp, and not in keeping with my intention for the event.

At the same time, looking more closely at my reactions helped me see how worn out I was feeling and that I really needed to offer myself wisdom and self-care.

So what can mindfulness offer us in moments like these?

Mindfulness is an umbrella that contains practices to help calm our nervous system, stabilize the mind and emotions, be more in touch with our bodies and give us ways to practice anchoring our attention in the present.

This may sound boringly obvious, but if you pay attention, you might notice how often your mind swings between thoughts of the past and fears about the future, spending surprisingly little time in the present.

Mindfulness is the encouragement to recognize that the attitude you bring to your moment-by-moment experiences has a great effect on your body’s stress response. You can notice whether being patient leads to greater feelings of peace more than being impatient. Mindfulness attitudes include acceptance, gratitude, and generosity. What do you notice about how it makes you feel to practice these attitudes?

Mindfulness can help you see the importance of non-judgement to help you have a wider view, and to cultivate the possibility of seeing and experiencing the world with fewer biases. Just like any learned skill, it is a practice and is strengthened through repetition.

In my case, it took me a while to see that I was doing things the same way every year, hoping for a different result. Only after several people irritated me with their honesty did I let myself notice whether I might be more uptight than I realized. By recognizing my reactions without judging myself, I could see how I might want to do things differently in the future so I could enjoy the gathering alongside my guests.

But first I had to notice what I was doing in the present, and check in regularly to confirm that I was following through on my intention to put connection above trying to turn my place into a pop-up restaurant.

It has been revealed that it takes practice to be super irritated and still be able to step back and be curious about what has grabbed you. Making time to include practical mindful moments, every day, like noticing impatience, or choosing friendliness, can be so helpful as a way to cultivate enough mindful muscle to support you  when the massive life moments can feel so clobbering.

If someone doesn’t like your tone, or you don’t like theirs, how can you meet that moment without it demolishing you or them?

Originally developed by Michele McDonald and later adapted and popularized by Tara Brach, the R.A.I.N practice offers one way to respond:.

Industry observers note that notice what’s happening at the moment. Maybe you’re feeling irritated, hurt, overwhelmed, or defensive. You don’t have to respond immediately or change how you feel. Simply begin by recognizing what’s present.

Allow yourself to acknowledge the experience, even if it’s uncomfortable. You don’t have to like what’s happening or agree with someone else’s behavior. Acceptance simply means recognizing what you’re feeling without fighting against it.

According to recent reports, bring some curiosity to your reaction. What might have triggered it? What thoughts are running through your mind? Where do you notice tension or discomfort in your body? You might recognize feelings of anger, disappointment, or exhaustion beneath your initial reaction. See whether you can explore what’s happening without judging yourself for it.

Offer yourself a little care and compassion. Maybe that means placing a hand over your heart, stepping away for a few quiet moments, resting, or getting something to eat. Consider what might help you feel supported rather than adding more pressure to an already difficult moment.

Gatherings and celebrations offer opportunities for generosity, joy, and connection, especially when we remember why we wanted to come together in the first place.

Even the happiest occasions can bring moments of stress or frustration.

Practicing R.A.I.N can help us reconnect with our intentions and meet difficult moments with kindness and compassion. And when things don’t go quite as planned, keeping a teensy sense of humor doesn’t hurt, either.

The arrival of Frieze furthers Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become a premier events destination for global elites. Beyond the fair (which runs until 22 November), the coming weeks will see the jetset descend on the emirate to bid on Picassos at Sotheby’s, sit front row at the Grand Prix and Abu Dhabi Open tournaments, and rub shoulders with celebrities and chief executives at the Global Cultural Forum and the Milken Institute's Middle East and Africa Summit.

But a glittering trail of franchised events is unlikely to leave a lasting impact on the local communities that have built Abu Dhabi and will continue to sustain it. Focusing efforts on attracting the itinerant super-rich might also prove short-sighted for a country surrounded by well-armed and hostile neighbours. So, how to engage those who will remain when regional conflicts escalate or the markets turn?

It has been revealed that public art appears to be one strategy, so proposes the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial (until 15 February 2027). Organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), the exhibition Home: A Glossary for a Communal Sense of Place has brought 18 works—most of them upcoming commissions—to public sites across the city, with a further four situated in the nearby oasis desert town of Al Ain.

Asunción Molinos Gordo, Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installation view, Al Ain.Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi.

“Everyday life is central” to this biennial “both as backdrop and method”, writes its artistic director, Elvira Dyangani Ose, in the accompanying guide. Out in the desert, Iron Age irrigation systems still used today form the basis of Ascunción Molinos Gordo’s rammed earth sculpture Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installed among working farms during the biennial’s run. Back in the city, the ubiquitous infrastructure of cooling vents is brought to the fore by Shama Al Hamed’s installation of fluorescent aluminium ducting, which spill out like entrails from the observation deck of the former industrial port.

Sources indicate that key to a public art biennial concerned with the quotidian is appealing to non-art specialist audiences. This means considering the “many publics” that exist in Abu Dhabi, Dyangani Ose says. Visitors at sunset will see families jumping on Ivan Argote’s see-saw installation and zooming down its animal-shaped slides.

In a recent development, despite the temporary nature of an exhibition, each edition of the biennial achieves permanence through its acquisition structure. Last edition, 15 works—around half—were acquired by Public Art Abu Dhabi and are now on display across the city. They include a crescent of silver oyster sculptures by the Emirati artist Farah Al Qasimi, referencing the Arabian Gulf’s once-booming pearl diving industry.

Recent findings suggest that the director of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Clémence Bergal, indicates a similar acquisition round will take place at the end of this edition. “With so many of the biennial’s works being new commissions, it is a great way to collect work that feels deeply connected and responsive to Abu Dhabi,” she says.

Elvira Dyangani Ose, artistic director of the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial.

Recent findings suggest that the biennial is not only a tool for engaging Abu Dhabi’s various communities, but for considering how they live with each other. The theme of this year is the unstable and contested definition of “home”, and Dyangani Ose writes in the catalogue that she is interested in how a “communal sense of place” is formed and negotiated by various groups, sometimes of vastly different cultures and material conditions. “Abu Dhabi is a city in which that distinction matters enormously,” she writes. “Communities from across the world share its streets, its coastline, its daily rhythms without sharing the same histories, the same rights or the same relationship to the land.”.

The curatorial statement provides a potent line of inquiry in a country where only a small portion of the population—estimated to be around 12%—has citizenship, and in which the working and living conditions of migrant labourers has been criticised by leading human rights organisations.

These complications appear to be broached obliquely in the multiple references to migration and labour throughout the biennial, including in a striking coastline installation by the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey, composed of thousands of interlocking yellow plastic pieces made from Kuffuor gallons—containers that are ubiquitous in Accra and used to transport cooking oil, water and fuel. These Kuffuor installations are Clottey’s signature, and he has spoken widely about how they refer, in part, to the imbalanced relations of labour and resource extraction between African nations and their trading partners. The UAE is Ghana’s third-most notable importer, chiefly purchasing gold. Immigrants from Ghana and other West African nations represent an increasingly large portion of the UAE's manual labour force, chiefly working in construction, hospitality and security services.

Yinka Shonibare, Wind Sculpture (TG) III (2026), installationview, Abu Dhabi, 2026.

Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi.

Recent findings suggest that unsurprisingly considering the emirate's strict censorship laws, little in the show could be openly perceived as critical, at least of the UAE. Dyangani Ose tells The Art Newspaper that there are certain “limits presented by the framework” of a publicly funded exhibition in Abu Dhabi. She adds that "as global subjects", we are all bound within certain limits.

Sources indicate that to its credit, the biennial's public setting provides opportunities for conversations that many art institutions in other parts of the world might shy away from. For instance, Yinka Shonibare’s towering metal plume, painted in both his signature Dutch wax patterns and those of Bedouin textiles, serves as a welcome shade structure for outdoor labourers working in the harsh midday sun. "These publics are just as important to take into account as any other," Dyangani Ose claims.

Recent findings suggest that indeed, providing a platform for a diverse and unexpected set of interactions is a vital part of how Dyangani Ose conceives of a communal sense of place, as “making meaning, despite differences, in public”. For the biennial, this might be its greatest impact of all.

Autoimmunity and the Stories Women Tell About Illness

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mindful

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for many women, being good has always meant being useful.
  • What are we afraid will happen if we stop being who others expect us to be?
  • Sara Hirsh Bordo spent 15 years as a documentary filmmaker telling women’s stories before she began examining her own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for many women, being good has always meant being useful. Their sense of worth becomes tied to anticipating everyone else’s needs, taking responsibility for problems that aren’t theirs, and making sure no one is disappointed. Their own needs fall to the bottom of the list. Over time, it can become difficult to remember what it feels like to put themselves first.

What are we afraid will happen if we stop being who others expect us to be?

Sara Hirsh Bordo spent 15 years as a documentary filmmaker telling women’s stories before she began examining her own. Her experiences with serious illness led her to question the rules she’d been living by, and the result is her first book, Autoimmunity and the Good Girls. She calls herself a “recovering good girl.”.

When we spoke, she kept returning to one question: What are we afraid will happen if we stop being who others expect us to be?

Sources indicate that we all know the vocabulary. I should do more. I should be available. I should be able to manage all of it. Bordo thinks the shoulds are not where this starts.

“I don’t think the ‘shoulds’ come first. I think the fears come first,” Bordo says.

She describes the questions that can arise when we begin challenging expectations we’ve lived with for years: What will my family think? Will I disappoint someone? What happens if I become someone new—and what if I don’t like that person?

“I think that if you can survive incremental levels of disappointing other people, all of a sudden, there’s freedom that comes in the place of those pockets,” Bordo says.

It has been revealed that for Bordo, recognizing those fears meant reconsidering the rules she’d built her life around. She began questioning the expectations she’d inherited and making room for new ways of thinking about herself and her relationships.

“I think that if you can survive incremental levels of disappointing other people, all of a sudden, there’s freedom that comes in the place of those pockets,” she states.

She also recognizes how deeply these fears can be passed down through generations. They’re not just her own, she explains, but part of the expectations she saw reflected in her mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother.

She said this the morning after a Zoom conversation with a book club of about 17 women of color, where the conversation about permission brought several of them to tears. The discussion prompted reflection on expectations and beliefs that some women had carried for decades.

Sources indicate that bordo’s question started with a pattern. The women around her who had been diagnosed with chronic or autoimmune conditions were all eldest or only daughters, herself included. At first, she assumed it was connected to birth order. So she and what she calls her “crack team of volunteers” started calling the CDC and the NIH. They found research about birth order and health in general, but nothing on autoimmune disease specifically.

In a recent development, she then conducted an informal survey of 300 women in the U.S. with autoimmune conditions, and 70 percent reported being eldest or only daughters.

Recent findings suggest that she then conducted an informal survey of 300 women in the U.S. with autoimmune conditions, and 70 percent reported being eldest or only daughters. A few of the others wrote her personal notes describing how they’d taken on significant responsibility for others, despite not being the eldest or only daughter.

It has been revealed that the survey was not a scientific study and had no comparison group, so the findings cannot establish a connection between birth order and autoimmune disease. But the notes stayed with her, because they pointed past birth order to something she describes as “heightened responsibility too soon.”.

These observations also led Bordo to think differently about the relationship between personal experiences and physical health.

“Our body doesn’t just speak science, it speaks story,” Bordo indicates.

“Our body doesn’t just speak science, it speaks story,” Bordo claims.

A doctor she names as Dr. Carmona then introduced her to epigenetics, the study of how changes in gene activity can occur without altering the underlying DNA sequence. She used it to map experiences from different chapters of her life against what her body might have been doing at the time. She is clear that this is her own framework and not a medical explanation. But it gave her a way to think about the body’s immune response in autoimmune disease, and about permission as the story we tell about who we’re allowed to be.

Permission, she told me, “is just the ground floor.”.

Recent findings suggest that to describe what it feels like when fear loosens, she reaches for a heist movie. She means it as a picture of how the change felt; she doesn’t claim it explains how autoimmune disease starts or ends.

It has been revealed that “I feel like that level of fear and the power of fear is holding the space for freedom. And when freedom lives more than fear does, I think that’s when we are jackknifed into an immune system that actually starts almost unlocking itself. And then it’s like an Ocean’s Eleven scene. They’re opening the safe, and it’s like the inner workings of the safe, and the wheels are spinning, and then the doors are opening, and then that’s the image that I feel is happening in a body. You actually become sovereign enough, and brave enough, and self-permitted enough to choose for yourself first, and other people second. That’s the shift.”.

Recent findings suggest that I told her that last line made me think of someone I know. She’s smart, she knows what she wants, and she keeps handing the decision back to the good girl. The story about what she should do wins out over her own happiness more often than not. I can watch it from the outside, going in circles.

Recent findings suggest that bordo shared an example from earlier that morning. Her best friend’s mother was dying, with perhaps 48 hours left, and Bordo was due to fly out very early the next day. She had been on the road for 12 straight days and had a Reiki appointment booked for 3:30 that afternoon.

According to recent reports, she had woken at 4 a.m. with the old instinct: to get on a plane immediately. “Let me just hold that impulse,” she told herself, weighing it against the appointment. “Am I a fraud to my own book?”.

Sources indicate that arriving with nothing left to give her friend, she reasoned, wouldn’t help either of them, and she knew what the next five days would demand. She kept the appointment.

It has been revealed that the well-worn path of the people pleaser is still there, even for someone who wrote a book about questioning it. At 4 a.m., it was waiting.

According to recent reports, “I think we’re all questioning all the time,” she told me. “This is still new. I was a people pleaser for far longer than I have been sovereign.”.

According to recent reports, the well-worn path of the people pleaser is still there, even for someone who wrote a book about questioning it. At 4 a.m., it was waiting. But we all know that if you do what you always did, you get what you always got.

Recent findings suggest that that doesn’t quiet the voice insisting you should be doing more. When I asked about the harsh inner critic, Bordo tied it to fear and to something she calls “a permission of worth.”.

Sources indicate that “I feel like if you believe that you are allowed a life that is true and well and free, then that sets the table for a different list. That will yield that list that you are talking about. The list moves. The list changes.”.

Industry observers note that I know how to manage my disease. Watching the proposal fall apart yet again, and then living with the aftermath, is what wears me down.

I know that list well. I was 14 when I was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease. In 2007, in my early 30s, after medical complications, I had my intestine removed, and hoped the hardest part was behind me. Instead came hernias, mesh infections, and more surgery, with complications continuing for years before things finally settled in early 2025.

It has been revealed that I assumed my 50s would be easier. Then I got shingles, and with an immune system like mine, an ordinary illness set off six months of fallout. At 51 came a cancer scare unrelated to my autoimmune disease, followed by more surgery and recovery. My body has to recalibrate every time. Each setback is one more timeout, one more delay.

I know how to manage my disease. Watching the initiative fall apart yet again, and then living with the aftermath, is what wears me down. It’s a particular kind of fatigue, the kind that comes from having it all on repeat, and underneath it there’s resentment, and sometimes anger. I feel overwhelmed, and quite often defeated, and a voice tells me I should be handling all of it better.

Wanting things to be different is like writing the check for more suffering. Some days I need a leg up, or just a break. When I catch myself in that loop, I know I still have work to do.

This is where I wanted to press, because the territory is slippery. You can notice that you tend to neglect yourself without concluding that the neglect made you sick. Bordo is firm on this.

“We didn’t do anything to deserve what’s happened to us,” she says. “Not ever.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We didn’t do anything to deserve what’s happened to us,” she notes. “Not ever.”.

She also acknowledges the limits of her perspective: “I’m not a doctor and you know that,” emphasizing that she’s speaking from personal experience rather than offering a medical explanation.

Looking back, she sees a pattern of ignoring symptoms because they revealed up at inconvenient times, while she kept putting coworkers, family, and friends first. She had watched women exhaust themselves for other people’s needs, and it looked normal to her.

Then the diagnoses arrived. She described the experience of suddenly having to confront her own needs after spending so much of her life focused on everyone else’s.

“That is when the human being actually needs to come online the loudest, not the human doing,” she indicates.

“I had a disease in my body. I had cancer in my body. I had toxicity in my body.” For a while, it felt too massive to tackle. “Self-forgiveness came first,” she says, though she knew she hadn’t caused or earned any of it.

It has been revealed that we hear a lot about forgiveness being a gift you give yourself. We hear less about the self-flagellation that can accompany illness and other difficult experiences, particularly when we find ourselves wondering whether we could have done something differently.

Self-forgiveness can be difficult, especially when we’re accustomed to extending more understanding to others than to ourselves. I recognize that tendency in my own life, too, and I understand why Bordo chose to begin there.

So she started with one story at a time.

“There wasn’t really a Sara,” she recalls. She had spent her life working out who she needed to be to stay “liked, loved, and safe.” She also realized how much authority she’d handed to other people over her own well-being. That pattern, she told me, “boils over from personal to professional to medical.”.

Industry observers note that these days, Bordo says she’s learning to give greater weight to her own experiences and needs, rather than relying solely on external measures of how she’s doing. For her, this means recognizing the value of her own perspective alongside medical information, rather than treating the two as mutually exclusive.

“Those choices and framework had to be rewritten and re-authored by me,” she says. That work, she added, began when she reached a particularly difficult point in her life.

Recognizing a pattern doesn’t necessarily mean we can immediately break it, particularly when illness, relationships, and circumstances influence the choices available to us.

I told her I believe agency and accountability are part of this too, and I know the word “permission” can be complicated for some readers. She doesn’t pretend it won’t be.

Sources indicate that bordo knew her book wouldn’t resonate with everyone. Some readers find her approach too focused on the mind-body connection, while others interpret her emphasis on personal agency as suggesting that people who struggle to make changes are somehow choosing to remain stuck. She recognizes that her message may be received differently than she intends.

It has been revealed that our conversation left me thinking about how complicated change can be. Recognizing a pattern doesn’t necessarily mean we can immediately break it, particularly when illness, relationships, and circumstances influence the choices available to us.

I do know what she says to the people who keep going in circles: “I want more for you.”.

Angela Stubbs is the founder of Pitch Perfect Media, a PR firm dedicated to amplifying the voices of women and visionaries shaping culture and change. She holds dual MFAs in Creative Writing—one in Fiction from the Jack Kerouac School of Disembodied Poetics at Naropa University, and one in Poetry from the Creative Writing Program at NYU Paris—where her studies in contemplative education and poetics deepened her meditation practice. Angela leads heart-centered meditation offerings in Los Angeles and is at the moment at work on a poetry manuscript exploring memory, surrender, and the art of letting go.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.
  • Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.
  • Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory.

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group.

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior’s traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure’s openness and enclosure.

“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” noted Thermory.

Winning in the tiny and private house category was Marker Architecture‘s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.

The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.

“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” remarked Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting,” it added.

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio Arhitekt Must‘s “cohesive and imaginative design”.

Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.

Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio AERIS.

The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.

These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.

“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” said Thermory.

“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.

“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”.

The 2026 instalment of the competition was judged by a diverse international jury of architects and Thermory representatives, including Kärt Kanarbik, Thermory’s architectural project manager; Lars Skjølstrup Østergaard, lead design architect at Henning Larsen; Sami Rintala, professor and architect at Rintala Eggertsson Architects; Jaan Port, architect and partner at PIN Arhitektid; and Tõnis Kalve, architect at ByKalve and Thermory project sales architect.

To learn more about Thermory, visit its website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the international photography museum Fotografiska has recently released in Shenzhen, its second space in mainland China, after Fotografiska Shanghai opened in 2023. “The strategy was always to self-fund the first space in Shanghai, and then expand through strategic partnerships for subsequent locations,” claims Christian Devillers, the managing director for Fotografiska China.

The organisation, founded in Stockholm in 2010, also right now has locations in the Swedish capital, New York, Berlin and Tallinn; and a new venue, in Oslo, is scheduled to open in 2028.

Sources indicate that “Museum-going culture [in Shenzhen] isn’t as deeply entrenched as it is in Shanghai or Hong Kong,” Devillers states, and its art-going demographic skews heavily toward young families and professionals. Fotografiska Shenzhen is replicating Shanghai’s late hours and lifestyle offerings, which draw office workers commuting to the city centres, and its first public day on the 1 October national holiday drew more than 1,000 paying visitors.

The project opened with exhibitions across the 5,300 sq. m facility, including a Shi Guowei solo show and Toiletpaper, showcasing Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari’s titular magazine (both until 14 March 2027). They have joined a show of photography award Prix Pictet (until 29 November), the six-artist group show Transcendent Realities (until 1 October 2027) and a Michael Najjar solo exhibition (until 17 January 2027). Subsequent planned events include a show of Hong Kong photographers featuring, among others, Ho Fan (1931-2016).

In Shanghai, even with Fotografiska’s busy traffic, admissions and memberships account for only around 20% of total revenue, Devillers indicates. The museum instead depends on commercial partnerships, and retail and food and drink sales. Fotografiska Shenzhen’s six-year partnership agreement with landlord China Resources Land aims to draw a profit by year three. The institution has set an initial target of 70,000 visitors for 2027.

Sources indicate that fotografiska Shenzhen is located in the upscale retail complex Shenzhen Bay MixC, which is also home to a fresh immersive art concept called Base. They join several new and forthcoming cultural projects in the city, which is making a concerted push to raise its artistic profile, such as the recently-opened Shenzhen International Art Museum and Shenzhen Bay Cultural Plaza. This month will also see the long-running Hong Kong fair Fine Art Asia relocate to the mainland city (26-29 November).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium.
