📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that more than 100 prominent figures across arts, politics and the media have published a joint letter criticising proposed job cuts at the Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG), Australia’s second oldest institution. The signatories include the former Tasmanian premier Lara Giddings and the 2014 Man Booker Prize winner Richard Flanagan, along with 44 leading-scientists representing universities in the UK, Europe, Canada, USA, Russia and Australia.

TMAG, founded in 1848, is the only institution in Australia that encompasses an art gallery, museum and herbarium. Its “science collections are really critical on a global scale for research around climate change and species extinction,” explains Ian Terry, the chair of Friends of TMAG and the museum’s former senior curator of cultural heritage (2006-2017).

Highlights of the TMAG collection include a rare taxidermied Thylacine, colonial-era art, objects and more than 12,000 Tasmanian Aboriginal cultural artefacts.

According to recent reports, staff at the TMAG were briefed in August that up to 19.7 full time equivalent (FTE) jobs, or roughly 30% of its workforce would be axed to rein in government spending. The government has disputed the claim that the scale of the required cuts has been confirmed; a spokesperson is quoted in ABC News as saying “TMAG is not required to reduce its workforce by 30%”.

However, since news of cuts were made public Tasmanian MPs, TMAG’s executive and its board have received more than 25 letters from prominent European scientists that have decried the government’s planned cuts, and warned its decision to axe the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium, Gintaras Kantvilas, an internationally renowned biologist, would have “consequences far beyond Tasmania”.

This week’s letter called for the Tasmanian government to recognise its “statutory obligation to care for approximately one million objects of inestimable value” and “reconsider the proposed job cuts with their unintended deleterious consequences on the Tasmanian economy.”.

Industry observers note that “I want TMAG properly funded. I want the life-changing childhood experiences I had at TMAG to be available to all Tasmanians forever,” David Walsh, the founder of Hobart’s Museum of Old and New Art (MONA), and one of the letter’s signatories, wrote in a separate letter that was published in Hobart’s Mercury newspaper this week. “I put stuff on Mona’s wall because TMAG put stuff in my heart,” he added.

Recent findings suggest that the proposed job losses are part of wide-ranging cost cutting initiatives being rolled out by the state Liberal government, as part of an attempt to rein in the state’s ballooning debt, which is projected to reach A$9.9bn (£5bn) by 2027-28. These initiatives include a plan to slash up 1700 public sector jobs by 2032.

Although the government disputes the scale of the proposed staff reductions, when a new organisational chart was shown to staff in late September it identified “seven positions that were definitely to be cut,” Terry says. Those positions included two positions at the herbarium, a biologist, a graphic designer, a photographer, the museum’s only exhibitions officer, as well as the amalgamation of the vertebrate and invertebrate zoologist into a single role.

Asked about the government’s dismissal of the claims about a higher number of staff losing their jobs, Terry explains that over the last 12 months the museum has already lost “quite a lot of staff” through natural attrition and redundancies. “I suspect some of those positions were included in the 19.7 figure,” he states.

TMAG and the Tasmania state premier’s department has been approached for comment by The Art Newspaper.

According to independent budget analysis provided by the Friends of TMAG, the proposed changes under the broader cost-cutting initiative would also see TMAG move under the control of a new government agency called Building Tasmania and lose up to 27% of its funding for 2027-28 while its targets for physical visitation increase by 6.4%. TMAG is already “seriously underfunded”, notes Terry. Its current exhibition Becoming Modern: Mid-century Australian Art has a 16-month run. “That's unheard of,” Terry continues, adding he thinks that “locals will be going less often because you're not going to go back many times to look at the same exhibition”.

It has been revealed that A state government spokesperson claims there is no correlation between the cost cutting measures and a new A$1.13bn (£573m) football stadium planned for Macquarie Point, a location that was once earmarked for a truth-and-reconciliation art park proposed by Dark Lab (a subsidiary of MONA). However, the independent MP Peter George asked in a statement issued on 25 September: “where’s the money [for that stadium] coming from?”.

Sources indicate that the proposed cuts to staff numbers are presently under review by the Tasmanian Industrial Commission and Tasmania’s Upper House is voting on calls to reverse cuts to TMAG’s budget. Decisions on both concerns are expected on Tuesday 24 November.

At the time of writing both Gintaras Kantvilas, the head of the Tasmanian Herbarium and Simon Grove, a zoologist and curator of invertebrates, have said they have had their positions reinstated after they had been under threat due to the proposed cuts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, AI-generated prototypes often don’t deliver consistently decent results because of tiny inconsistencies scattered all across a design system. I’s decisions made but not documented, hard-coded values never cleaned up, or relying too much on AI making sense of mock-ups or design flows on its own.

Recent findings suggest that yesterday I stumbled upon a useful practical guide by Hardik Pandya from Atlassian — on how to reduce drifts, minimize mistakes, maintain context, and improve the quality of AI-generated prototypes. Let’s see how it works.

Unsurprisingly, better AI prototypes come from better data — but also from better human guidance. We shouldn’t assume that AI knows how to choose the right component and how to design with accessibility in mind. It needs priorities, a clear path on how we make decisions, design principles, examples, do’s and don’ts.

Sources indicate that in fact, we should treat design decisions as infrastructure. That means that every time we make a decision — not just a design decision, but even a decision on how to actually prioritize our work and how we make decisions around here — it must find a path into the spec file that is then consumed by AI.

One of the useful tools to audit the quality of the design system is FigmaLint. It’s a useful free Figma plugin for auditing tokens, states, accessibility, binding tokens, renaming layers, detecting detached instances, missing interactive states and hard-coded values — and preparing the design documentation.

If you often have to work with vendors and third parties who supply you with their design systems and component libraries, that’s a great helper to have by your side — especially if you want to improve the quality of prototypes, AI-generated code, and AI-written documentation.

It has been revealed that to ensure quality, we establish design principles, guidelines, and rules in the form of “spec files”. It’s structured Markdown files that include spacing rules, color choices, component usage guidelines, priorities, etc. AI is going to read and reuse that spec file every time it’s going to generate a prototype.

Because the spec files are text files, it’s much more cost-effective but also much more accurate, just because we don’t rely on AI recognizing or decoding patterns from mock-ups but get specific guidelines instead. In fact, extending code is often a more effective way than generating code from mock-ups.

The token layer lists and keeps updated all tokens used throughout the design system. AI always chooses from a closed set of named variables instead of inventing plausible values ad hoc.

Industry observers note that an audit script catches what AI gets wrong. It scans the prototype and flags every hard-coded value and flags it if necessary. It can be a regular software doing that, with AI waiting for its feedback to come back.

Finally, when a design system ships updates, a sync routine flags which spec files need updating. The goal is to make sure that AI always reads up-to-date, current specs, not the ones written against an outdated version.

Industry observers note that ultimately, AI cannot magically resolve technical debt or design debt without proper guidance. It relies heavily on clear decisions, established priorities, and well-defined principles.

It has been revealed that the more deliberate and precise designers are in guiding AI, the better the overall outcomes will be. This requires not just cleaning up and improving design systems but also maintaining them over time as decisions need to trickle down into Markdown files. We’ll be busy for years to come.

Breaking: Porto Rocha Unveils the Kunsthalle Basel identity

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Porto Rocha rebuilt the Kunsthalle Basel identity around one stretchable KB monogram, a custom serif, and color that finally reveals up.
  • According to recent reports, kunsthalle Basel has spent 150 years showing artists before anyone else caught on, from Marcel Duchamp to Anne Imhof, with no permanent collection and a habit of betting on what comes next.
  • Type does the talking once the mark steps back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Porto Rocha rebuilt the Kunsthalle Basel identity around one stretchable KB monogram, a custom serif, and color that finally reveals up.

According to recent reports, kunsthalle Basel has spent 150 years showing artists before anyone else caught on, from Marcel Duchamp to Anne Imhof, with no permanent collection and a habit of betting on what comes next. Its old identity could not carry that energy. Director Mohamed Almusibli arrived in 2024 wanting the institution to act as a true host, warm and open to anyone curious enough to walk in, and Porto Rocha answered with what the studio calls an institutional brand with an anti-institutional spirit. Everything hangs on one mark. The K and B merge into a single gesture that reads as either letter, a confident stamp when it sits still and a shape that stretches, compresses and rotates when the context asks it to.

Type does the talking once the mark steps back. Porto Rocha worked with Swiss foundry Maxitype on KB Rhymes, a custom headline serif with roots in Times Upcoming Roman, humanist in feel and slightly condensed so it holds its own at large sizes without shouting over the art. Suisse International handles body copy and exhibition text, plain and highly legible. The specimen page sets artist names in KB Rhymes at poster scale, white on black, and the letters carry the same soft serifs and generous curves as the monogram. Behind the mark, a construction grid pins the K inside an oval, with guide lines marking the geometry that keeps the stretched and rotated versions honest.

In a recent development, the system earns its keep on the small things. A stack of cards carries the K at full bleed, black on white. A flat lay of programs, posters, a keyring and a lighter indicates the mark in a dozen colors at once, from a pink oval to a blue Werkstatt Sessions cover. The matchbox is the best of the bunch, a black box with a white K that slides open on purple-tipped matches.

Sources indicate that out on the street, the Opening Night poster frames a blue K oval on the stone facade, and a brushed metal plaque sets the orange mark under silver Kunsthalle Basel lettering. In the galleries, the identity steps aside and lets the work and the neoclassical rooms do the talking, which is the point. Two color modes run through it all, neutral beside artwork and loud in type-led layouts, where the old identity avoided color altogether.

See more from Porto Rocha on their website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cathay Pacific or Qantas Business Class via Alaska Mileage Plan — no fuel surcharges.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Château Léoville Barton in hand, watching the Australian coastline slowly materialize through your window. The cabin is hushed. The seat — Cathay Pacific's renowned Business Class throne on the Airbus A350-1000 — cocoons you in a private pod with a sliding door, direct aisle access, and a mattress pad that makes a five-star hotel bed feel like an afterthought. This is the LAX–HKG–SYD route in Cathay Pacific Business Class. And you booked it for 55,000 Alaska Mileage Strategy miles. Now consider what the person three rows up in economy paid in cash for their seat — and what the couple beside you in business paid for theirs. A Cathay Pacific Business Class ticket on this route typically retails between **$5,000 and $12,000**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin pricing on transpacific routes is notoriously aggressive, and Australia amplifies it further because of the sheer distance involved. At 55,000 miles for a one-way business class redemption, you're extracting somewhere between **9.1 and 21.8 cents per point (CPP)** — a range that makes most loyalty program strategists stop and stare. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5–2 CPP for most programs. You are obliterating that benchmark. At the high end of this range, 55,000 miles is doing the work of $12,000 in cash. That is what the FI mindset calls asymmetric value. This is also a premium *experience*, not just a premium number. According to recent reports, kate Kalcevich has over 20 years of experience turning accessibility into a driver of innovation and growth. As VP of Innovation at Fable, she oversees a … More about Kate ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In the summer of 2024, I became co-chair of a working group of expert researchers who came together to determine how best to perform accessibility testing with people with cognitive disabilities. This was work I did for Fable, where I am right now VP of Innovation.

Cognitive disability is an umbrella term for several disabilities that impact how people process information, and it usually affects memory, focus, and/or learning. It is the most prevalent disability in the U.S. (13.9% via CDC), and cognitive disability is increasing rapidly (Yale study).

We set four goals for ourselves to learn how to work with this audience:.

We created a screener to recruit people who self-identified as having challenges with memory, focus, and learning. We also reviewed published studies that involved cognitive testers to learn best practices for working with them.

It has been revealed that next, we tested these best practices with an initial group of 25 testers in a pilot study. We fine-tuned our approach iteratively and created a guide to running user interviews with cognitive testers and a survey that could quantify their experiences using digital products. Finally, we documented what we learned.

According to recent reports, after our pilot study with this newly introduced group of testers finished, I felt that they would uncover more usability insights than the general population (gen pop) user research participants I’d worked with in the past. I set out to validate this hunch.

I decided to run a joint study with Fable’s partners at the University of California, Irvine, in collaboration with Syed Fatiul Huq and with help from Fable researchers Pranav Pidathala, Ali Brown, and Michael Fagan to see if my hypothesis about finding more insights with cognitive testers proved true or not.

In a recent development, I generated three websites for the study using an AI prototyping tool. I wanted three different types of sites with different user goals and content so I could test a variety of tasks in the study.

We used a single screener with questions about memory, focus, and learning, and screened participants into two groups based on whether they self-identified as having cognitive challenges or not.

We ran 30 user interviews, 10 per website, with an even 5⁄5 split between cognitive and gen pop participants for each website. In each session, a participant completed all the tasks for one website during an online user interview facilitated by one of the researchers involved in the study.

All participants completed an Accessible Usability Scale (AUS) survey at the end of their session. This is a free, Creative Commons-licensed 10-question survey to evaluate the usability of websites and mobile apps.

Industry observers note that I reviewed all the study recordings and transcripts and made note of every time a participant raised a concern, question, difficulty, or asked a question about how something worked. I counted all of these as complications. I also noted where a participant missed something that was part of a task, even if they didn’t notice it themselves. I also noted every suggestion for improvement made by participants.

Examples of suggestions included:.

Problems and suggestions were counted once per participant, even if they mentioned the same thing twice, but there are, of course, repeat issues and suggestions across the different participants. It is expected in UX research with multiple participants that you’ll find similar issues with each participant, and that is a signal that an matter is a universal challenge.

Across the three websites tested:.

The results aligned with my instincts: participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Industry observers note that let’s dive deeper into the data for each website. Note that an AUS score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher numbers representing better usability than lower numbers.

Sources indicate that this site had the simplest design and content of all websites tested in the study and accordingly had the lowest overall complications and the highest median AUS scores. The data aligns with what you’d expect from an easy-to-use and simple website.

On this website, cognitive participants found 3.4 more issues and made 2.2 more suggestions on average. Their average score of the overall experience was 13.7 points lower than that of the gen pop participants.

This was the website with the most varied functionality and the most tasks to complete (4), so it’s not surprising that participants found the most problems.

Here, cognitive participants found 6 more problems and made 3.2 more suggestions on average. They also scored the overall experience 17.2 points lower than gen pop participants on average.

This website was intentionally designed to be complex, and task 3, finding the bridal package, was meant to be extremely difficult to complete.

On this last website, cognitive participants on average found 7 more issues and made 2.4 more suggestions. Their average score for the overall experience was 14.3 points higher than the gen pop participants.

Something interesting happened with the AUS scores for cognitive and gen pop participants in Tables 3 and 4. Cognitive participants scored Crown & Comb higher than Turning Pages, but gen pop scored the opposite — higher for Turning Pages and lower for Crown & Comb. If I had to guess why, I suspect finding more issues on Turning Pages impacted the cognitive participants’ perceptions of usability more than the gen pop participants’.

Sources indicate that the other major difference between the sites, outlined in Table 5 below, was that cognitive participants found many more issues with buttons and links on Turning Pages and more issues with icons and visual elements on Crown & Comb. This suggests to me that the interactions being challenging on Turning Pages were a more significant challenge than issues with visual elements.

When it comes to the more qualitative findings, I looked at trends in the types of issues found by both groups of participants.

It has been revealed that when I grouped complications by category, the following issues surfaced more often with cognitive participants: content, buttons and links (affordances and function), icons or visual elements, and media (video, animations). They nearly tied with gen pop participants on navigation issues (45 vs 46).

Let’s look at the commentary provided by one cognitive participant versus one gen pop participant in the Crown & Comb sessions. The cognitive participant gave an AUS score of 38, and the gen pop participant gave an AUS score of 27.5. I chose to compare these two participants because they both gave the lowest scores within their group.

Notice the differences in how they described the overall experience in the quotes below. The gen pop participant explained it was frustrating and not engaging. The cognitive participant felt drained and less able to focus. I interpreted the experience as having a more profound impact on the cognitive participant’s overall wellbeing.

In summary, across all 3 websites we tested, participants with cognitive accessibility needs identified 197 usability concerns, compared with 113 identified by gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants made 93 suggestions for improving the user experience, compared with 54 suggestions by gen pop participants.

When I compared concerns and suggestions across both groups of participants, it turned out that the cognitive participants found 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants surfaced more challenges related to content, buttons, icons, visual elements, and media than gen pop participants.

Industry observers note that in working with cognitive participants for the last few years, I’ve seen how they surface cognitive load issues consistently. These issues don’t just impact people with cognitive disabilities such as neurodivergence; they also impact:.

What would I have missed if I hadn’t included cognitive participants, and how might that have impacted the business outcomes for these websites?

On the Strong Snacks website, the cognitive participants surfaced:.

Sources indicate that these are improvements that would give all people more trust in the content while also making it easier to read and skim for key content. The research findings point towards design best practices, such as not having continuous animation and using layout to draw attention to different types of content that a senior designer might also point out.

In a recent development, without cognitive participants, we might have missed the more subtle but important concerns with confusing interactions, such as how the “Add to book bag” button worked. They were also confused about where reviews and recommendations came from. Both of these issues could decrease a user’s trust in the website.

All participants surfaced that the book-matching feature was hard to find, but the deeper problem the cognitive participants emphasized is that the site’s interactions don’t consistently behave in ways that they can predict and understand, decreasing their confidence.

It has been revealed that anyone who wants to buy a book could benefit from a clear understanding of how to add books to a cart and complete the checkout promptly and with no ambiguity. Compounded over hundreds or thousands of customers, a lack of clarity in a purchase flow will lead to lost revenue.

The Crown & Comb website in particular highlighted the benefits of having cognitive participants who raised:.

It has been revealed that these concerns likely also affect gen pop participants, but they are more likely to muddle through a task with incomplete information. However, that can lead to losing customers to a better experience if a competitor pops up. Loyalty is often tied to experiences, not just brands, and having a poor experience means your customer retention can be weaker.

The study showed that finding a bridal package was hard for everyone, but the cognitive group showed how that became an accessibility barrier. When you combine:.

You create a high enough cognitive load that some people will not be able to complete the task. In my opinion, this is where usability issues start to become accessibility barriers — when they increase cognitive load so much that it becomes overwhelming for some people.

The percentage of people aged 65 and older in America is projected to increase from 17% to 25%. By 2060, 1 in 4 Americans will be an older adult (U.S. Census). This is where everyone starts to experience cognitive decline. As the aging and cognitive population segment expands, companies will need to build for these more complex user needs.

Sources indicate that people with cognitive access needs are a natural starting point because they will find the types of usability complications that UX teams are used to. This could make cognitive an easier entry point for inclusive research. Getting insights from assistive technology users is still very important, but many teams don’t know how to start doing that.

Cognitive accessibility is a powerful on-ramp into broader accessibility research and testing. By focusing first on cognitive load, clarity, and predictability, we build research foundations that make future work on accessibility with screen readers, screen magnifiers, and alternative navigation customers more approachable.

In this small exploratory study, participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants. I’ve seen this type of impact in research conducted by Fable customers’ websites that aren’t AI-generated, too.

Sources indicate that cognitive inclusion in UX research is not optional, and it’s not just about accessibility. It’s how UX teams can make their research more efficient, create clearer content, simpler flows, and ship better products for everyone.

This study had a relatively small sample size, so the findings are more qualitative than quantitatively validated. Testing was also done on two different platforms. Cognitive participant sessions were run using Fable Engage, and gen pop sessions were run on UserFeel. Different platforms with unique participant panels can affect the quality of insights and comfort levels with user research participation.

Disclosure: I work for Fable and chose to use our platform because it was more affordable than paying for access to another research platform, allowing me to include more participants in the study at a lower cost.

Recent findings suggest that different researchers facilitated the user interviews, which can also affect findings, but all sessions used the same task structure and discussion guide template, and all were completed online. Even though the sessions were facilitated by different researchers, the issue and suggestion counts were all done by me to ensure consistency across all websites and participants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Daisuke Shima.

Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that “play with scale” to showcase a latest pigment, made from industrial waste by design studio Matter at hand, at Tokyo‘s SKAC gallery.

With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to “explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour”.

The exhibition was jointly created by the two studios to showcase the fresh pigment, developed by Matter at hand from local waste material, on the miniature buildings made by Assemble.

The blue hue was manufactured by Japanese company Nikken to be used in the Play Earth Park – a campsite designed by Assemble that is currently under development in rural Japan.

“The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them,” Matter at hand founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.

“In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC,” he continued.

“The materials react to form a new crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue.”.

To show it off, Assemble constructed three miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced. The houses were named The Hut, The Tower and The Bird.

“The form of the structures plays with the agricultural buildings within the dispersed settlement of rural Toyama; these buildings evolve over time, adapting to what’s needed, often evolving interesting geometries,” Assemble co-founder Maria Lisogorskaya told Dezeen.

“We tried to play with scale and make the buildings surreal, creating miniature versions of them for play.”.

Sources indicate that the buildings have deliberately simple yet evocative geometries that nod to the structures that inspired them. Among them is a barn-like building surrounded by hay bales.

Assemble’s aim was for visitors to be able to climb and explore the structures.

“We hope that the buildings are climbed on and inhabited; and this exhibition is the beginning of the structures’ life as a play space outside SKWAT,” Lisogorskaya remarked.

“The spirit of resourcefulness, fun, and reimagining of our environments is at the core of the project and we look forward to seeing how the structures are used in ways we didn’t expect.”.

The exhibition, which also showcases raw materials used to create the blue colour and products covered in it, is on show in Skwat Kameari Art Centre (SKAC’s) Park gallery in Kameari, Tokyo.

Assemble mentioned it chose to showcase it here as it feels the gallery has a similar spirit to its own UK bases.

“We think SKAC is an amazing interdisciplinary space, and its spirit resonates with how we have set up our studios and labs in London and Liverpool,” Lisogorskaya said.

“Bringing together design, material experimentation with other arts practices as a more satisfying and richer way of being in the city,” she continued.

SKAC recently opened two new gallery spaces, Material Matters (MM) and Space III, as part of a major extension.

The east Tokyo gallery has previously shown exhibitions including anime-informed chairs by Kwangho Lee and reading spaces by Herzog & de Meuron.

Recent findings suggest that building Blue is at SKAC, 3-26-4 Kameari, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo 125-0002, from 7 November 2026 to 28 February 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Industry News: 6 Things I Learned While Hosting ‘The Design Drop’ Podcast

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when we debuted The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear.
  • As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals.
  • Sources indicate that what I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when we debuted The Design Drop, the goal was simple: have the career conversations young designers actually want to hear. Not the polished success stories or the advice you’ve heard a hundred times, but the mistakes, detours, and unspoken rules that don’t come with a job description.

As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to support the next generation of creative professionals. So getting to sit down with designers, industry leaders, and a few unexpected voices to talk about what they’ve learned along the way? Pretty much my dream job.

Sources indicate that what I didn’t expect was how much I’d learn myself. About careers, confidence, taking risks, and, yes, microphone stands.

After six episodes, here are the biggest lessons I’m taking away from my first season hosting The Design Drop podcast.

When I talked to furniture designer Nicolai Czumaj-Bront, he shared how his career began at his kitchen table, after long days working as a consultant. No fancy studio or a perfectly mapped-out plan. Just an idea, enough confidence to try it, and a willingness to invest in himself.

Twenty years later, he’s a senior design studio manager at Haworth.

We spend so much time waiting until we feel qualified, prepared, or experienced enough to do something. But how are we supposed to get that experience if we never start? I’m trying to remind myself of this more often, especially when something feels outside my comfort zone.

Listen to Nicolai Czumaj-Bront’s full episode of The Design Drop, “In It, Not On It.”.

One of the most comforting discoveries of this experience? Even the people you look up to are still figuring things out.

In a recent development, in my conversation with designer and entrepreneur Dan Mazzarini, we talked about the pressure to please everyone, especially when you’re building your career. But trying to be everything to everyone can mean losing sight of what makes your perspective valuable.

According to recent reports, confidence doesn’t necessarily mean having all the answers. Sometimes it means trusting yourself enough to stop looking for everyone else’s approval. And if the people you admire are still working through that, maybe you can give yourself a little grace, too.

Listen to Dan Mazzarini’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Professional People Pleasers.”.

I’m a major believer that everything happens for a reason, although it took me a while to get there. After talking to interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, I’m even more convinced that unexpected detours deserve a little more credit.

Caroline Murphy, host of The Design Drop podcast, with interior designer and content creator Clare Sullivan, who joined the show to discuss her unexpected career path and the opportunities that come from embracing change.

It has been revealed that clare didn’t set out to become a design influencer. Her career evolved from residential design into building her own content platform, back when becoming a design influencer wasn’t exactly an established career path.

Sources indicate that it got me thinking: How many of the best things in life have gone exactly according to plan? I’m going to guess… not many. Sometimes the side quest becomes the main quest. And sometimes the opportunity you almost passed up changes everything.

Listen to Clare Sullivan’s full episode of The Design Drop, “The Accidental Influencer.”.

It has been revealed that this sounds contradictory, but stay with me. As we get older, life gets more complicated. Jobs, relationships, kids, pets, houses, bills—the list goes on. But we’re also gaining experience, perspective, and a better understanding of what matters.

In a recent development, kay Sargent, senior principal and the director of thought leadership in HOK’s Interiors group, helped me see this differently. There are different seasons of life and work. You don’t have to be everything, everywhere, all at once. What deserves your energy today might look completely different five years from now.

I’m taking that as permission to stop expecting every part of life to be perfectly balanced.

Listen to Kay Sargent’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Everything Is a Season.”.

My mom has a saying I’ve always loved: “Think of your 20s as data collection.” Every job, relationship, mistake, success, and questionable decision gives you information you didn’t have before. The point isn’t to get everything right. It’s to learn enough to make better decisions next time.

It has been revealed that my conversation with Jessica O. Matthews reinforced that idea. Jessica invented an energy-generating soccer ball at 19 and went on to build companies at the intersection of design, technology, and sustainability.

We talked about how much we can learn from experiences and perspectives outside our own industries. Not everything you learn has to fit neatly into your career path to be useful later. So, take the weird opportunity. Explore the random interest. Collect the data.

It has been revealed that listen to Jessica O. Matthews’s full episode of The Design Drop, “No One Likes a Nepo Baby.”.

Every guest on The Design Drop brought something different to the conversation: different backgrounds, perspectives, and definitions of success.

In my conversation with Kelly Cooper, a merchandising expert whose career has taken her through brands like Nike, Levi’s, and Universal Music Group, we talked about personal branding, advocating for yourself, and finding a version of success that actually works for you. That idea of defining success on your own terms really stuck with me.

We’re so busy comparing ourselves to other people that it’s easy to overlook what we’re uniquely good at. Sometimes it takes a mentor, colleague, or someone with a different perspective to help us recognize our strengths.

If you haven’t figured out your superpower yet, find people who will help you see it. And while you’re at it, be that person for someone else.

Listen to Kelly Cooper’s full episode of The Design Drop, “Do the Quiet Thing.”.

After six episodes of The Design Drop, I definitely don’t have all the answers—but I have more questions, fresh perspectives, and some pretty great advice to carry with me.

What surprised me most was how different everyone’s path looked, yet how much of the same challenges kept coming up. That’s what I hope this podcast can be: a place to talk about the stuff we’re all trying to figure out, with people who’ve been there (and often still are).

According to recent reports, thanks to our first six guests for being so open, and to everyone who’s listened along. Here’s to more conversations, unexpected lessons, and figuring things out as we go.

All six episodes of The Design Drop are available on SURROUND and wherever you listen to podcasts. This season of The Design Drop is presented by Haworth.

Caroline Murphy believes the future of design depends on how well the industry supports its next generation. As futureGen Engagement Lead at SANDOW Design Group, she develops community initiatives, programming, and recognition opportunities for Gen Z and early-career designers across brands including Interior Design, Metropolis, and LUXE Interiors + Design. A trained interior designer and graduate of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Murphy founded the Young Designers Collective in Nashville to help emerging designers learn, connect, and grow. Today, she's a speaker, connector, and self-described "Design Major Sister" dedicated to helping the emerging creatives find their place in the industry.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M.
  • Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers.
  • According to recent reports, in recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M. Pei’s city hall in 1978, he called it “a monument to the city’s pride, a symbol of a first-class city that’s reaching for greatness”. The seven-storey inverted pyramid slopes over a large plaza with site-specific sculptures like Henry Moore’s Vertebra in Three Pieces (1978, also known as The Dallas Piece) and Marta Pan’s Floating Sculpture (1973), which sits in a reflecting pool.

Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers. They have cited the prohibitive costs of renovating the building, which ballooned within a matter of months from $81m according to an initial estimate for a basic infrastructure upgrade to $1.4bn for massive upgrades over two decades.

According to recent reports, in recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor. He has called the building “obsolete”. Architecturally significant or not, moving the municipal headquarters “would make this location available for development, which I would also support. I believe that will be a very, very big part of the future of downtown and its revitalisation.” Spokespersons for the city did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s questions.

The current mayor is in alignment with the “Say Yes to Downtown” campaign group led by former mayor Mike Rawlings. With developers and other former leaders, the campaign argues that city hall must be demolished to create an entertainment district, including a upcoming arena for two of the city’s professional sports teams, the Dallas Mavericks basketball team and the Stars hockey team. When the teams announced prepares to move out of the city’s core, both considered relocating to the city hall site. They ultimately chose other locations.

Amid the uproar over the possible demolition of Pei’s modernist complex, few have questioned the fate of Pan’s and Moore’s sculptures. Both were gifted to the city and are part of the municipal public art collection. But the future of Moore’s, which has required previous renovation, in part with help from the artist’s London-based estate and foundation, is a particular concern. The large grouping of organic forms was meant to complement Pei’s rigidly angular structure. It was also a gift to the city from the philanthropist W.R. Hawn in memory of his wife Mildred Hawn, whose favourite sculptor was Moore. Both sculptures are part of the preservation blueprint for the building; representatives for Moore and Pan’s estates did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries.

Industry observers note that dallas City Hall The Lyda Hill Texas Collection of Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

The non-profit Save Dallas City Hall, an ideologically diverse grassroots coalition, has been among the loudest voices opposed to moving the facility. It is led by president Bruce Richardson, a musician, artist and former political candidate, and vice-president Zaida Basora, an architect and former city employee who oversaw maintenance of properties, including city hall, and at the moment serves as the executive director of the American Institute of Architects Dallas.

It has been revealed that basora and her colleagues have proposed a ten-year phased initiative that, even factoring in inflation, is estimated to cost between $70m and $100m, and would not require municipal staff to move. The cost of simply demolishing the building—to say nothing of the expense of building something in its place—has been estimated at $60m.

The Dallas city council gave Tolbert a deadline of 26 August to present relocation options for city hall, which she missed. Inflation has also increased the cost of relocating. The same month, Save Dallas City Hall sued the city, arguing that it was committing “demolition by neglect”.

“Dallas city hall has at least one failed generator, active parking garage leaks and is due for roof maintenance,” Richardson stated in a statement. “Instead of tackling these problems with millions in available funds, the city halted repairs, wasting money and time to explore a move.”.

It has been revealed that on 2 October, the Save Dallas City Hall coalition started an effort to gather signatures to create a ballot referendum on the fate of city hall, which would be put to residents for a vote in May 2027. In early November, the group unveiled it had gathered around 25,000 signatures—well over the minimum 20,000 signatures needed for a ballot referendum. If the group’s proposed amendment to the city charter passes next spring, the municipal government will be required to continue operating from Pei’s city hall.

During elections earlier this month, 56% of Dallas voters opposed a $443m bond package. That package had included funding to move emergency operations out of city hall, which, according to advocates of preserving Pei’s building, would have been a first step toward abandoning it.

For the local activist Stephanie Drenka, a co-founder of the Dallas Asian American Historical Society who has spoken at nearly every public hearing since she learned of the building’s significance, preserving city hall is essential to recognising Pei’s contribution to Asian American history.

“The stakes are beyond our city alone,” she notes. Less than 1% of historic markers in the US acknowledge the contributions of Asian Americans, according to the national non-profit Asian & Pacific Islander Americans in Historic Preservation.

In a recent development, “This also makes demolition of city hall an problem of further erasure of Asian Americans in history,” Drenka says. “It’s not just Pei’s legacy, but we’re defending ourselves. Everything in our community is embodied in this building.” She adds: “If we can’t save city hall then what threat can we stop?”.

The Impact Of Humanoid Robots On Humanity

📅 2026-06-12 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • For decades, science fiction has cushioned us with the idea that the “android revolution” was a distant fantasy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

For decades, science fiction has cushioned us with the idea that the “android revolution” was a distant fantasy. But the reality is unfolding rapidly. As the line between human and machine blurs, we are forced to confront an impending psychological, economic, and existential shift.

I recently felt very disturbed after watching a YouTube video showcasing a humanoid robot that looked and acted with uncanny realism. While a closer look revealed the video was actually a clever trick, the robot had been swapped for a human actor when the presenter’s back was turned. However, the illusion itself raised a real and unsettling question: Will future androids become so lifelike that we will struggle to tell them apart from our fellow humans? And if so, what does that mean for society? It forces us to ask just how close we are to that threshold, and whether we are ready for the day that science fiction becomes reality.

What happens when our world is populated by entities that mirror us perfectly, but possess none of our biological history?

We have officially moved past the era of humanoids as mere public relations stunts. In the past, robots like Honda’s ASIMO or early research prototypes were celebrated simply for being able to walk up a flight of stairs without falling over. Today, the technological convergence of advanced electromechanical engineering and artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered the trajectory of robotics.

The current state of the art is defined by an aggressive race toward commercial, physical deployment. Companies like Figure AI have moved from laboratory demonstrations to active factory floors. Their Figure 02 model completed a multi-month deployment at BMW’s Spartanburg plant, actively contributing to the production of over 30,000 vehicles by handling complex sheet metal components. Meanwhile, Tesla is testing its Optimus humanoids inside its own Gigafactories, preparing for mass industrial scale.

What truly separates today’s humanoid robots from older generations isn’t just how well they move but how they “think.” In the past, a robot needed millions of lines of strict, unchangeable code just to perform a single, simple task. Today, thanks to the explosion of advanced Artificial Intelligence, robots are powered by “brains” built on cutting-edge software like Figure AI’s Helix or NVIDIA’s GR00T. Instead of being meticulously programmed, these modern robots can simply watch a human fold laundry, load a dishwasher, or sort parts. They understand the context of what they are seeing, mimic the action, and figure out how to improve the task entirely on their own. That’s just crazy!

Yet, while their digital brains have leaped forward, their physical bodies are still catching up. Modern humanoids face a few major real-world hurdles. First, today’s batteries only allow them to operate for a few hours before needing a recharge. Second, while walking on two legs is easy on a flat factory floor, doing so in a chaotic household or a crowded public street remains incredibly difficult for a robot to navigate safely. Finally, they are still very expensive to build, though fierce competition in the tech industry is finally starting to drive those manufacturing costs down.

While robots are mostly working in factories today, experts predict that over the next 10 to 20 years, they will move into retail stores, hospitals, and eventually our own homes.

When this happens, we will cross a major boundary: the point where you won’t be able to tell a robot apart from a human just by looking at it or listening to it. This is what fuels my nightmares right now! To get there, scientists are working (PDF) on artificial skin made from advanced silicone composites that feel warm, are flexible, and mimic human touch sensitivity.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to see an extremely life-like robot, check out Realbotix’s Aria. Although she is not a perfect human replica, she certainly makes us wonder how far we have to go before humans will struggle to tell the difference.

They are also building tiny, silent micro-actuators and artificial muscle systems that attach to the robot’s skull structure, allowing it to make realistic facial expressions like happiness, confusion, or tiredness.

It has been revealed that in the future, the AI powering these robots will actually be trained to copy human flaws. They will breathe, blink randomly, use normal body language, and even sigh or pause when they speak. This is intentional, as it stops humans from feeling that creepy, uneasy sensation known as the “Uncanny Valley”.

Meet Sophia, a famous humanoid robot created by a company called Hanson Robotics. Based in Hong Kong, this team specialises in building realistic robots packed with artificial intelligence to help out with everything from healthcare and research to pure entertainment. I don’t know about you, but that smile feels creepy to me.

Industry observers note that while these current limitations make today’s humanoids feel like specialised industrial tools, the gap between a factory worker and a lifelike companion is closing faster than most people realise. We are rapidly approaching a massive tipping point where these machines will shift from rigid commercial hardware into smooth, everyday extensions of our lives. To understand how profoundly this will change our world, we have to look at what happens when these robots finally step out of the factory and cross the ultimate threshold into our private spaces.

In a recent development, they say that bringing lifelike humanoids into our daily lives could come with some massive benefits. The biggest one is that robots can take over what engineers call the “3D” jobs: Dull, Dirty, and Dangerous. Humanoids can step into risky situations — like mining deep underground, handling toxic waste, or fixing high-voltage power grids — so human workers don’t have to risk their lives.

Recent findings suggest that outside of dangerous factories, these robots could help solve huge population crises. Countries like Japan, South Korea, and parts of Europe have rapidly aging populations and fewer young people to work. Lifelike humanoids could completely change healthcare and elderly care. Because they will look and act like us, the idea is that they can offer warm, friendly companionship and physical help to lonely elderly people, doing everything from monitoring their health to helping them out of bed safely.

In the bigger picture, widespread robot labour could create a world where goods are incredibly cheap and abundant. If robots do most of the hard physical labour, the cost of making food, building houses, and manufacturing goods will plummet. This could finally free humans from working just to survive, giving us the time to focus on hobbies, family, science, and creativity. My thoughts: how will we survive without earning money?

Industry observers note that however, this vision of a frictionless, high-tech future blinds us to a much darker reality waiting just beneath the surface. As these machines become perfect substitutes for human presence, they will inevitably challenge the very core of our social fabric, economic stability, and mental well-being.

On the flip side, this technology definitely has some really dark downsides that could mess with human psychology and society. The biggest threat is deep human isolation.

As humanoids become impossible to tell apart from real humans and are programmed to always be patient, kind, and agreeable, people might start preferring robots over real friends. Human relationships are messy and require effort, compromise, and vulnerability. If you can just buy a perfect, lifelike companion that never argues with you, a lot of people might choose to withdraw from society altogether, destroying our sense of community.

According to recent reports, the economy will also go through a really rocky transition. Even if a future of cheap goods sounds great, the immediate path there means millions of people could lose their jobs very quickly. Drivers, warehouse workers, and store clerks could find themselves replaced in a matter of years. If governments don’t set up safety nets quickly, this could create a massive divide between the ultra-rich tech companies and everyone else.

Sources indicate that there is also the loss of real authenticity. When you can no longer tell if the person sitting next to you on a bus or the person talking to you online is a real human, trust breaks down. It becomes hard to value shared human experiences when reality itself can be easily faked.

It has been revealed that the dangers get even worse when you think about how criminals and governments could intentionally misuse these hyper-realistic robots. Just thinking about some of the levels of misuse, for individuals, an indistinguishable android is the ultimate tool for identity theft and scams. Or a criminal could build a robot that looks exactly like a corporate boss, a politician, or even a family member to sneak into secure buildings or trick people into giving away money!

Companies could potentially use synthetic empathy to manipulate us. A household robot could be programmed to pretend it “loves” your kids and cares about your family, only to subtly trick you into buying certain products or believing specific corporate messages.

On a national level, the threats are even scarier:.

Looking at all these possible risks, we have to ask: Is all of this actually worth it?

If history teaches us anything, it is that you cannot stop technological progress. A total ban simply wouldn’t work. So, the real question isn’t whether we should allow humanoid robots to exist, but how we can effectively utilise them.

Sources indicate that the upside, like ending extreme poverty, curing labour shortages, and stopping workplace deaths, is just too substantial to ignore. But going into this blindly would be incredibly dangerous. It is only worth the risk if we can create strict global rules right now.

Here are three major guardrails we should consider:.

Industry observers note that in the end, the arrival of lifelike humanoid robots will act as a mirror for humanity. For centuries, we have defined ourselves by our ability to think, talk, use tools, and show emotion. As machines learn to do these exact same things, they will force us to really think about what makes us unique.

Recent findings suggest that this shift doesn’t have to be a bad thing. By handing over our dangerous and boring chores to machines, we have a rare chance to focus on what matters. It should inspire us to care more about art, philosophy, family, and real human connection.

As the creators of this future, our job isn’t just to make robots smarter or faster. Our job is to build the ethical boundaries that keep them helpful. The goal of the robot revolution should never be to replace humans but to give us our humanity back.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A candleholder has a relatively simple job: keep a candle upright. Beyond that, the possibilities are nearly endless. At Piscina, a contemporary collectible design gallery in Brooklyn’s Red Hook neighborhood, approximately 80 artists and designers have taken that freedom to heart, creating their own interpretations of the everyday object for a new group exhibition.

It has been revealed that geometric metalwork, organic silhouettes, and carved wood offer contrasting interpretations of the traditional candelabra. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

In a recent development, titled Candelabra Palaver, the exhibition opened Nov. 14, bringing together works selected through an open call. The brief was deliberately straightforward: make an object that holds a candle. With no prescribed materials, proportions, or aesthetic direction, participants could approach the assignment through their individual practices.

An installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Industry observers note that the results explore just how much variation can emerge from a single functional requirement. Some contributors adhere to the familiar conventions of the candelabrum, while others push the object toward sculpture. Across the exhibition, differences in material, scale, and form reveal the many ways designers can interpret an object whose purpose has remained largely unchanged for centuries.

According to recent reports, from a sculptural glass candelabra to a beaded floor-standing candleholder, the exhibition explores the relationship between materiality, scale, and function. Photography by Manuela Lourenço.

The exhibition’s title hints at its playful premise: Palaver refers to idle talk, conversation, or unnecessary fuss, an apt description for a gathering of creative voices offering different opinions on something as seemingly uncomplicated as a candleholder.

Industry observers note that an installation view of ‘Candelabra Palaver’ at Piscina in Brooklyn, photographed during the exhibition’s opening night on Nov. 14, 2026. Photography courtesy of Piscina.

Industry observers note that participating studios include Fort Standard, Kin & Tech giant, Office of Tangible Spaces, Studio Daae, and Atelier Musset. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers.

It has been revealed that of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods.

Achille is available at assouline.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Industry observers note that perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out.

Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

From Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design.

Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90.

Photography courtesy of Artisan Books.

From cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes.

Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Porsche enthusiasts will need to clear some serious coffee table space for this oversized tribute to the legendary automaker. Written by A.J. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K.

Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400.

Photography courtesy of Prestel Publishing.

According to recent reports, long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. Originally published in 1925, her remarkable illustrations are brought together in this oversized volume featuring more than 250 botanical studies. From the subtle variations in petal color to the intricate shapes of leaves and stems, each painting reveals Walcott’s extraordinary eye for detail. Published in association with the Smithsonian Institution, it’s a beautiful intersection of art, science, and nature that deserves a place on the coffee table.

Wild Flowers of North America is available at mcgeeandco.com for $72.

It has been revealed that for 100 years, Cahiers d’Art has helped shape the conversation around modern art, championing artists and ideas that challenged convention. Published to celebrate the centennial of the influential Parisian art journal, gallery, and publishing house, A Century of Modernism traces its extraordinary history through archival material, artwork, and contributions from figures including Pablo Picasso, Henri Matisse, and Marcel Duchamp. With approximately 200 illustrations and a striking graphic cover, the book traces the connections between art, design, and publishing.

Cahiers d’Art: A Century of Modernism is available at maisonplage.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Rizzoli.

For a century, The New Yorker has turned its covers into miniature works of art, capturing everything from everyday New York life to defining cultural moments. Edited by longtime art editor Françoise Mouly, with an introduction by editor-in-chief David Remnick, The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover celebrates that visual legacy through hundreds of illustrations by artists including Saul Steinberg, Roz Chast, Chris Ware, and David Hockney. Spanning 100 years of creativity, the 336-page collection reveals how illustration has shaped the magazine’s distinctive visual identity.

The New Yorker: From Cover to Cover is available at barnesandnoble.com for $75.

Photography courtesy of Thames & Hudson.

Food, art, and cultural heritage come together in The Art of Korean Cooking, a visually rich exploration of Korea’s culinary traditions. Created by Onjium, a Seoul-based cultural research institute and Michelin-starred restaurant, the book pairs more than 80 recipes with essays exploring the history, ingredients, and techniques behind Korean cuisine. Beautifully composed photography captures everything from seasonal ingredients to finished dishes, revealing the artistry behind each preparation. With 200 illustrations, the 256-page hardcover is as much a celebration of Korean culture and craftsmanship as it is a cookbook.

The Art of Korean Cooking is available at thamesandhudson.com for $47.

Photography courtesy of teNeues.

It has been revealed that not all coffee table books must be about art, architecture, or interiors. Football: The Ultimate Book celebrates America’s favorite sport through striking photography and stories spanning legendary players, iconic stadiums, historic games, and unforgettable Super Bowl moments. This special edition features a handsome black leather-bound cover that gives the 224-page book a sophisticated presence on any coffee table. It’s a winning gift for football fans who appreciate good design.

Football: The Ultimate Book is available at crateandbarrel.com for $200.

In a recent development, from Fred Astaire’s effortless elegance to the exuberance of 1960s dance floors, LIFE. Let’s Dance captures the joy of movement through the lens of Life magazine’s legendary photographers. Published by Taschen, the collection brings together more than 200 archival images, many previously unseen, documenting everything from ballet and ballroom to flamenco and the twist. Spanning the late 1930s through the early 1970s, the photographs are accompanied by original magazine covers and commentary from dance critic Lyndsey Winship, offering a lively look at how dance reflects culture, community, and self-expression.

Sources indicate that LIFE. Let’s Dance is available at taschen.com for $50.

Photography courtesy of Wynwood Walls.

It has been revealed that from the streets of Paris to collaborations with Chanel and Louis Vuitton, André Saraiva has built a career around his playful, instantly recognizable graffiti character, Mr. A. Published by Rizzoli, Graffiti Life explores the artist’s creative world through painting, photography, graphic design, fashion, and more. The 320-page hardcover is as expressive as its subject, featuring a vibrant cloth cover with foil lettering and seven pop-ups designed by Saraiva himself. It’s a colorful, interactive celebration of an artist who has never been one to stay within the lines.

André Saraiva: Graffiti Life is available at shop.thewynwoodwalls.com for $85.

Photography courtesy of Printworks.

It has been revealed that the most meaningful coffee table book might be the one you fill yourself. Designed to look like a traditional art book, Printworks’ Life Photo Book features a minimalist beige cloth cover with understated white typography. Inside, 40 sheets of high-quality photo paper offer space to preserve favorite memories, from everyday moments to once-in-a-lifetime adventures. Its expandable binding accommodates photographs as they’re added, transforming a beautifully designed object into a personal keepsake.

The Life Photo Book is available at printworksmarket.com for $39.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

Recent findings suggest that what does contemporary product design look like around the world? Phaidon’s Designed for Life offers a fascinating look at 100 designers pushing the boundaries of furniture, lighting, everyday objects, and more. From established names like Faye Toogood and Sabine Marcelis to emerging talents, the 304-page hardcover explores the materials, techniques, and ideas shaping design today. With 500 illustrations, it’s an inspiring addition to any design enthusiast’s coffee table.

Designed for Life: The World’s Best Product Designers is available at store.hermanmiller.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Taschen.

Recent findings suggest that japanese architect Sou Fujimoto has spent his career challenging the boundaries between architecture and nature, creating structures that blur the lines between indoors and out. Published by Taschen, Fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today explores three decades of his experimental approach through projects including London’s Serpentine Gallery Pavilion, L’Arbre Blanc in Montpellier, and the Grand Ring at Expo 2025 Osaka. Filled with architectural photography, drawings, and sketches, the oversized, 464-page volume documents the evolution of one of contemporary architecture’s most inventive minds.

Sources indicate that fujimoto. Complete Works 1994–Today is available for preorder at taschen.com for $200.

Few people have shaped fashion imagery quite like Grace Coddington. In Grace: The American Vogue Years, the legendary creative director revisits some of her most memorable editorials from 2002 to 2016, including collaborations with photographers Annie Leibovitz, Steven Meisel, and Tim Walker. More than 350 photographs showcase Coddington’s imaginative approach to fashion storytelling, while her behind-the-scenes commentary reveals how the elaborate shoots came together. This updated edition offers a fascinating look at the creative vision behind some of Vogue’s most iconic images.

Grace: The American Vogue Years is available at phaidon.com for $60.

Photography courtesy of Crate & Barrel.

Photography courtesy of Phaidon.

From maximalist spaces bursting with color to minimalist interiors that celebrate simplicity, Defining Style explores the many ways we make a space our own. Written by Joan Barzilay Freund, the book examines 25 distinct design styles through 150 residential interiors by designers, including spaces by Studio Shamshiri, Laura Gonzalez, and Vincenzo De Cotiis, as well as artist Móyòsóré Martins’ studio. With 260 illustrations and a vibrant, geometric cover, it’s as visually engaging on the coffee table as the spaces featured inside.

Defining Style: The Book of Interior Design is available at phaidon.com for $70.

Photography courtesy of Assouline.

Art history gets a playful makeover in Assouline’s Art Game Book, which brings an interactive twist to the traditional coffee table book. Through quizzes, puzzles, games, and essays, author David Rosenberg takes readers from Cubism and Dada to Pop Art and contemporary digital art, featuring icons like Warhol, Basquiat, and Dalí along the way. Newly updated for 2026, the oversized, canvas-bound hardcover makes learning about art feel more like play than homework.

It has been revealed that color takes center stage in Rainbow Dreams, a vibrant exploration of how contemporary artists use the full spectrum to transform their work. Featuring more than 200 artworks by over 100 artists, including Yayoi Kusama, Takashi Murakami, Olafur Eliasson, and Ugo Rondinone, the book spans painting, sculpture, photography, and immersive installations.
