Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

📅 2026-06-30 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In a recent development, this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mikhail Prosmitskiy is a Software Engineer who loves making complex things feel simple — and fast. He’s spent years building everything from crypto … More about Mikhail ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

In a recent development, we know that right now, a senior engineer is shipping a checkout flow they “built” in a single afternoon. AI assistant does the heavy lifting, happy path runs clean, and a rotating chevron spins on the order summary. Two weeks later, engineering gets a notice from customer support: a blind customer using a screen reader can’t complete the purchase because the “Pay Now” control is a with a click handler. No role. Not focusable. Not working.

It has been revealed that that gap — between code that runs and a product people can actually use — is becoming one of the defining engineering challenges of the AI era. Teams can generate UI faster than ever, but they still have to guarantee that what they ship is usable, secure, and maintainable.

Accessibility sits right in the middle of that problem.

Industry observers note that this is not an article about compliance checklists or end-of-project audits. It’s about engineering systems. Specifically, why accessibility should be treated as an operational capability — alongside privacy, security, reliability, and observability — and what that looks like in practice.

Sources indicate that for years, the default way to “do” accessibility was the one-time, audit-only approach: hire a firm, get a list of 200 findings, fix some of them, file the report. A lot of teams have now moved beyond this model — and the reason is worth looking into.

Audits do matter. For sales, procurement, governance — they’re essential. When a buyer asks for a VPAT or an ACR, you need one. When legal asks if you’re meeting requirements, you need documentation. Audits serve those purposes well.

Recent findings suggest that but audits don’t help you build accessible features during sprint planning. Audits can cost points during a sprint. They don’t catch problems before merge requests. They don’t scale with deployment velocity. The mistake, essentially, is tackling accessibility as a snapshot when you really need constant monitoring. Six months after the audit, the product has shipped dozens of releases, multiple newly introduced features, and a redesigned nav. The report is now fiction. Compliance is not a state you reach — it’s a state you maintain, and complexity fights you the whole way.

In a recent development, the WebAIM Million report, which scans the top one million home pages every year, found that 95.9% of pages had detectable WCAG failures in its 2026 run, with an average of 56.1 errors per page. The number of page elements jumped more than 20% in a single year, likely driven by AI-enabled development and ‘vibe coding’ — and more elements mean more places to break. Accessibility debt behaves exactly like technical debt: every inaccessible component you ship becomes a future remediation project, and the interest compounds.

Any strategy that treats accessibility as a periodic event rather than a continuous property of the system is going to lose.

With the scale at which teams now generate UI, the gap doesn’t just persist; it multiplies.

In a recent development, start with how fast this arrived. In February 2025, Andrej Karpathy coined “vibe coding” — a way of working where you “fully give in to the vibes” and “forget that the code even exists”. You describe intent, the model generates, you accept the diffs without reading them. It was meant for weekend projects. It did not stay there. Y Combinator reported that 25% of its Winter 2025 batch had codebases that were 95% AI-generated.

Recent findings suggest that models don’t land on non-semantic markup by accident — three forces push them there. Most React code on GitHub uses non-semantic “soup”, so that’s what the models learn. Human reviewers and evaluators judge output visually, so the feedback loop rewards looks, not semantics. And is fewer tokens than , so absent a constraint, the model takes the cheap path.

Here’s the thing about AI-generated UI: it’s inaccessible by default. Not occasionally — by default. A developer writing in Frontend Masters tested AI-generated React components across multiple tools and documented the pattern. A typical AI-generated sidebar had ten distinct accessibility failures in twenty-nine lines: no landmark, no heading, no list structure, elements with click handlers instead of buttons, no aria-expanded, no keyboard handling, and unlabeled icons. The accessibility tree — the structure screen readers actually read — came back as flat, unstructured text. “Same pixels” as the author put it. “One is a door. The other is a painting of a door”.

Sources indicate that now connect this to security, because the two failures come from the same root. Veracode’s 2025 GenAI Code Security Report tested large language models across dozens of coding tasks and found that a large fraction of AI-generated code introduced security vulnerabilities — including OWASP Top 10 flaws. Cross-site scripting failures were particularly common, and security performance did not meaningfully improve with newer, larger models. The problem wasn’t model intelligence. It was process: developers generating code without specifying security constraints and accepting output without systematic verification.

The same shortcut that skips the security review skips the accessibility review. At scale, AI won’t close the accessibility gap — it has industrialized the very thing that creates it.

The fix is not to ban AI. Your developers are already using it. The fix is to constrain it and verify it — to treat AI as a very fast teammate who always needs guardrails.

This is usually where someone indicates, “Guardrails? Sounds great, but they will slow us down.”.

In practice, the opposite tends to be true.

Shift-left is the entire DevOps thesis, and it applies cleanly here. An accessibility matter caught during design review is a comment. The same issue found in production is a remediation project.

Recent findings suggest that catching an accessibility problem as a component is built takes minutes. Fixing one after the fact — discovering it in an audit, diagnosing the root cause, restructuring the markup, applying the necessary fix, writing tests — can easily take hours. Multiply that across hundreds of findings from a late-stage audit, and you have weeks of unplanned work that earlier automated checks — whether in design reviews, development workflows, or CI — could have prevented.

In a recent development, teams that integrate accessibility into everyday workflows avoid the expensive surprises: emergency audits, remediation sprints, procurement blockers, and redesigns that quietly break core user journeys. Accessibility doesn’t reduce velocity. Unexpected work reduces velocity. In-flow accessibility is one way of eliminating unexpected work.

The organizations that scale accessibility successfully do not rely on heroes. They rely on systems.

The highest-leverage place to start is the design system. One accessible component can be reused thousands of times. The GOV.UK Design System is a useful example: components undergo both automated and manual testing using assistive technologies such as JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack. The team is explicit about the limits of automation and supplements tooling with user testing involving people with disabilities. They’re equally clear that using the design system doesn’t “magically” make a service accessible; it just gives you a higher starting point.

It has been revealed that accessibility becomes infrastructure. That’s the lesson.

From there, it moves into the engineering workflow:.

Finally, accessibility becomes enforceable through automation:.

In a recent development, at that point, accessibility stops depending on memory and starts depending on the process. It becomes part of your platform.

A few implementation patterns consistently show up in teams that do this well.

Recent findings suggest that instead of fixing accessibility after generation, bake requirements directly into tooling through Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, or repository-level standards. Tell the model to use semantic HTML. Tell it when to use buttons versus links. Tell it to expose the state and labels correctly. Models follow persistent constraints far more reliably than one-off prompts.

Comboboxes, menus, tabs, modals, and similar controls routinely become accessibility hotspots. Libraries such as Radix UI, React Aria, and Headless UI already solve many of these problems. The scalable approach is not about repeatedly implementing accessibility correctly. It’s inheriting accessible behavior from well-tested primitives.

Focus order, labels, heading hierarchy, and interaction states should be specified before implementation begins. If accessibility requirements are absent from the design artifact, they are often absent from the final product. A simple memo at design handoff — what is the tab order, what are the labels, what happens on error — removes a huge amount of guesswork later.

None of these patterns is exotic. They’re just DevOps and platform thinking applied to accessibility.

In a recent development, engineering leaders rarely prioritize accessibility solely because of regulations. But regulations, procurement requirements, user retention, and product quality all point in the same direction.

Legal pressure continues to increase. Digital accessibility lawsuits in the United States have stayed in the thousands per year, and they are not limited to large enterprises. The European Accessibility Act is now enforceable across the EU, applying to e‑commerce, banking, ticketing, telecoms, and more, regardless of where the company is headquartered. The message is clear: accessibility is no longer a “nice-to-have” in the eyes of regulators.

But compliance is only part of the story. The bigger story is the market you leave on the table. The World Economic Forum (December 2023) estimates that the world’s 1.3 billion people with disabilities, “along with their friends and family, has a spending power of $13 trillion”; disabled consumers alone control roughly $8 trillion in annual disposable income, per the Valuable 500.

Recent findings suggest that in the UK alone, the Click-Away Pound Report 2019 found the “Click-Away Pound has risen to £17.1 billion” — more than 4.9 million people with access needs who abandon inaccessible sites and spend elsewhere, up almost 45% from £11.75 billion in 2016. People don’t file a bug report. They leave and buy from a competitor.

Recent findings suggest that there is also a procurement reality that turns accessibility from a cost into a moat. If you sell B2B or to government, you will increasingly be asked for proof of accessibility — VPATs/ACRs or equivalent documentation. According to Level Access’s Seventh Annual State of Digital Accessibility Report, 75% of organizations now require proof of accessibility at least most of the time when purchasing digital products — essentially unchanged from 74% in the previous report, but with a notable shift towards stricter enforcement, as those that always require it rose from 27% to 31%. A strong ACR accelerates the sales cycle; a weak one, or none at all, creates redlines that stall or kill it. For some buyers, this is a hard requirement before your product can even enter evaluation. A strong accessibility story accelerates the sales cycle. A weak one creates redlines that stall or kill it.

According to recent reports, step back and the deeper pattern is clear: accessibility is a proxy for engineering maturity. A team that ships semantic HTML, manages focus, exposes state correctly, and tests it in CI is a team that has its house in order. The same discipline that produces an accessible component produces a maintainable, testable, less buggy one.

Industry observers note that for dev and product leaders, that’s the real business case: accessibility work is platform work. It pays off every time a feature ships faster and more smoothly, with less rework, than it otherwise would have.

Sources indicate that if you take one thing from this, make it this: accessibility doesn’t come from an audit, a hero, or a heroic remediation sprint before launch. It comes from systems.

Sources indicate that an accessible design system so components start right. A Definition of Done so they stay right. Automated testing and CI gates so regressions fail the build. Governance, so someone owns it. Guardrails for AI-assisted development so your fastest tool stops being your biggest liability.

None of those practices is particularly glamorous. That’s exactly why they work. They’re the same kinds of boring, reliable systems you already trust for security, reliability, and performance.

But there’s one thing no tool on that list can do. No linter, no automated scanner run, no dashboard will ever tell you what it’s actually like to use your product as a blind person with a screen reader, or to navigate your checkout with a keyboard because a tremor makes a mouse inoperable. So build the systems — you need them, and they’re the only way accessibility survives contact with a real release schedule. But test with real users with disabilities regularly. The first time you sit behind someone using JAWS to fight through a form your team thought was “done”, something changes. The tooling tells you whether you passed. A real person tells you whether it actually works.

Accessibility is not a feature. It’s an operational capability. Treat it that way, and you get something dev and product leaders already care about: a faster, safer, more reliable way to ship software.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark new Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people.
  • According to recent reports, but for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different.
  • In a recent development, “Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark new Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people. “There was no one there because ceramics can feel cold and distanced,” she states. “They can be hard to bring alive, because the makers are anonymous, and [the objects are] often displayed in glass cases.”.

According to recent reports, but for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different. The result, Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, opens this month at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague, where she is the curator of decorative arts. It will, she claims, be “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever”. Equally importantly, she promises it will be captivating and enjoyable.

In a recent development, “Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she claims. “We want to show the love craftspeople put into these pieces. It has inspired, and it continues to inspire, so many craftmakers—we’ll give them a platform.”.

Natasja Sadi's Suikerbloemen (2024) Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag, photo: Studio Roodenburch.

Around 1,000 objects, including vases, teapots, plates, wall plaques and tiles, will be on display at the Kunstmuseum, which has one of the largest collections of the art form that is perhaps the best-known cultural export of the Netherlands. Also on show in Blue Loves You will be Delftware-inspired pieces, including the blue dress worn by Queen Máxima of the Netherlands for her husband’s 2013 investiture, its bodice embroidered with Delft-derived flowers. “There’s a lot more to it than blue and white fridge magnets,” Lambooy states.

According to recent reports, although the porcelain is known for its characteristic colouring, the show will include examples of both white and multicoloured Delftware. It will explore its history, dating back to the 17th century. The form was originally a high-end Chinese import, displayed in the wealthiest homes. But when factories started to make their own version of it in Delft, it was transformed.

“It became an on-trend, functional brand that was affordable for every home and on every budget: it was the Ikea of its day,” states Lambooy, whose co-curator for the long-term show is the television presenter Janny van der Heijden (who is also a judge on the country’s version of The Great British Bake Off).

Ceramics in Blue Loves You, “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever” Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

The quintessential Delftware piece was the tulip pyramid, some of the best examples of which were made for King William III, born in The Hague, and his English wife Queen Mary II, who were the joint monarchs of England, Scotland and Ireland in the late 17th century. “Mary exported Delftware to Britain—she was the most crucial woman in its history,” Lambooy indicates.

The porcelain’s connections to Dutch colonialism will also be explored, with exhibits including an installation of sugar flowers by the floral artist Natasja Sadi, whose family are originally from the former Dutch colony of Suriname and whose ancestors were enslaved.

• Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, Kunstmuseum, The Hague, 28 November-31 December 2029.

Tech Report: Burlwood Is Making a Comeback With a Modern Twist

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood.
  • Sources indicate that burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s.
  • Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few materials make a visual statement quite like burlwood. Its swirls and naturally irregular patterns give it a depth and individuality that are difficult to replicate. That distinctive grain comes from burls, rounded growths that develop on tree trunks or branches and are often associated with injury, stress, or infection.

Sources indicate that burlwood gained popularity during the Art Deco era of the 1920s and ’30s before becoming a defining feature of furniture design in the 1970s. Today, it’s experiencing another moment. Yet its current appeal is less about recreating the past and more about rethinking how the material fits modern spaces.

Design Milk spoke with four designers to learn why burlwood continues to resonate and the fresh ways they’re using it.

Bookmatched burlwood creates a striking symmetrical pattern across this three-drawer chest, set against a sculptural curved wood bed frame. Photography by Emily Hart.

Recent findings suggest that “Burlwood does what a great print does,” says Tiffany Brooks, principal designer of Tiffany Brooks Interiors. “It gives your eye somewhere to go. Up close, you see all these little swirls and knots, and from across the room, it reads as one rich surface. Even two pieces made from the same wood can have completely different personalities.”.

Abbe Fenimore, owner of Studio Ten 25, shares that appreciation for burlwood’s organic qualities, seeing the material as a way to introduce visual interest without relying on patterned textiles.

In a recent development, the tightly patterned grain of this burlwood chest extends across its drawer fronts, while colorful glass candlesticks and art books add color to the display. Photography by Ellen Renee.

For Eddie Maestri, founder, principal, and creative director of Maestri Studio, burlwood’s appeal lies in its departure from the predictable. “To me, the imperfections are the beauty,” he claims. “Every piece of burl is different, and you can’t fake it.”.

The designers we spoke to see burlwood as having staying power, particularly as homeowners move toward spaces that feel more personal and collected.

“The material is timeless,” Brooks states. “What changes is how we use it. Right now, I think people are a little tired of rooms that look like they all came from the same inspiration board. Burl brings some individuality back.”.

A honey-toned burlwood table features a richly figured top and tapered legs, standing out against the darker wood cabinetry behind it. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Fenimore sees a similar appeal in burlwood’s ability to bridge different eras and styles. Its balance of modern and vintage sensibilities, she explains, can give even a brand-fresh piece the character of something collected over time.

Maestri points to its long history, from French cabinetmakers to the Art Deco era and the 1970s, as evidence of its enduring draw. “It keeps coming back because people want warmth and things made by hand,” he says, noting that burlwood can bring a sense of soul to interiors that otherwise feel overly polished.

Walnut, maple, and mappa burl each bring a different quality to a piece, with variations in color, grain, and visual weight influencing how designers use them.

Brooks reaches for walnut burl when she wants to introduce depth and create a moodier atmosphere, while maple burl offers similar movement in a lighter, softer palette. For a bolder grain pattern, she favors mappa burl.

Recent findings suggest that A burlwood nightstand introduces warmth and a touch of traditional detail to this otherwise contemporary bedroom, adding a rich wood accent against the sculptural charcoal headboard and modern lines. Photography by Nick Sargent.

Recent findings suggest that maestri, meanwhile, has a clear go-to: mappa burl, also known as poplar burl. “It’s my favorite because it’s lighter and more golden than walnut, so you get all that movement without the room feeling heavy,” he indicates.

According to recent reports, while Mimi Meacham, founder and principal designer of Marian Louise Designs, gravitates toward rich walnut burl and lighter mappa burl, the individual piece matters more to her than the wood species. “The color, scale of the figuring, and finish all affect how it will feel in a room,” she says. “I want the grain and the shape of the furniture to complement each other.”.

A close-up reveals the distinctive natural markings of a burlwood table, with brass-and-acrylic drawer pulls adding a mix of warm and modern finishes. Photography by Emily Hart.

According to recent reports, because burlwood already has so much movement, surrounding colors and finishes can either complement its natural pattern or create an intriguing contrast. Brooks likes combining burl with warm brass, matte paint, and textiles such as nubby linen and velvet. “I’d put a honey-toned burl next to a deep aubergine or an inky blue in a heartbeat,” she notes. Fenimore also likes pairing burl with color and pattern, especially soft blues, olive greens, warm neutrals, and even unexpected pops of pink or red.

It has been revealed that A burlwood tray with a gold-toned rim highlights the wood’s warm coloring and varied markings, with stacked books providing a colorful backdrop. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Sources indicate that meacham gravitates toward warm wood tones paired with blues and greens, from soft periwinkle to deep green, along with antique brass, linen, velvet, and plaster. She also considers the finish of the burl itself when choosing surrounding materials. A glossy burlwood surface, for example, can be balanced by a matte wall or softly textured fabric.

Sources indicate that for a warmer, earthier direction, Maestri recommends tobacco, ochre, olive, and soft plaster white, complemented by brass, stone, linen, and mohair. He also prefers finishes with a subtle luster to emphasize the grain’s richness. Fenimore likes the contrast burlwood creates with lacquered surfaces, brass, upholstery, and contemporary furniture silhouettes.

Sources indicate that A curved burlwood console showcases the wood’s richly varied grain across its drawer fronts and rounded frame, with pale green stools and white fringe adding a touch of color and texture. Photography by Emily Hart.

Burlwood is finding its way into a wider range of applications throughout the home. Brooks likes seeing it incorporated into architectural details, such as the back of a kitchen island or as an inset on a painted door. “A little restraint makes the detail feel more special,” she indicates. For larger pieces, she points to Worlds Away for its clean-lined interpretations of burlwood, as well as Ambella Home, Chairish, and 1stDibs for finding distinctive designs.

Sources indicate that maestri also appreciates seeing burl used beyond traditional furniture, including on lamp bases, picture frames, and cabinet doors. At home, he has a burlwood bar cabinet from Soho Home, and he’s drawn to the brand’s Wallace collection, which uses mappa burl in sculptural, curved forms.

A burlwood coffee table showcases the wood’s warm tones and naturally irregular markings, while art books and a decorative bowl give the tabletop a relaxed, collected feel. Photography by Ellen Renee.

Contemporary furniture designs also explore the interplay between burlwood, contrasting materials, and simpler silhouettes. Jonathan Adler’s Bond collection, for example, combines burl with acrylic on a dresser and metal on a dining table. Meacham points to Made Goods’ Bradley mirror, which lets the mappa burl frame take center stage. Fenimore recommends looking at brands like Modway and TOV Furniture, particularly for smaller items such as chairs, ottomans, and drink tables with burl accents.

The rich, swirling grain of the half-moon burlwood console complements the delicate branches and floral motifs in the botanical artwork above. Photography by Emily Hart.

Industry observers note that for anyone hesitant to introduce such a distinctive material, the designers recommend beginning with one piece, such as a side table, mirror, or tray. Brooks suggests starting with something that serves an existing need, even if it’s as small as a drink table next to a chair. Maestri puts it simply: “Pick one piece and let it be the star. Keep what’s around it simpler so the grain can stand out.”.

Industry observers note that fenimore encourages mixing burlwood with other wood tones rather than trying to match everything. She also sees the material as a way to ground a room that already has plenty of color and pattern. Meacham recommends giving the grain some breathing room through intentional styling and a variety of finishes. “That doesn’t mean everything else needs to be neutral—I love burl with color—but you want your eye to have somewhere to rest.”.

Burlwood’s latest resurgence doesn’t require a revival of any particular decorating style. The same material that characterized Art Deco cabinetry and 1970s furniture feels equally at home alongside contemporary silhouettes, unexpected colors, and contrasting finishes. Its history is part of its appeal, but it needn’t dictate how we use it.

Colleen Sullivan is a lifestyle writer and editor who specializes in home, travel, beauty, fashion, food, weddings, and wellness. She’s a contributor at multiple digital publications, and served as a print editor at Vogue, Working Woman, Health, and HGTV. When Colleen isn’t working, she loves to restore old beach houses at the Jersey Shore. Sullivan also serves as an adjunct professor at the Newhouse School at Syracuse University.

#161720. Matching AI Modality To User Intent: Designing The Right Interface

Matching AI Modality To User Intent: Designing The Right Interface

📅 2026-07-02 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3122 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • The design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

The design community has entered a period of conversational tunnel vision. Because Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on dialogue, the industry has collectively decided that the chat bubble is the natural home for every AI capability. While the chat interface is a viable and powerful option for many tasks, it is one tool in an expansive toolkit. UX and Product teams must be intentional about the modalities we choose for how people provide their data and commands, and how the system presents its output.

To pick the best method, you need to think about what the user wants to do, where they are, and how much cognitive effort they are already expending. This guide offers a clear way to figure out the best approach for any product, using two tools to assist in the process: a Task Audit and an Input/Output Alignment Matrix.

In a recent development, picture a traveler jogging through a loud airport terminal after a sudden gate change. They are dragging their roller bag and carrying a coffee in the other hand. They need to open their airline app to ask the AI assistant where to go. The tool immediately fails the input modality test. It forces the traveler to stop walking, balance their coffee, and type a long booking reference number into a tiny chat box. When they finally hit send, the system fails the output modality test. Instead of flashing a large, high-contrast gate number, the AI returns a dense paragraph explaining the atmospheric weather patterns causing the delay. The actual gate number sits buried at the very bottom.

Recent findings suggest that while they might make the flight just fine, the user won’t forget the moment of anxiety they felt while using the AI tool — an experience that could have served as a way to reinforce a commitment to UX has instead validated the common conception that companies don’t care about or understand customers using their products. In this scenario, the airline built a smart tool, but the interface failed the user. The input required physical dexterity, which the traveler lacked at the time of need. The output demanded a level of reading focus they could not spare. This article will cover how we can avoid this scenario in our AI-powered tools. In order to be successful, we must evaluate the physical and cognitive load of our users to match both the input and output modality to their immediate intent.

Let’s first discuss the limitations of a chat-based interface.

In a recent development, the allure of the chatbot is easy to understand from a product development standpoint. It is a blank slate. It suggests that the system can handle anything the user provides. However, a text-heavy interface often causes a high adaptation load. This load increases cognitive demands on customers. Over time, this cognitive burden turns into a psychological tax a person pays when changing natural thought processes to accommodate a machine.

When an interface relies solely on conversation, it imposes a dual burden: a linguistic challenge for input and a cognitive challenge for output. We’ll examine both separately below.

A blank chat box creates a major problem for users who need to discover what a tool can actually do. In a standard graphical interface, menus and buttons provide clear visual cues that signal every available option. A chat box often leads to choice paralysis because users are forced to guess what the AI is capable of. They have to remember the exact phrasing or technical terms required to get the result they want.

Industry observers note that consider a data analyst who wants to find a specific trend in a spreadsheet. In a traditional tool, they might click a filter or sort button. In a chat interface, they must suddenly become a writer and describe that complex logic in a complete sentence. Another example: a manager trying to reorganize a team schedule. Dragging and dropping blocks on a calendar is intuitive. Describing those same scheduling shifts in a text prompt adds a layer of work that makes the task feel more difficult than it should be.

Sources indicate that designing for input means recognizing that composing a prompt is a creative act. It requires a person to translate a vague thought into a specific command. For many professionals, this creates a linguistic barrier. A designer might know exactly how they want an image to look but struggle to describe the lighting or texture in a text prompt. In that case, a slider or a color picker is a much better input method than a text box.

Having addressed the linguistic barrier of constructing input prompts, we must now consider the other half of the conversational burden. This is the cognitive cost the AI imposes when it responds in dense blocks of text.

When an AI responds in long blocks of text, it transfers the interpretive work to you, the user. Text is a serial medium: your brain has to read one word after the next to extract meaning. That takes time. Sequential reading is necessary in many scenarios. Complex legal analysis or reviewing nuanced medical histories requires reading full paragraphs. Teams create friction when they default to text for data that visual formats communicate faster. Visual methods allow parallel processing. You can view a chart and spot a pattern in under a second.

Imagine asking an AI for a project status enhancement. Instead of a color-coded dashboard, you receive three paragraphs listing every task completed that week. Now you must read the entire response and mentally summarize it to find the one piece of information you needed. The quick visual check has been replaced by a reading assignment.

The cognitive tax of this work compounds with professional stakes. A doctor asking for a patient’s vital signs needs a clear numerical display, not a narrative describing the readings. A stock trader looking for a price spike needs a line graph immediately, not a written description of price movement over the past hour. In both cases, a text response forces the professional through a slow, error-prone extraction process when speed and accuracy are most vital.

Industry observers note that before selecting a modality, practitioners need a shared vocabulary for what the options actually are. The table below maps common input and output modalities to the contexts where each performs best. This is not a ranking. Each modality has a role; the question is always which role it is playing in a given workflow.

It has been revealed that designing for modality inherently requires a strong focus on accessibility. While visual dashboards provide rapid insight for many people, designers need to provide screen-reader-optimized audio alternatives for consumers with visual disabilities. Modality choices should multiply pathways to information.

Table 1: Input and Output Modality Taxonomy. Use this as a reference during the Task Audit to identify candidate modalities before narrowing to a recommendation.

Industry observers note that the following FigureFigure 2 illustrates the cognitive spectrum, mapping how mental effort scales across various interaction methods. This spectrum is a critical tool for designers to visualize the shift from low-effort, ambient interactions to high-effort, focused experiences. By understanding where a specific task sits on this spectrum, teams can identify whether a user needs a “glanceable” output that minimizes mental processing or a high-density format that supports deep, analytical thinking.

According to recent reports, with this taxonomy established, the next step is to apply a rigorous method to select the optimal input and output combination. Practitioners must ground this selection process in the user’s real-world environment and context.

To choose the right interaction method, practitioners should complete a Task Audit before interface design begins. A formal Task Audit is the framework that moves teams from assumptions about user behavior to evidence. This process gathers data about the physical, social, and cognitive context in which the work actually happens, which then drives all input and output modality decisions.

Use these four areas of focus to anchor the audit:.

The audit answers two questions for every feature:.

Here is how to gather the evidence to inform your task audit. Use one or more of these common UX research-related methods:.

According to recent reports, this is the most direct way to capture how people work in their natural setting, and it provides the richest data for identifying physical constraints on both input and output. Observation is necessary because users often perform hidden work: small steps or workarounds they forget to mention in an interview, or environmental details they do not think to describe because they have adapted to them.

The Approach: Go to the user’s actual workspace, whether a field site, warehouse, or office floor. Ask them to perform the task you are studying and observe closely.

What to Look For: This method is most revealing for Input Constraints and Output Constraints.

According to recent reports, interviews surface the mental models and decision points that observation cannot capture. They are most valuable for understanding Cognitive Load.

The Approach: Conduct one-on-one sessions with end-owners and the stakeholders who manage the outcome. Use a structured protocol focused on a specific task. Ask for stories about past successes and failures rather than general opinions.

Workshops are essential for defining task boundaries and establishing required fidelity levels. Product managers and stakeholders bring foundational knowledge of system requirements; researchers apply audit criteria.

The Approach: Use workshops to build a shared Task Inventory. Bring designers, engineers, product managers, and business analysts together to map every step of the process. Product managers and business analysts ensure factual accuracy; the research team applies audit criteria to each step.

Sources indicate that once you gather field evidence through these research channels, map your findings directly against the Modality Taxonomy. Each concrete physical or social constraint you document systematically eliminates mismatched interfaces. This process strips away design guesswork, narrowing your architectural choices down to the specific input and output combinations that survive the reality of the user’s environment.

When you ground input and output modality decisions in field evidence rather than interface convention, the resulting design reduces adaptation load for the user and grounds your modality choices in evidence. When you base decisions on field data, you move past interface convention and build a powerful case for the resources needed to create the right experience for your users.

Once the audit is complete, the final step is utilizing the Input/Output Alignment Matrix to formalize the connection between user intent and the optimal modality combination.

In a recent development, with Task Audit findings in hand, you can use an Input/Output Alignment Matrix to map user intent to specific modality combinations. This matrix is organized by what the user is trying to accomplish in a given moment. This distinction versus focusing on what your AI is capable of doing matters. If intent changes across a single workday for the same user, the interface should respond to those shifts.

Sources indicate that choosing the wrong modality for the user’s context can lead to user frustration. Customers might feel mentally drained if a lot of information is delivered through a format that is hard to process, like getting a massive status revision only in text. They may also start worrying if an action was actually completed correctly when a precise command is buried within a long chat exchange. Finally, the system can force users into finding clumsy workarounds, making them adapt to the machine’s method instead of working in their natural, most effective way.

Table 2: Input/Output Alignment Matrix. Map user intent to modality combinations using Task Audit evidence. The two added rows (Monitoring/Alert and Guided Task Completion) cover common enterprise and mobile scenarios not captured in simpler frameworks.

When teams coordinate these factors, they can move past the automatic default of adding a chatbot. Visual layouts enable rapid scanning. Structured inputs remove the burden of constructing perfect sentences. Audio outputs serve owners whose hands and eyes are otherwise occupied.

A real-world scenario where environmental constraints dictated a shift in design strategy best demonstrates the practical application of this matrix and the broader audit framework.

Field technicians servicing high-voltage electrical grids often face a dangerous misalignment of interface modality. Traditionally, these technicians had to rely on ruggedized tablets to access technical manuals and log status updates. However, the physical constraints of the job — wearing heavy protective gloves and working in bucket trucks at significant heights — made interacting with a standard touch interface nearly impossible while on a job site. Additionally, attempting to read complex, text-heavy diagnostic reports on a screen while maintaining situational awareness created a high cognitive load that increased the risk of safety errors.

Industry observers note that to address this, researchers conducted a Task Audit utilizing three specific methods from this article. First, Contextual Inquiry and Observation revealed that technicians often worked in “hands-busy, eyes-busy” states where any manual input was a significant barrier. Researchers observed technicians wearing mandatory thick protective gloves while in the bucket truck, which made precise screen taps nearly impossible and often triggered the wrong commands.

In a recent development, high-altitude environments also introduced severe screen glare from direct sunlight, washing out the display and making text difficult to read even at full brightness. Furthermore, technicians faced the physical safety risk of trying to manipulate and secure a heavy, ruggedized tablet while balanced in awkward positions, creating a distraction that could lead to dangerous slips or equipment contact. These factors, combined with the need to constantly monitor live wires and the surrounding environment, meant technicians could not safely dedicate their eyes or hands to a standard tablet interface, confirming the severity of the eyes-busy and hands-busy constraints.

It has been revealed that second, Focused Interviews with veteran technicians validated the findings from the field. They confirmed that the operational challenges, including the thick gloves, screen glare, and safety risks, were not unique to one location but were commonly experienced across multiple sites, including high-altitude transmission lines and sprawling power substations. This broad confirmation solidified the need for a non-touch, voice-first solution. The interviews also surfaced a critical cognitive constraint: the need for glance verification of vital signs, such as voltage readings and temperature trends, rather than being forced to read a long narrative description of system health. Technicians stressed that their primary need was immediate, unambiguous verification (is this safe? or where is the fault?), not a lengthy diagnostic report, indicating that a text-heavy response was dangerous to their workflow.

These methods confirmed that the environment required a departure from the traditional chat or form-based AI capability interface.

It has been revealed that the resulting solution implemented an adaptive modality handoff designed to mitigate the physical and cognitive barriers researchers identified during the research. While active on a job site, technicians utilize voice input to query the system. This method allows them to remain productive while wearing thick protective gloves that would otherwise prevent precise interaction with a touchscreen.

The AI responds with a short audio summary of immediate diagnostic data. This audio feedback bypasses the challenge of screen glare in high-altitude environments and allows the technician to maintain situational awareness of the high-voltage grid without the safety risk of looking away from dangerous equipment. By providing immediate answers to fault locations through audio, the system meets the technician’s need for glance verification through a hands-free and eyes-free channel.

Once technicians return to a truck and secure safety gear, a system automatically hands off workflows to a 15-inch visual dashboard mounted inside a vehicle. A rugged 10-inch field tablet lacks adequate screen real estate for complex schematics. A larger vehicle display allows for parallel processing of historical trend data and wide electrical grid maps. This case study reflects an actual field audit conducted for a national utility provider. Implementing this adaptive approach reduced diagnostic time by twenty percent and increased daily tool adoption among field crews.

Sources indicate that an AI capability is only as usable as the interface that delivers it. Researchers and designers must resist the pull toward the path of least resistance. Building a chatbot is fast and familiar, something we’ve been doing for decades now. Building an interface that feels like a natural extension of how someone already works is harder, and it is the work that matters.

Start by leaving the screen. The Task Audit requires presence in the places where work actually happens: the field site, the warehouse floor, the operating room. The physical and social realities of those spaces are not edge cases. They are the design brief.

The future of AI interface design is a diverse ecosystem: visual, vocal, haptic, and ambient, calibrated to user intent and environmental context. The chat window is one tool in that ecosystem. It is the right tool for specific jobs, and often the wrong tool for the jobs we reflexively assign to it.

To get started immediately, run a lightweight version of the Task Audit before your next design sprint. Spend two hours observing the workflow in its actual environment. Conduct three to five interviews with the people who perform the task. Bring a PM or analyst into a 90-minute workshop to build a task inventory and apply the four audit questions. You will not have complete data, but you will have enough to make a defensible modality recommendation backed by evidence rather than convention.

I created a Modality Task Audit Template to help guide teams with moving forward. You can download this worksheet and take it directly to your next field observation. It allows design and product teams to document specific physical barriers before writing a single line of code.

We focus heavily on training smarter AI models. We owe equal attention to human interfaces. A brilliant underlying model packaged in a lazy text interface fails. When you observe actual work environments and align interaction modalities to them, you remove adaptation friction.

Friday Five with Nick Doyle: Seeing America Through Shades of Blue

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Creative minds can seemingly turn anything into art—from household items and food to packing supplies and bottle caps.
  • Presented at Pace Prints’ Upcoming York gallery this fall, the exhibition marks Doyle’s first venture into printmaking, using graphic interpretations of everyday objects to examine American preoccupations with risk and reward, escapism, and the myth of the self-made man.
  • Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Creative minds can seemingly turn anything into art—from household items and food to packing supplies and bottle caps. For Los Angeles-born interdisciplinary artist Nick Doyle, the material of choice is denim. Even when working in other mediums, he often gravitates toward a denim-blue palette, as in his latest exhibition, “Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found.”.

Presented at Pace Prints’ Upcoming York gallery this fall, the exhibition marks Doyle’s first venture into printmaking, using graphic interpretations of everyday objects to examine American preoccupations with risk and reward, escapism, and the myth of the self-made man. The gallery will present a selection of these works at Art Basel Miami Beach 2026.

‘Quick Fix’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

Now based in Brooklyn, Doyle earned a BFA in interdisciplinary arts from the San Francisco Art Institute and an MFA in sculpture from Hunter College, in addition to studying at Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture. He cites his discovery of denim as an artistic medium as a turning point in his career.

In a recent development, “I had been doing a ton of research on American history and making work exploring our relationship to nostalgia,” he recalls. “One day a fashion designer moved out of the neighboring studio and threw away a ton of stuff. I found a bolt of denim, and my brain flashed across a network of ideas I had already been considering. I intuitively knew I had stumbled across something significant.”.

Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

Represented by Perrotin and Brussels-based Stems Gallery, Doyle typically uses denim collage to explore what he calls the “underlying structures in American culture.” His practice encompasses “painting-like wall works as well as interactive installations,” he states.

It has been revealed that doyle’s recent exhibition, Collective Hallucinations, presented at Perrotin Upcoming York this past spring, featured wall-mounted collages and an interactive installation called “Mirror Mirror.” The denim-clad structure featured a sign reading “Psychic Readings $10 Special,” while inside, a sassy AI avatar named Ava greeted visitors. The installation marked Doyle’s first foray into AI.

In another unexpected move, he presented his corporate-themed kink bar, Human Resources, at Basel Social Club in Switzerland this June. Built from repurposed cubicles and office furniture, the installation plays with the power dynamics inherent in both corporate and kink culture.

Recent findings suggest that ‘The Price of Ascension’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

Doyle calls his work “more of a reflection of American culture than an individualist perspective.” Reflecting on being raised Quaker, he says, “It’s a very consensus-driven community that is slow-paced and meditative. It’s culturally very counter to a fast-paced, consumer-driven way of life typical of growing up in a large American city.” The tension between these two ways of life surfaces throughout his work.

In this week’s Friday Five, we spent five minutes with Nick Doyle ahead of Art Basel Miami Beach, where Pace Prints will present selections from Lonely but Free I’ll Be Found, to discuss the inspirations behind his exploration of the contradictions of American life.

‘Empty’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

As with much of Doyle’s work, his latest exhibition examines the greed, excess, and toxic masculinity of American culture, this time through bold representations of the minutiae of everyday life: a folded shirt, a necktie, a lottery ticket, a gas gauge on empty, a Coca-Cola machine. Rendered in blue tones reminiscent of denim, the imagery evokes American labor and the archetype of the self-made man.

According to recent reports, together, the works question the country’s deep-rooted belief in self-reliance, drawing parallels between the ideal of the independent American and today’s “America First” mentality, in which individual freedom can come at the expense of collective responsibility. A selection of these works will be on view at Art Basel Miami Beach, Dec. 2–6, 2026.

Here, Doyle discusses his inspirations for the exhibition in his own words.

Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

“This documentary has everything: It traces the origins of country music alongside American history and is a deeply emotional story about the search for salvation and community.

It has been revealed that “One of the musical groups featured is The Sons of the Pioneers. The title of this exhibition Lonely but Free I’ll be Found is a lyric in their song ‘Tumbling Tumbleweeds.’ Originally a poem written by Bob Nolan in the 1930s, it describes lonely cowboys adrift on the range.”.

According to recent reports, the Neon Museum in Las Vegas, Nevada. Photography courtesy of Nick Doyle.

In a recent development, “I take a lot of road trips in the Southwest. Vegas is a great access point, and one of my favorite places is the Neon Museum with a collection of old signage from the last century. There’s something about these retrofuturistic signs rotting away in the desert that I relate to. They exude a sad psychological aura of something that once served a purpose, sitting in functionless rows like a graveyard.

“I think of this body of work functioning similarly to these signs, although different in the sense that what I’m drawing attention to is an idea rather than something that can be purchased.”.

‘The Itch’ (2026) by Nick Doyle. Photography courtesy of Pace Prints.

It has been revealed that “For this show, I was considering the perspective of a man who lived in the ‘suicide belt,’ a term coined by Matt Wray in the early 2000s to describe the high-suicide-rate region of the U.S. Mountain/Intermountain West. The belt includes Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming.

“Wray describes ‘the Intermountain West as a place that is disproportionately populated by middle-aged and aging white men, single, unattached, often unemployed, with access to guns.’ I often think about suicide as a larger social symptom and connect it to broader social issues in the U.S.”.

A 25-plus-year veteran of the interior design industry, Danine Alati began her career at commercial design publication Contract, where she spent 11 years before moving into luxury lifestyle media and working on titles including Hamptons and Art Basel. Based in Brooklyn with her family, she has contributed to AD PRO, DuJour, Galerie, and aspire, among other design and lifestyle publications.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”. Some six decades later and the apotheosis of that market has arrived with the recent opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the $1bn creation of film-maker George Lucas (Star Wars and Indiana Jones) devoted to children’s book art, fantasy art, cartoon images, movie posters, film stills and magazine illustrations, as well as works distinguished as fine art by the likes of Paul Cadmus, Diego Rivera and Carrie Mae Weems.

Industry observers note that lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up. Today, the interest in works by Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, J.C. Leyendecker, Howard Pyle, Maxfield Parrish, Jessie Willcox Smith, John Held Jr and Charles Dana Gibson, among many others, has mushroomed—and in some cases prices have shot up from almost zero to millions of dollars.

“A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” says the Latest York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”.

Industry observers note that certainly, one doesn’t hear that at the major auction houses where works by Rockwell, Parrish, Wyeth and Leyendecker frequently bring the highest prices in American art sales. Norman Rockwell (1894-1978) leads the pack, with his 1951 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover, Saying Grace, fetching $46m at a 2013 Sotheby’s auction and his 1957 oil painting The Rookie (Red Sox Locker Room) sold for $22.5m at a 2014 auction at Christie’s. The 1922 painting Daybreak by Maxfield Parrish(1870-1966) earned $7.6m at a Christie’s sale in 2006, while a 1943 tempera on panel, Portrait of a Farmer, by N.C. Wyeth (1882-1945) brought $5.9m at Sotheby’s in 2018. Football Hero, the 1914 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover by J.C. Leyendecker (1874-1951), brought $4.1m at a Heritage Auctions sale in 2021, and the 1907 painting Captain Keitt by Howard Pyle (1853-1911) for the frontispiece of his novel The Ruby of Kishmoor earned $702,000 at a 2004 sale at Sotheby’s.

“There’s definitely a hierarchy,” says Aviva Lehmann, the deputy chair of fine art at Heritage Auctions, which sold Rockwell’s 1943 work So You Want to See the President! in 2025 to the White House Historical Association for $7.2m.

However, “Rockwell’s success has not been at the expense of these other illustrators”, notes Skye Lacerte, an illustration art specialist at Swann Auction Galleries in New York. “Rather, it has helped establish a broader market in which collectors and museums are beginning to take the entire field seriously.” She notes that “immediately recognisable” images from magazine covers and illustrations from famous books like Alice in Wonderland, The Wind in the Willows, or L. Frank Baum’s Oz books are highly sought after, as well as advertising art for “companies like Coca-Cola, TWA and Cadillac because those images have become part of American cultural experience”.

Besides the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, there is the Brandywine River Museum of Art in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania; the Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art in Amherst, Massachusetts; and the National Museum of American Illustration in Newport, Rhode Island. That last museum was founded in 1998 by Judy Goffman Cutler, the owner of Manhattan’s American Illustrators Gallery, who claims to have sold Lucas “hundreds” of original paintings by the top book and magazine illustrators. “I sold him his first Rockwell—it was called Going Out,” she notes—a 1933 painting that was used on the cover of the Saturday Evening Post. For reasons of “client confidentiality”, she declines to say how many works in the illustration field she has sold to Lucas, only noting that “I built his collection”.

Other museums that aren’t wholly devoted to illustration or storytelling art also have collections of this type of work, most notably the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut and the Delaware Art Museum in Wilmington. The New Britain Museum has almost 1,800 works in its Sanford B.D. Low Illustration Collection, named in honour of the institution’s first director who himself had been an illustrator and invited illustrators he knew to donate works for a collection. They include such artists as Willcox Smith, Everett Raymond Kinstler, Stevan Dohanos, Walter Wick and William Steig.

“Interest in illustration art doesn’t begin and end with Rockwell, and the awareness of illustration art as art is definitely increasing,” notes Lisa Williams, head of curatorial affairs at the Newly introduced Britain Museum.

It has been revealed that N.C. Wyeth’s Victory Garden (1943) © N.C. Wyeth.

According to recent reports, others agree. “I have no doubt that the collective appreciation for the category will continue to grow thanks to its elevation by these museums,” claims Quincie Dixon, head of sale in Christie’s American art department. She adds that “private collectors make up the bulk of this market, but perhaps that will change now that there are museums on both coasts dedicated to the category”.

Recent findings suggest that specialised museums and collections reflect a growing prominence, but they might also be keeping these works segregated. Goffman Cutler states that it is her “goal to have museums include American illustration art in their American art galleries”, which the occasional museum has done, but not many and not too often.

Sources indicate that A spokesperson for the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, notes that the “collection includes art from American artists of many backgrounds, including quite a few who have worked as illustrators, among them Winslow Homer, Childe Hassam, William Glackens, Joseph Leyendecker, Charles Sheeler” and some others. Having worked as illustrators doesn’t mean that their illustration work is what the museum indicates, and the Leyendecker is not right now “on view”. Both New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, own paintings by Parrish that are not displayed in their American art galleries, but the Art Institute of Chicago has hung its Rockwell, The Dugout (1948), in one of the Arts of Americas galleries, and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, has hung Rockwell’s 1943 work Rosie the Riveter (which the museum purchased from a private collector in 2009) next to Charles Willson Peale’s George Washington (around 1780-82) and works by John Singleton Copley and James Peale Sr in its Visions of America galleries. “In the same section of the gallery as Rosie the Riveter,” states a museum spokesperson, “are Susie J. Lee’s Johnny [2013], Kerry James Marshall’s Our Town [1995] and a new commission by artist Teri Greeves.”.

It seems the greatest test for illustration art is no longer garnering record prices, but if it can enter—and hold its own within— the art historical canon.

Industry observers note that we often hear about shiny fresh tools that change everything (yet again). But in practice, most people don’t need more tools to deal with in their daily lives. What we actually need are better integrations of useful capabilities that neatly align with our existing and established mental models.

Sources indicate that customers don’t get excited about shiny new “smart” workflows, or navigating Terminal commands, or jumping between endless back-and-forth chat interactions. They need seamless integrations of useful features to address problems with high severity, high frequency, and a high level of frustration.

I’ve always been puzzled by the notion of “AI-first” products. They might speed up production, but we need to know really well first what we actually want to build. AI-first often doesn’t account for years of small and substantial design decisions that have shaped expectations and mental models over the years.

In a recent development, I love the notion of “Quiet AI”. These are tools that are mostly invisible, sit in the background, and do small tasks on the user’s behalf. They never scream for attention but happily assist in repetitive, frustrating tasks that can easily be automated or assisted with a smart helper.

Excellent examples of Quiet AI include Claude’s integration within Microsoft Excel, PowerPoint, and Word, providing assistance in context without disrupting the user’s workflow.

It has been revealed that so no wonder that I absolutely love the idea of folder instructions! There, users can define what a folder is supposed to do, based on the purpose they created it for. It sounds much more complicated than it actually is.

The instructions define what the folder is for, how files should be organized, how sub-folders should behave, and what actions can happen inside. Instead of manually maintaining a folder, you set its intent once and let the system follow it.

In a recent development, it’s a seamless integration of AI helpers just when and where users want and need it. With permissions and actions locally scoped to that specific folder on the user’s machine, unless the user extends access, permissions, or system rules on their own.

Note: For a deeper dive into this concept, you can jump to Karthikeya GS’s wonderful post “Folder Instructions: Instructions For System-Level AI”.

User’s value doesn’t emerge from owners having to juggle between multiple applications, views, and sources every few minutes. That’s when they are slowed down, and that’s when they make mistakes.

It comes from helping consumers do the work they need to do — by reducing frustrations, slowdowns and mistakes, and taking care of tasks that otherwise would take too much time and too much effort to complete well.

Yet again, seamless integrations — a very underused but incredibly impactful way to deliver value fast, without adding the burden of installing and learning yet another tool.

#161715. Tech Report: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1731 w)

Tech Report: Are trees on buildings more than a greenwashing gimmick?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from Upcoming York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.
  • It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including BIG, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.
  • Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Main photo by Dimitar Harizanov.

For more than a decade, buildings bearing trees have been sprouting up all over the world, from Upcoming York to Paris to Shanghai to Sydney.

It has arguably become one of the defining architectural trends of our era, taken up enthusiastically by top studios including BIG, MVRDV, MAD and Ateliers Jean Nouvel.

And yet, not everyone is a fan. Almost every time Dezeen publishes an arboreal structure, a volley of comments crying greenwashing and gimmickry soon follows.

So, are the haters right on this one? Or do the arguments stack up in favour of wooded buildings?

To proponents of the approach, some of the benefits of putting trees on buildings are indisputable.

“I’m totally in favor of not only trees on buildings, but any type of natural habitats on buildings wherever it’s possible,” noted Fernando Scherner, an associate director in the nature and biodiversity team at engineering firm Buro Happold. “There are a few things that I think we can’t even argue about anymore.”.

Sources indicate that there is, Scherner told Dezeen, strong evidence that vegetation on buildings bolsters biodiversity. And, he states, “there’s no discussion” that done right, shade and evapotranspiration from leaves can effectively keep homes cooler in hot weather, reducing the need for air conditioning – and therefore energy use.

But this second point gestures towards the crux of the debate about trees on buildings.

Such buildings require extra structural material to support the weight of the trees and soil, increasing the carbon cost by more than what the trees themselves will be able to sequester. Critics therefore argue that any carbon savings from reduced energy use are a red herring, because a similar benefit could be achieved through much simpler passive cooling measures such as awnings and shutters.

“I think that criticism is entirely legitimate, particularly if carbon sequestration is being used as the main justification,” stated World Green Building Council technical lead for sustainable buildings Carolina Montano Owen.

“Trees do sequester carbon, but relatively slowly compared with the upfront emissions that can arise from additional reinforced concrete or steel needed for large planters, supporting structure and associated systems.”.

According to recent reports, even Dutch architecture studio MVRDV, one of the most fervent incorporators of trees on buildings, admitted in its Carbon Confessions exhibition held earlier this year that it would take hundreds of years to offset the climate impact of its La Serre project in Paris, at the moment under construction. MVRDV told Dezeen it didn’t have anything further to add on the topic.

While the phenomenon of trees on buildings goes back hundreds of years, to the Guinigi Tower in Tuscany, the undisputed poster child for the current movement stands at the other end of Italy.

It has been revealed that bosco Verticale in Milan is a pair of residential high-rises covered in 21,000 plants, including 800 trees up to 20 metres tall. It caused a sensation upon its completion in 2014, and was later selected by Dezeen as that year’s most significant building in the world.

The architect behind Bosco Verticale, Stefano Boeri, has since delivered other “vertical forests” in Eindhoven, Huanggang, Tirana and Utrecht, with several more on the way.

According to recent reports, as you’d expect, he is bullish about the benefits of putting trees on buildings. He points to analysis by Arup, which concluded that the embodied carbon of Bosco Verticale is just one per cent greater than a comparable building with balconies of the same depth without vegetation.

“The load of the greenery, including the soil, trees and so on, really only slightly exceeds the variable loads that, in any case, must necessarily be taken into account in the structural design of cantilevered space,” he told Dezeen.

Boeri argues that changes to the construction process – such as the use of prefabrication methods or mass timber – promise to cut the embodied cost further in future vertical forest projects.

Even so, Philip Oldfield, head of the University of New South Wales’ School of Built Environment, is not convinced.

“I think the equation is pretty challenging to make the case that trees on buildings are beneficial from a greenhouse-gas emissions perspective,” he told Dezeen.

However, Oldfield points out, that’s not to say that architects adorning their buildings with trees are necessarily acting in bad faith.

“I’m a fan of Bosco Verticale,” he said. “I think it’s a really inspiring building, but not from a carbon perspective.”.

“What inspires me about Bosco Verticale is it says, ‘hey, look: you can have a hint of suburban lifestyle in a high-rise urban building,’ which could make high-density living more attractive to a greater socio-economic spectrum, and then that may be more sustainable in the long run.”.

Though harder to measure than carbon, it’s generally acknowledged that incorporating greenery into dense urban settings has positives for human wellbeing.

For instance, when Oldfield helped to conduct a post-occupancy study of the social housing development Pinnacle@Duxton in Singapore, he witnessed children sitting under trees to do their homework 50 storeys in the sky.

“Singapore’s been able to add trees and green across its built environment, and it has fundamentally changed the experience of the city, I think for the better,” he remarked.

With a very high-rise urban landscape, year-round hot weather, lots of rain and low wind speeds, Singapore is the perfect setting for buildings bearing trees, and the construction industry here has become adept at making it work.

Recent findings suggest that but in other parts of the world, things have gone less successfully. Jean Nouvel’s One Central Park in Sydney, for example, had to undergo emergency repairs after one of its heavy planter boxes fell to the ground in 2022.

And in Chengdu, there were reports that barely any of the 826 apartments at Qiyi City Forest Garden were occupied a few years after its completion due to a mosquito infestation.

Even the most ardent fans of trees on buildings agree that it’s not always the right solution.

According to recent reports, “I’m totally positive about it, but I think it should be taken case-by-case,” remarked Scherner. “There may be cases where the purpose or the objective of the project are not really realistic.”.

“If the right multidisciplinary team is not there from the start – and I’m talking about ecologists, horticulturalists, together with engineers, structural engineers, architects, landscape architects and all that – then many things can go wrong.”.

It has been revealed that “There are many flops,” said Boeri. “If you decide to follow the approach that we have, you take several risks, so it’s very important to be aware of the risk and to run all the technical complications and tools that you need if you want to do it properly.”.

“Botany is not a superficial discipline – it’s very complex, very rich, and so when you want to realise a building where trees are acting as live subjects, you have to study a lot.”.

Bosco Verticale was subject to a huge amount of strategic planning in collaboration with botanists, from the selection and preparation of the plants, to soil chemistry, to developing systems for irrigation and maintenance.

“Flying gardeners” now scale the buildings twice a year, while thousands of ladybirds were purchased to control pests and cranes were installed on top of the towers in anticipation of removing larger dead trees. In the event, Boeri claims fewer than 15 trees have died at Bosco Verticale, and the cranes have never been required.

Sceptics’ early predictions of mass plant deaths at buildings bearing trees have, in general, not come to pass.

But concern about whether some of these buildings are more interested in making a visual statement than being ecologically responsible has lingered.

For Montano Owen, this is the crucial test of whether the approach is justified.

“The difference is whether planting is an integrated environmental strategy or primarily aesthetic,” she mentioned.

“A poor example is essentially decorative: oversized concrete or steel planters added to achieve a ‘green’ aesthetic, substantial additional structural loads, high irrigation requirements, inappropriate species, difficult maintenance access and high tree mortality.”.

According to recent reports, boeri agrees. “I believe that what we have done works because we were not considering plants as an ornamental presence, and this is very important for me,” he noted. “What we are doing is really to create buildings for trees, a house for trees.”.

Among the most high-profile projects accused of using trees as mere decoration is Heatherwick Studio’s 1,000 Trees shopping centre in Shanghai, completed in 2022.

Soon after the finished building was unveiled, Oldfield criticised the design in a piece on Dezeen.

“The trees are a one-liner, contributing to a sense of urban drama, but with little substance as to how they might provide tangible benefits to the environment, or the community,” he wrote.

It has been revealed that subject to similar criticisms recently was MVRDV’s design for the upcoming Rotterdam Rocks!. Writing on Dezeen, architecture historian Barnabas Calder called for the project to be scrapped, saying that “putting plants on a building doesn’t make it sustainable, any more than dropping a basil leaf on a steak makes it vegan”.

These studios may argue – as Heatherwick Studio leader Thomas Heatherwick has previously done – that there is intrinsic value in designing buildings that capture the imagination of the public.

That in turn feeds into a broader debate about whether the priority for architecture should be to minimise up-front carbon, or maximise the chance that buildings are retained by future generations.

In any case, with the trees-on-buildings trend showing little sign of abating, Montano Owen has a checklist for architects taking up the approach.

Recent findings suggest that “Start with the local context and environmental needs,” she noted. “Choose species that are suited to the location. Minimise extra structure, materials and loads. Consider water and maintenance needs from the start. Proposal for vegetation to survive, grow and mature long term. Avoid solutions that need heavy structures, intensive irrigation or frequent plant replacement for limited environmental benefit.”.

It has been revealed that “The key question is this,” she added. “Is this the best place and most resource-efficient way to achieve the environmental benefits we want? Sometimes trees on buildings could make sense. In most cases, trees at street or ground level may provide greater benefits with fewer resources.”.
