This year Simon Skinner was named emerging designer of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, he selects five projects that showcase his work.

Swedish designer Skinner set up his studio in 2020 and has rapidly become known for his sculptural furniture and installations that explore rethinking and reusing found materials.

“My practice is centred around material culture, exploring the relationship between objects, meaning and everyday life,” Skinner told Dezeen.

“What connects my work is an interest in how forms carry associations and how these can be reshaped to offer new perspectives on things we know and take for granted.”.

Skinner finds that the things that excite him about design are also “the same things that make me suffer”.

“You never quite know what’s coming next when running your own practice, but there’s also something exciting about that uncertainty,” he said.

“A material or an object you’ve overlooked for years can suddenly become the starting point for a whole body of work.”.

Over the coming year, along with creating newly introduced collections and public installations, Skinner hopes to dedicate more time to research.

“I want to make more room for research and experimentation, and give myself time to follow an interest before knowing exactly where it might lead,” he noted.

“When I started researching Afro combs at Konstfack, I became aware of how much history and symbolism an everyday tool can hold. That experience still informs how I work,” he continued.

“I want to keep exploring the objects and forms we take for granted, looking at the meanings they’ve inherited and what happens when you change their material, scale or context.”.

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning Skinner, as described by the designer:.

“An ongoing project in which vintage glass sourced from flea markets and second-hand shops is brought together in sculptural lighting compositions.

“Drawing on the memories and associations embedded in these found objects, the work explores the relationship between material, memory and light.”.

“Crafted in my studio, these combs celebrate rituals and traditions surrounding textured hair.

“Informed by historical references and personal experiences, they reimagine an everyday object through distinctive forms and symbols.”.

“Extending the exploration of beauty rituals within the Syntax collection, the Vanity Table offers an alternative reading of an object associated with personal grooming.”.

“These one-of-a-kind pieces, a daybed and an armchair, are upholstered in hand-dyed canvas in deep magenta hues.

“Combining traditional upholstery techniques with an experimental approach to colour and detail, the pieces embrace the irregularities of the dyeing process, making them an integral part of their character.”.

In a recent development, “This piece of furniture explores our relationship to the mechanical lock. The lock is integrated into the leg, with keys used to secure the connection between the leg and the seat.

“The keys can also serve as hooks for keychains and personal belongings, inviting individual expression.”.

Weaponizing And Defending The React Flight Protocol: Deserialization Sinks In RSCs

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, durgesh Rajubhai Pawar is a freelance developer dedicated to building high-performance, accessible web applications. He specializes in orchestrating complex … More about Durgesh ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Sources indicate that react Server Components don’t send HTML to your browser. They don’t send JSON either. When a server component renders, what actually travels over the wire is a custom streaming protocol called Flight. It’s a line-delimited format with its own type system, its own reference resolution, and its own rules for reconstructing executable behavior on the client.

Most React developers have never opened the Network tab and actually looked at a Flight payload. It looks like a mix of JSON fragments, dollar-sign-prefixed references, and module pointers that the React runtime silently reassembles into a live component tree. The framework handles it, so nobody questions it.

I’m not sure most teams have thought carefully about what that trust actually implies.

It has been revealed that I started pulling apart the Flight protocol after CVE-2025-55182 dropped in December 2025. The security community called it React2Shell, and for good reason. It was a CVSS 10.0, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability sitting in the Flight deserialization layer. One crafted HTTP request to a Server Function endpoint, and an attacker had shell access. No credentials needed.

The federal Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Agency (CISA) added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Sysdig tied in-the-wild exploitation to North Korean state-sponsored actors deploying file-less implants through the Ethereum blockchain. That’s the kind of CVE that gets your attention.

After spending time in the source (mostly getOutlinedModel and getChunk, which is where the resolution logic that matters actually lives), I realized React2Shell wasn’t a one-off parsing bug. It was a symptom. Flight reconstructs executable references, lazy-loaded components, server RPC endpoints, and async state from a stream of text. That’s a deserialization system.

The attack surface extends well beyond a single missing hasOwnProperty check. This article covers how Flight works on the wire, where the deserialization sinks are, what attackers have already weaponized, and what’s still exposed.

This leads to a ranked, practical set of defenses for your own Server Components: schema validation on every Server Action, the server-only package, cross-site request forgery (CSRF) hardening beyond framework defaults, and an assessment of what the Taint API and Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) provide.

Open your browser’s Network tab on any Next.js App Router page and look for requests returning Content-Type: text/x-component. That’s Flight. It’s not a single JSON blob. It’s a streaming, line-delimited format where each line is a self-contained “row” that the client-side React runtime processes as it arrives over the connection.

Here’s what a simple Flight payload looks like in practice:.

In a recent development, row 1 is an import directive. It tells the client to load ClientComponent.js from the bundler’s chunk map. Row 2 is a JSON tree that constructs an HTML element, and the "$1" inside children is a reference back to chunk 1 (the imported component). Row 0 defines the server execution context, marking this as a RootLayout running in the Server environment. Even in this tiny example, you can see the mix of structural data, module references, and cross-chunk pointers that makes Flight different from plain JSON.

Every row follows the same syntax: :\n. The row ID is a numeric identifier that other rows can reference. The tag is a single character (or short string) that tells the parser what kind of data follows. The payload is the actual content.

Here are the row tags I found while reading through the source:.

So far, this might look like a benign structured data format with some custom tags, but the real complexity and attack surface live in the prefix system.

This is where I started paying closer attention.

It has been revealed that when the client-side parser encounters a string value starting with $, it doesn’t treat it as literal text. It intercepts the string, checks the prefix, and routes it through a type-specific resolution path. The parseModelString function in ReactFlightClient.js is where this happens. It’s essentially a substantial switch statement on the character after $.

Recent findings suggest that every other prefix resolves a chunk and gives you the parsed result. $@ hands you the raw internal Chunk object instead, the wrapper React uses to track resolution state, pending callbacks, and internal metadata (which is why it’s used for Promises and why exploits use it to get a mutable handle). Exposing framework plumbing through the protocol looks like a design mistake to me, though I’d be interested to hear the rationale if there is one.

It has been revealed that and $: (property access) is the other critical prefix. It lets the protocol specify a path like $1:user:name, which tells the parser to resolve chunk 1, then access .user, then access .name on the result. That’s arbitrary property traversal driven by data in the stream. If you’ve spent any time auditing JavaScript for prototype pollution, that pattern should feel familiar.

Flight is not JSON with extra steps. JSON gives you data. Flight gives you behavior. It reconstructs module references that trigger client-side code loading, creates server action endpoints the client can invoke as RPC calls, sets up Promise chains that the React runtime will await, and builds lazy-loaded component boundaries that execute on demand.

In a recent development, whether React developers think of it that way or not, the mechanics look very similar to deserialization systems that have historically caused problems. The stream doesn’t just describe what the UI looks like. It instructs the client runtime on what code to load, what functions to call, and what to trust.

According to recent reports, if you want to read the implementation yourself, fair warning: the chunk resolution path is miserable to follow. State transitions bounce between helper functions, and the naming obscures what the code is actually doing. I gave up on static reading and just set breakpoints. The key files are react-client/src/ReactFlightClient.js for the client-side parser (look for parseModelString, getChunk, reviveModel, and getOutlinedModel) and react-server/src/ReactFlightServer.js for the serialization side. The reply handler for Server Actions lives in react-server/src/ReactFlightReplyServer.js.

The deserialization pattern is familiar: Java’s ObjectInputStream gave us ysoserial, Python’s pickle executes code on load(), PHP’s unserialize chains __wakeup and __destruct methods, and .NET’s BinaryFormatter was deprecated entirely.

So JavaScript should be immune to this, right? JSON.parse() only produces plain data objects. No constructors fire. No magic methods run. You get back exactly what the JSON string describes, nothing more.

According to recent reports, that’s true for raw JSON.parse(). But it stops being true the moment a framework wraps custom deserialization logic around it. And that’s exactly what Flight does.

According to recent reports, javaScript uses prototype-based inheritance. Every object has a __proto__ link to its prototype, and property lookups walk up this chain. If an attacker injects __proto__ or constructor.prototype as a key during reconstruction, they modify the shared base prototypes that all objects inherit from. Downstream code reads attacker-controlled values without knowing.

Recent findings suggest that flight’s $: prefix performs property traversal on deserialized objects. The getOutlinedModel function walks colon-separated paths like $1:user:name by iterating through each segment and accessing it on the parent object. If those path segments include __proto__ or constructor, the traversal walks straight up the prototype chain. That’s not a theoretical risk. It’s exactly how React2Shell worked.

The V8 engine (and the JavaScript spec) treats any object with a .then property as a Thenable. When you await something, the runtime checks for .then and calls it if it exists. No class check. No internal slot verification. If .then is callable, it gets invoked.

Sources indicate that flight resolves chunks asynchronously. If an attacker constructs an object with a manipulated .then property and gets it into the chunk resolution pipeline, the runtime calls the attacker’s function during normal await behavior. The language semantics do the work.

I initially focused on $F because forging Server Action references seemed like the obvious attack surface. After tracing the resolution path, $: property traversal looked much more interesting. I also spent a few hours examining chunk status transitions (pending, blocked, resolved, errored) to see if you could force a chunk into an unexpected state, though that approach didn’t yield any results.

Recent findings suggest that these two risks converge in Flight because the protocol doesn’t just deserialize data. It deserializes behavior. The $ prefix system dictates which execution path the parser takes: $F creates a callable server endpoint, $L sets up lazy code loading, $B triggers a blob handler, $@ exposes internal framework state. The parser’s control flow is driven entirely by what’s in the stream.

If an attacker can influence the stream’s content, they control which functions the parser calls, which objects it constructs, and which internal state it exposes.

This is the CVE that proved the theory. CVE-2025-55182, nicknamed React2Shell, is a CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in the Flight deserialization layer. One HTTP request, no login required, full shell access.

I want to walk through the entire gadget chain because understanding it reveals how much power the Flight protocol hands to an attacker who can control the stream.

Recent findings suggest that the vulnerability sits in getOutlinedModel, a function responsible for resolving deep property paths from the $: reference system. The instance used in the exploit chain lives in the server-side reply handling code (ReactFlightReplyServer.js). When the parser encounters a reference like $1:user:name, it splits on the colons and walks the path segment by segment. Here’s the vulnerable loop:.

Two lines. No hasOwnProperty check. No validation that the property exists on the object itself rather than somewhere up the prototype chain. Just parentObject[reference[key]] and move on.

So an attacker supplies $1:__proto__:constructor:constructor, and the loop traverses from a plain JSON object up through Object.prototype to the Object constructor to the Function constructor. Function in JavaScript behaves like eval(). Function("arbitrary code")() executes.

No allowlist on property names. No check for __proto__. I searched reviveModel and the chunk initialization path for any filtering. Nothing.

Getting from “I can reach the Function constructor” to “I have RCE” requires chaining several Flight protocol features together. The Resecurity write-up covers the full chain in detail; here’s the high-level sequence:.

In a recent development, each step uses a legitimate Flight protocol feature in a way the designers didn’t anticipate. There’s no single “broken” feature. The vulnerability emerges from how these features compose when an attacker controls the input.

The numbers on this one are stark:.

It has been revealed that exploitation was immediate. Sysdig published research linking EtherRAT deployments to North Korean state-sponsored actors who weaponized the vulnerability within hours of disclosure. EtherRAT is a file-less implant that uses the Ethereum blockchain for command-and-control communication — a technique researchers call “EtherHiding” — making takedown nearly impossible because you can’t seize a blockchain.

Separately, Palo Alto’s Unit 42 documented a backdoor called KSwapDoor that masquerades as [kswapd1] on infected Linux systems, blending into process lists alongside the legitimate kswapd0 kernel swap daemon; their analysis confirms KSwapDoor uses RC4 encryption to protect its internal strings and configuration data, while C2 communications run over AES-256-CFB with Diffie-Hellman key exchange across a P2P mesh network. The speed and sophistication of these campaigns — state-sponsored actors deploying novel implants through a single unauthenticated HTTP request — underscores why a CVSS 10.0 in a deserialization layer demands immediate patching, not triage.

In a recent development, the React team’s patch is clean and targeted. The core change caches the genuine hasOwnProperty method at module load time:.

Then every property check in the deserialization path uses .call() to invoke the cached reference:.

Even if an attacker shadows hasOwnProperty on a malicious object, the check uses the original prototype method. The prototype chain traversal that powered the gadget chain is blocked. This fix shipped in React 19.0.1, 19.1.2, and 19.2.1.

Recent findings suggest that the fix is correct. But reading through the patches, I noticed the React team hardened ownership checks while leaving the property traversal model intact. The $: prefix still walks colon-separated paths; it just validates each step now. I think exposing arbitrary property traversal through a network protocol was a design mistake, and the patch treats the symptom. If future bugs emerge, they’ll likely come from this same area.

Sources indicate that the framework patch closes the known gadget chain, but it doesn’t change the fundamental dynamic: the Flight protocol still reconstructs behavior — executable references, module imports, RPC endpoints, async state — from a stream of text. That reconstruction happens before your application code runs, before your validation logic fires, before your auth middleware even sees the request. Relying solely on the framework to protect your Server Components means trusting that every edge case in a complex deserialization parser has been found and fixed. The defenses that follow are the practical steps you can take to limit the blast radius on your own.

Some of these close real attack paths. Others mostly make you feel safer than you are. I’ve ranked these from most-to-least impactful based on what I’ve seen in the vulnerability research. If you only have time for one change, start at the top.

Recent findings suggest that this is the single most impactful thing you can do at the application level. The Flight deserializer processes raw, unvalidated network input before your code takes control. Strict schema validation is your primary defense against whatever the protocol reconstructs.

It has been revealed that put a schema validation call at the very top of every Server Action, before any business logic runs — and I mean before anything, including logging. If you log an argument before validating it, and that argument triggers the stringification bug from CVE-2025-55183, you’ve leaked source code before your validation even had a chance to run.

Zod and Valibot both work well for this. Validate types, shapes, string lengths, numeric bounds, and enumerated values. Reject anything that doesn’t match. Use .safeParse(), not .parse() — the throwing variant can surface internal error details in the response if you’re not careful with your error boundaries.

In a recent development, one crucial nuance: If your Server Action accepts a plain object argument (not FormData), validate the whole argument — don’t destructure first and validate fields individually. Destructuring before validation means you’re already accessing properties on the unvalidated input, which is exactly the kind of operation the Flight deserializer can exploit.

Sources indicate that if your Server Action doesn’t start with a schema parse, it’s a vulnerability waiting to happen. I’d argue this should be a lint rule — and if you’re running eslint-plugin-react, consider writing a custom rule that flags any "use server" export without a validation call in its first statement.

The server-only package is straightforward and effective.

Industry observers note that import server-only at the top of any file that contains database credentials, raw API calls, internal business logic, or anything else that should never cross the server-client boundary. If a Client Component tries to import that file (directly or transitively), the build fails with a clear error.

The failure mode to watch for is barrel files. If you re-export a server-only function through an index.ts that also exports client-safe utilities, any Client Component importing from that barrel will pull in the server-only module transitively and break the build — or worse, if the barrel doesn’t include the server-only import itself, it may silently let server code through. Keep server-only modules in separate files with their own import paths.

Sources indicate that it also won’t protect you from data leaking through return values. If a Server Component calls getUser() and passes the full user object (including passwordHash or internalRole) as props to a Client Component, that data rides the Flight stream to the browser. The server-only guard prevents the code from crossing the boundary, not the data the code returns. You must explicitly filter your return shapes.

It has been revealed that after CVE-2026-27978, relying solely on Next.js’s built-in Origin vs. Host header check isn’t enough. The Origin: null bypass showed that framework-level CSRF protection has edge cases.

For state-changing Server Actions (anything that writes data, deletes records, or modifies permissions), layer your own protections on top of the framework’s defaults.

Explicit CSRF tokens.For high-value operations (password changes, role assignments, payment actions), generate a per-session CSRF token on the server, embed it in a hidden form field or custom header, and validate it in the Server Action before proceeding.

The allowedOrigins gotcha.Never, under any circumstances, add 'null' to experimental.serverActions.allowedOrigins in your Next.js config (even if the officially advisory is more nuanced, saying “unless intentionally required and additionally protected”). That string literal matches Origin: null — the exact header that sandboxed iframes send — and it reopens the CVE-2026-27978 bypass. If you’re seeing CSRF failures from legitimate requests, the fix is to configure your reverse proxy to set the correct Origin and Host headers, not to weaken the validation.

I covered this in detail in the React2Shell section. The fix is correct, and it completely neutralizes the known gadget chain. It shipped fast, which I respect.

The action item here is to verify you’re actually running a patched version. The RCE fix landed in React 19.0.1, 19.1.2, and 19.2.1. Check your lockfile:.

Recent findings suggest that if you see 19.0.0, 19.1.0â€“19.1.1, or 19.2.0, you’re vulnerable to the RCE. Upgrade immediately. And don’t stop there: the DoS fixes (CVE-2025-55184, CVE-2025-67779, CVE-2026-23864) require 19.0.4+, 19.1.5+, or 19.2.4+. If you updated after React2Shell and then stopped paying attention, you may still be running a version vulnerable to the DoS variants.

It’s a reactive patch, not a structural redesign.

Note: More on that in Where This Goes Next.

According to recent reports, react’s taintObjectReference and taintUniqueValue functions register objects or strings with the runtime. If tainted data tries to pass through the Flight serializer, it throws an error. The idea is to prevent sensitive data — user records, API keys, tokens — from accidentally leaking into the client.

Here’s how it looks in practice:.

If a Server Component passes the tainted user object as props to a Client Component, React throws it at serialization time with your custom error message. That’s genuinely useful as a development-time guardrail.

According to recent reports, the catch — and it’s a significant one — is that taint tracks object references, not data content. Any derivation breaks the tracking:.

Industry observers note that taintUniqueValue works on specific strings (like API keys), but it’s also reference-based. If the same key value appears in a different variable, the taint doesn’t follow.

Industry observers note that think of taint as a development guardrail, not a security boundary. It catches honest mistakes: a developer accidentally passing a full user object to the client. It won’t stop an attacker who can influence what gets serialized, and it won’t survive routine data transformations that your own code performs. It’s a useful defense-in-depth layer, but shouldn’t be your primary boundary.

Web Application Firewalls can add a detection layer for known attack patterns. They can inspect POST requests carrying the Next-Action header, block payloads containing constructor:constructor or __proto__ chains, and flag error responses containing E{"digest" patterns that indicate the server is leaking internal error details.

If you’re running a WAF, here are specific patterns worth adding:.

But attackers know about WAF inspection buffers, and they’re usually around 128KB. Prepend 130KB of padding before the malicious payload, and the WAF inspects the padding, finds nothing, and lets the request through. Chunked Transfer-Encoding tricks accomplish the same thing.

According to recent reports, the failure mode is treating WAF coverage as a security boundary rather than a noise-reduction layer. WAFs catch automated scanners and low-effort attacks, and that has real value. But a motivated attacker will bypass them with padding or encoding tricks. The defenses that actually stop sophisticated attacks are the ones earlier in this list: validating input before it reaches your business logic, keeping sensitive code off the wire, and staying on patched versions.

React2Shell wasn’t the end of it. The security audits that followed the December 2025 disclosure shook out a series of related vulnerabilities in the same deserialization surface. None of them are as severe as the original RCE, but they’re worth tracking because some of them required multiple rounds of patching.

It has been revealed that the DoS pair (CVE-2025-55184 and CVE-2025-67779) is a textbook example of why deserialization parsers are hard to patch correctly. The first fix shipped, researchers found edge cases it missed, and a second round was needed. CVE-2026-23864 added a third DoS vector through unbounded memory allocation rather than CPU exhaustion. (See the defenses section above for specific version checks.).

CVE-2025-55183 is the sneaky one. It’s a source code exposure bug that triggers when a Server Function calls JSON.stringify (or any implicit stringification) on one of its arguments. Developers do this constantly for logging, debugging, or error reporting.

The attacker sends a crafted argument that, when stringified, causes the deserialization parser to reflect the function’s own source code back in the response. Business logic, database queries, and any hardcoded secrets sitting in Server Action files become readable by anyone who can send an HTTP request.

CVE-2026-27978 is a different class of bug entirely. It’s a CSRF bypass in Next.js’s Server Action handling. Next.js validates that the Origin header matches the Host header to prevent cross-site request forgery. But when a request comes from a sandboxed , the browser sends Origin: null.

The CVEs above have patches. But some of the risk is structural, baked into how Flight is designed to work.

Man-In-The-Middle (MITM) On The Flight Stream

If an attacker can sit between server and client (CDN compromise, cache poisoning, rogue proxy), modifying the Flight stream in transit looks feasible. The format is plain text with a predictable structure.

Assuming stream control, an attacker could alter $I (Import) rows to redirect component loading to a different module in the webpack chunk map. They could inject $F (Server Reference) tags to embed hidden RPC triggers in the rendered UI. They could modify D (Data) rows to change component props, and if the target component uses dangerouslySetInnerHTML, that’s a direct XSS vector.

Flight escapes $ prefixes in user-supplied strings to prevent data from being interpreted as protocol instructions. But that only applies to data flowing through the serializer. A MITM attacker writes raw protocol directly into the stream. The escaping doesn’t help.

Server Action IDs are obfuscated hashes generated at build time. They look random. But server-reference-manifest.json maps every action ID to its source implementation. A public manifest hands an attacker a complete API map. This exposure usually stems from misconfigured hosting, an exposed .next directory, or path traversal.

Known action IDs expose Server Actions to standard IDOR and parameter tampering attacks. An attacker can forge direct requests with manipulated arguments. Developers often trust these inputs blindly because they originate from React’s internal machinery. The architectural consequences of that misplaced trust will be the focus of my next piece.

When a Server Action captures variables from its surrounding scope (closures), Next.js encrypts them before sending to the client. The key is in NEXT_SERVER_ACTIONS_ENCRYPTION_KEY, AES with a base64-encoded key (16, 24, or 32 bytes). decryptActionBoundArgs handles decryption on each invocation.

By default, this key regenerates every build. But multi-server setups often use a static key. If an attacker gets file read access (path traversal, SSRF), they extract the key, decrypt the closure state, modify it (changing a userId, a role, a query parameter), and re-encrypt. The server accepts the forged closure as legitimate.

Supply Chain Activation via Module IDs

I haven’t demonstrated this end-to-end, but the theory is straightforward.

Flight references client components by module ID, something like ["360","static/chunks/app/page-7f3480.js"]. The bundler assigns these IDs at build time based on the module graph. A compromised npm package sitting in node_modules as a transitive dependency gets bundled into a chunk but never loaded because no component references it. Inert.

But if an attacker injects $I import references into the Flight stream (via MITM, cache poisoning, or server-side injection), the parser should load that dormant module. There may be chunk-level validation I’m not seeing. But if the module ID is valid and present in the manifest, I don’t see what stops it. The attack doesn’t require the package to be imported anywhere in your code. It just needs to exist in the bundle output.

React Flight isn’t the first framework to invent a custom serialization format for server-client communication and then discover it’s an attack surface. And it won’t be the last.

Google Web Toolkit (GWT) used a custom RPC protocol to sync Java objects between browser and server. BishopFox demonstrated that attackers could manipulate the wire format to achieve arbitrary deserialization; GWT eventually disabled binary serialization entirely. It took years.

Java Server Faces (JSF) and ASP.NET both serialized ViewState to the client as a hidden form field. When cryptographic signing was weak or missing, attackers tampered with the serialized state and achieved remote code execution. Microsoft and Oracle patched it repeatedly. The underlying pattern kept resurfacing.

The pattern is always the same: a framework invents a custom wire format to move rich, stateful, sometimes executable data between server and client. The designers assume the server is the sole producer of that data and the client is a trusted consumer. Then someone demonstrates that the wire format can be manipulated in transit, or that the server can be tricked into deserializing attacker-controlled input. React Flight is the latest entry in this pattern. It is not an anomaly.

The React Flight protocol solves a genuinely hard problem: streaming interactive component trees from server to client in a way that enables progressive hydration, async data loading, and server-driven code splitting. It works. I don’t want to lose sight of that.

But it works by serializing executable references, async state, module pointers, and RPC endpoints over a streaming text protocol, and then trusting the structure of that stream on both ends. The React team has patched the known gadgets. The hasOwnProperty fix is correct. The DoS fixes are in place. The source code exposure bug is closed.

I think exposing arbitrary property traversal and executable Thenable reconstruction through a network-facing protocol was a design mistake. $:, $@, and $B are powerful internal primitives that were reachable through a parser that didn’t validate ownership of the properties it traversed. One check was missing, and the result was CVSS 10.0.

As more frameworks adopt server-driven UI patterns, the industry is going to need stronger primitives than “the server is trusted”: cryptographic validation of serialized payloads, signed component trees, and content integrity checks on the Flight stream itself.

Hoping the parser handles every edge case hasn’t worked historically, and I don’t see why it would start working now.

The code is in react-client/src/ReactFlightClient.js. If you ship Server Components, read it. Know what your framework is trusting on your behalf.

Alphamarkâs web design for Studio Plato pairs a locked split-screen diptych with rippled glass transitions and stark white project pages.

Industry observers note that studio Platoâs homepage doesnât scroll at all. Designed and developed by Alphamark for the interior architecture practice, the landing screen locks into a full-viewport 50/50 diptych where two views of the same room share one frame. On the opening slide for Tiny Apartment in Newly introduced York City, a dark walnut kitchen and sheer linen curtain anchor the left column while a wide living area sits on the right. Navigation floats straight across the photography in white: a bold uppercase PLATO wordmark beside a two-line tagline on the left, four crisp links and a frosted Letâs Connect button on the right. Moving from slide 01/03 to 02/03 triggers the siteâs quiet signature. Horizontal rippled bands warp the outgoing room like fluted architectural glass before settling onto Residence Lumiereâs thatched courtyard in Zwevegem, Belgium, and later the dark-paneled lounge of San Franciscoâs D Residence. Minimal controls in the lower-right corner keep that pacing tight.

Sources indicate that stepping past the homepage flips the whole tonal register. On the Selected Projects â24 â â26 index, full-bleed atmosphere gives way to a bright white page and black header chrome, accented only by a solid-black Letâs Connect box and a thin rule beneath the active link. Alphamark staggers the portfolio across two uneven columns so large scenes like Singaporeâs Kage Matcha Bar carry visual weight beside smaller, lower-set previews of Residence Lumiere. A feathered blur along the bottom edge softens incoming rooms and gray one-line captions before they clear into focus. Opening Tiny Apartment pulls back even further: the project title sits alone above an edge-to-edge shelving detail, letting natural light and book spines hold the viewport without sidebar clutter.

Industry observers note that that same web design discipline carries into the Studio and Services pages. On the Studio route, a centered three-line statement rests above a stepped five-image strip of stone, travertine, weathered timber, and terracotta vessels, while the paragraph underneath clears gradually from a soft blur as reading continues. Services trades photographic drama for a three-column editorial split separated by a single faint vertical hairline. Left holds Contemporary Interior Design and a black Learn More button; middle lists six plain deliverables from Concept Development to 3D Visualization; right grounds the layout with one vertical room plate. Itâs a calm bit of web design that lets architectural materiality breathe while keeping every link one click away.

#161699. Breaking: Thinking Outside The Box: Digital Design In The AI Era

Breaking: Thinking Outside The Box: Digital Design In The AI Era

📅 2026-07-28 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at MacPaw who not only believe that making great products requires seeing the world in a different light, but also strive to innovate and create incredible software ecosystem for owners’ Macs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Oleksii Hrzhehorzhevskyi is a Senior Character Producer at MacPaw, specializing in character design, animation, and visual storytelling. He right now leads the … More about Oleksii ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that this article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at MacPaw who not only believe that making great products requires seeing the world in a different light, but also strive to innovate and create incredible software ecosystem for owners’ Macs. Thank you!

Sources indicate that the phrase “artificial intelligence” has many excited, especially those in tech. But for those of us in creative fields like digital art and design, AI can be more concerning than it is exciting.

Recent findings suggest that AI-generated art, videos, and images have flooded the internet, raising questions about whether more companies will turn to tools like OpenAI’s Dall-E, Midjourney, Leonardo.ai, and more, rather than employing human artists. What’s more, the fact that these AI models are trained on real artists’ work without their consent leaves many feeling as if they have no choice but to accept AI into their work and lives.

It has been revealed that in a digital world increasingly dominated by faceless AI chatbots, agents, and features, it can be easy to get overwhelmed by all the technology. AI will certainly play a huge role in reshaping many industries, including design. We can’t deny this. But at the same time, humanization, empathy, and having a person at the wheel have never been more vital.

Rather than viewing AI as something that replaces human creativity, we at MacPaw saw an opportunity to explore how we could make AI feel more personal and accessible — all the while keeping humans at the center of the experience. That led us to rethink how AI assistants are created.

Traditional AI assistants like Claude and ChatGPT typically take the form of a conversational textbox or webpage on screen, as this is how users have interacted with their devices. It’s comfortable and familiar. While extremely useful for a variety of tasks, interacting with these AI assistants can feel transactional and technical.

Recent findings suggest that using the same textbox format across all AI assistants does provide consistency. But we wanted to create a newly introduced, more personal and differentiated experience for consumers. But what format would be best? Even if we change how an AI tool looks, it still needs to be useful and intuitive to use.

As humans, it’s easier to understand and connect with things that resemble us. This is why we often find ourselves drawn to things like animals and characters: they have traits that we recognize within ourselves. Understanding this, we saw an opportunity to combine these values: utility and personality.

Enter Eney: a new proactive AI assistant. MacPaw didn’t want Eney to simply be another AI tool for users, but rather one that proactively assists within a user’s workflow. The vision was to help users connect with Eney more easily than with other AI tools, so we decided to create a character users could interact with. We wanted Eney to be expressive, friendly, and to emote as humans do. But we needed to strike an important balance: making Eney cheerful without it being overly goofy or childish.

Recent findings suggest that this is where human animation and intervention played a critical role. While challenging, it was crucial because an overloaded character UI could turn owners off and make navigating Eney difficult. To avoid this, the design team chose to create a select set of emotions and gestures for Eney to express, ensuring that its expressions conveyed useful information. For example, when working on a task, Eney’s figure resembles a loading icon. To do this, we worked to reduce Eney’s on-screen movement to make sure it wasn’t distracting or excessive.

Recent findings suggest that after exploring a few different shapes and styles for Eney, we settled on a circular figure, as it felt the most approachable. It was simple and helped create the feeling of a calm, floating digital companion, rather than another rigid interface element on a user’s desktop. Eney’s minimal face design also plays an notable role in connecting with the user. Its eyes are the main emotional connector — a key feature in showing emotions without being cartoonish.

The color choice for Eney was also crucial. Many AI assistants and companies use blue in their products, as it’s typically associated with intelligence. Blue is a great color, but we wanted Eney to stand out. We still wanted the color to be warm and inviting while slightly more visually stimulating, which led us to choose the color pink. Among dozens of other AI products that choose a more blue aesthetic, Eney was designed to catch a user’s eye and stand out in their mind (and on their screen).

All in all, we wanted to create a character that was present but not attention-seeking; a warm and supportive digital helper that enhances a user’s workflow rather than distracts from it. Eney’s character gives personality to otherwise invisible processes.

While those who aren’t design professionals may assume there wasn’t much significance behind Eney’s character creation, this couldn’t be further from the truth. Like many other products, all these elements — style, design, emotion, size, name, and more — were intentionally chosen, not by machines but by humans.

Even though AI has streamlined many design processes, namely enabling faster design, there are still many things it can’t do well. Even when designing Eney, while technology supported the process, human designers controlled every step and decision.

As designers, it’s more key than ever to have good judgment, artistic direction, integrity, and emotional sensitivity when working in the field. Technology like AI can help us work faster, but it can’t replace the values that inspire and shape our work.

What’s more, while anyone can easily generate something by typing a prompt into an AI image tool, there’s a true beauty and talent when intentionally crafting something through manual design.

As designers, we shouldn’t stray away from the latest tools. Rather, we should learn them and see how they could potentially help us within our creative workflows. Personally, I like to use AI tools such as Perplexity and ChatGPT for research purposes in the early stages. However, we need to remember that they’re just that: tools. At the end of the day, technology like AI cannot, and should not, replace human artistry. It should help us express our visions, not replace us entirely.

If there’s one thing to take away from this piece, it’s that curiosity helps build taste over time, and taste becomes more valuable, not less, in the AI era.

Industry News: Munch museum appoints Thorsten Sadowsky as newly introduced director

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Munch museum in Oslo, dedicated to the work of the Modernist artist Edvard Munch, has appointed Thorsten Sadowsky to be its next director.
  • Industry observers note that sadowsky arrives with experience leading several prominent European institutions.
  • In a recent development, “My experience at the Kirchner Museum Davos has taught me that the distinctive strength of a museum dedicated to a single artist can also be its greatest challenge,” Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Munch museum in Oslo, dedicated to the work of the Modernist artist Edvard Munch, has appointed Thorsten Sadowsky to be its next director. Sadowsky, who joins Munch from Stiftung Schleswig-Holsteinische Landesmuseen Schloss Gottorf (Schleswig-Holstein State Museums Foundation Schloss Gottorf) in northern Germany, will begin his newly introduced role on 1 May 2027.

Industry observers note that sadowsky arrives with experience leading several prominent European institutions. His current position involves the management of multiple museums in the Schleswig-Holstein area, including the Museum of Art and Cultural History Schloss Gottorf and the Jewish Museum Rendsburg. Previously he has also directed the Museum der Moderne Salzburg, Museum Kunst der Westküste in Alkersum and the Kirchner Museum Davos, which is focused on the life and career of the German Expressionist Ernst Ludwig Kirchner.

In a recent development, “My experience at the Kirchner Museum Davos has taught me that the distinctive strength of a museum dedicated to a single artist can also be its greatest challenge,” Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper. “Such a museum offers an exceptional opportunity to engage with an artist’s oeuvre with a degree of intensity and depth that is rarely possible in an art museum with a more broadly based collection. The challenge, however, is to ensure that the focus on a single artist does not lead to intellectual or curatorial narrowness.”.

Sadowsky adds that his task is therefore “to continually open up new perspectives, reveal unexpected connections and bring the artist’s work into dialogue with other artistic practices, historical experiences and contemporary concerns”.

Sources indicate that the Munch museum, which opened in a sprawling fresh home on Oslo’s Bjørvika waterfront in 2021, houses nearly 27,000 works of art by Munch. Alongside its permanent displays, the museum hosts a temporary exhibition programme that has brought Munch’s work into dialogue with that of contemporary artists such as Tracey Emin, Katherina Grosse and Alice Neel, as well as events such as concerts and conferences. It has welcome more than 700,000 visitors so far this year, according to a release.

Sadowsky tells The Art Newspaper that he first encountered Munch’s work at the Hamburger Kunsthaller, while he was a university student. The opportunity to direct the museum, he states, is exciting thanks to "the extraordinary richness of [Munch’s] artistic legacy. Beyond the familiar image of Munch as a painter of anxiety, loneliness and existential uncertainty, there is still much to discover. His work speaks equally of vitality, human relationships, our experience of nature and the social transformations of modernity.“.

“Few artists have succeeded so convincingly in transforming individual experiences into images of universal human significance,” he adds. “In the realm of sculpture, Alberto Giacometti is another artist who achieved something similar.”.

Sources indicate that in his previous role as director of the Museum der Modern Salzburg, Sadowsky spoke about the importance of widening the scope of the programme and collection. He told the Austrian art magazine Parnass in 2022: “During my tenure as director, a major focus has been on broadening our perspective beyond the Western European canon and incorporating more postcolonial viewpoints.”.

Recent findings suggest that in his new role, Sadowsky says his immediate priority will be to “listen, to learn and to develop and deeper understanding“ of the institution and its people. “Over the coming years, I would like to further strengthen the Munch Museum as the world’s foremost centre of expertise on Edvard Munch, while continuing to develop it as an internationally minded, intellectually vibrant and socially relevant cultural institution,” he adds.

Sources indicate that the Munch museum is owned by the city of Oslo. Mehmet Kaan Inan, Oslo’s vice mayor for culture and business development, states in a statement: “I am delighted that Munch [museum] will be led by a director with such strong international experience and outstanding expertise in the arts. Sadowsky has headed several highly respected art museums and has demonstrated a strong talent for audience development, collaboration, and engaging broad and diverse audiences. His exceptional interest in Edvard Munch’s artistic legacy also provides an excellent foundation for leading Munch [museum] into the future.”.

Industry observers note that sadowsky takes over from Henrik Svalheim, who has served as interim director since Tone Hansen departed in October. Hansen left to lead Moderna Museet in Stockholm.

The Munch museum directorship runs as a six-year term, with the potential for one renewal.

#161697. The Bull And Bear Case For Digital Design In The Age Of AI

📅 2026-07-29 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1894 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

The Bull And Bear Case For Digital Design In The Age Of AI

📅 2026-07-29 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, andy is a design founder turned startup investor and coach.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Designers have spent years saying they would do better work if the organisation got out of the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, andy is a design founder turned startup investor and coach. He loves speaking at conferences like Smashing Conf and is a founding member of the Adobe Design … More about Andy ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Designers have spent years saying they would do better work if the organisation got out of the way. Not always in those exact words, obviously. It usually comes out as something more reasonable: we didn’t get enough engineering time, product had already decided the solution, the roadmap was too packed, leadership only cared about this quarter’s numbers, research got cut, the experiment was never run properly, the design debt was known about, but nobody wanted to spend a sprint fixing it.

Recent findings suggest that much of this is true. Most designers have worked inside that awkward middle space between product and engineering. Product frames the problem, or at least thinks it does. Engineering decides what is feasible, or at least what is affordable. Design is expected to make the thing clearer, simpler, more coherent, more usable, and occasionally more desirable, while also being careful not to disrupt the plan too much.

That position has always been uncomfortable.

They can spot the broken onboarding flow, the confusing upgrade path, the empty state that makes users feel stupid, the feature that looks reasonable in a product review but makes no sense in real use. Seeing the problem is one thing. Getting it fixed is another.

Industry observers note that so design often becomes an argument. You make the case. You annotate the flow. You bring the research clip. You point to the support tickets. You show the Figma prototype. You explain why the “small edge case” is actually the first-run experience for half your new consumers. Then everyone nods, agrees it matters, and moves on to whatever had already made it onto the roadmap.

This is one reason AI is more interesting for design than the usual “will it replace designers?” debate suggests. The real change is not that designers can make more screens. Nobody needs more screens. The interesting change is that designers may need less permission.

A good designer can now move from “we should fix this” to “I fixed this, and pushed it live.” They can prototype the alternative onboarding flow, write and test clearer product copy, build a rough working version of the interaction, clean up small pieces of design debt without waiting three months for a roadmap slot, and make the better thing visible enough that it becomes harder to ignore.

Industry observers note that that changes the politics of the work. Design has often relied on persuasion because designers lacked direct means of production. AI weakens that dependency. Not everywhere, and not for everything. Complex products still have architecture, infrastructure, data models, permissions, security, compliance, legacy systems, and all the other unglamorous reasons software is hard. But the boundary is moving.

It has been revealed that in this version of the future, designers become less permission-dependent: less reliant on product to bless the problem, less reliant on engineering to make every small improvement real, less trapped in the role of internal critic, taste-provider, or Figma operator. More able to make, test, repair, and ship.

In a recent development, the best designers start to look less like traditional product designers and more like hybrid product leaders. They still care about interaction, hierarchy, language, flow, brand and craft, but they also understand the commercial shape of the problem. They can make trade-offs. They can prototype in code, or close enough to code. They can use AI to explore options promptly, then use judgment to throw most of them away. They can sit with a founder or PM and move from a vague product concern to something tangible by the end of the day.

There may be fewer of these people, but they will be harder to ignore. The current design-org model was partly built around scarcity: scarce engineering time, slow production, expensive prototypes, handoffs between specialists, heavy coordination across teams. If AI reduces some of that scarcity, it probably reduces the need for some of the roles that grew around it. The optimistic case is not that every designer keeps their job and gets a productivity boost. That feels like wishful thinking. The more believable version is that the total number of designers goes down, but the designers who remain have more direct influence over the product.

In a recent development, that is not a bad outcome for the strongest designers. It may even be the thing many of them have wanted for years.

According to recent reports, autonomy has teeth. If AI gives designers more room to act, it also removes some of the cover. The same constraints that held good designers back have also protected weaker ones from being tested too directly.

For years, it has been easy to say: I had a better idea, but we never got the engineering time. Sometimes that was exactly what happened. Sometimes the better idea was never really more than a critique. It had not been made concrete. It had not been tested. It had not dealt with the awkward trade-offs. It sounded strong because it lived safely in opposition to the shipped thing.

According to recent reports, if you can prototype the recommendation, the recommendation has to get better. If you can make the alternative flow, the flow has to survive contact with details. If you can test the product copy, you have to care what happens when users read it. If you can fix the small piece of design debt, you have to decide whether it was really worth fixing.

According to recent reports, some designers are not as strategic as they think they are. They have learned the language of strategy without the discomfort of owning outcomes. They can talk about user needs, business goals, systems thinking, and product quality, but struggle when asked to make a call. They want influence, but not the exposure that comes with it.

Sources indicate that the profession has spent a long time arguing that design deserves more power. Fine. But more power means fewer excuses. It means the work is judged less by the elegance of the argument and more by the quality of the thing you made, tested, or changed. That is a better standard, but it will not be kind to everyone.

Recent findings suggest that there is a second bear case, and it is probably the one large design teams should worry about most. Product and engineering already have more institutional power than design in most companies. They own the roadmap, the technical architecture, the sprint machinery, the metrics, and usually the language leadership understands. Design often has to translate its concerns into someone else’s terms before they count.

Sources indicate that AI may not rebalance that power. It may hand product and engineering enough design capability to make design easier to bypass. A PM who can generate a decent flow, decent copy, and a decent prototype may not feel the same need to involve design early. An engineer who can use AI to produce a reasonable interface may decide the design system covers enough of the decision-making. A founder who can get to a polished demo in an afternoon may confuse polish with product thinking.

According to recent reports, the problem is not that these people will suddenly become great designers. The problem is that many companies do not know the difference between great design and plausible design. Plausible design is dangerous. It looks coherent in a product review. It uses the right components. The spacing is fine. The copy is not embarrassing. The flow mostly works. Nobody in the meeting feels strongly enough to object. So it ships.

If a manufacturer already thinks design is mostly screens, prototypes, and polish, AI gives it a cheaper way to get those things.

In that world, design does not gain more agency. It gets narrowed. The remaining designers manage the design system, police component usage, review flows that have already been decided, tidy the interface, maintain brand consistency, and get pulled into high-stakes debuts, executive demos, and the occasional messy cross-platform problem. Useful work, but a smaller surface area. Less shaping the product, more maintaining the furniture.

This is why the “AI will automate the boring 20%” argument feels too comforting. In some companies, perhaps that is what happens. But in large tech organisations, where design teams grew around coordination, production and process, the cut could be much deeper. Not 20%. Maybe 50%. Maybe more. Especially in places where leadership never really understood why the design team had grown so large in the first place.

It has been revealed that the painful part is that both futures can be true at the same time. AI can make the best designers more capable and many average designers less necessary. It can give design more agency while reducing design headcount. It can help a small number of designers move closer to product leadership while pushing others into governance and clean-up work. It can free designers from waiting for permission, then reveal that some were more comfortable waiting than acting.

Sources indicate that the designers who do well will not be the ones who merely use AI to produce more options. Options are cheap now. They will be the ones who know which option is worth pursuing, why it matters, how to test it, what to cut, where the product is lying to itself, and when “good enough” is quietly damaging the business.

Sources indicate that they will have taste, but taste will not be enough. They will need product judgment, technical curiosity, commercial awareness and the nerve to make decisions before every variable is settled. They will need to be comfortable moving between a customer conversation, a prototype, a pricing concern, a brand question, and a messy implementation detail without insisting that all of those belong to someone else.

I’m not completely sure where we end up. I hope it is closer to the bull case: fewer permission structures, more making, more agency, better designers finally able to show what they can do without being held back by the machinery around them.

I fear it may be closer to the bear case: product and engineering absorb much of the work, companies decide plausible design is good enough, and design loses status, headcount, and strategic ground.

Industry observers note that in reality, it will probably be some uncomfortable mix of the two. Some designers will use AI to gain more agency. Some companies will use it to need fewer designers. Some teams will produce better work because the distance between judgment and execution gets shorter. Others will ship more plausible mediocrity because nobody in the room can tell the difference.

For years, designers have stated they could create more value if they were less constrained by the organisation around them. AI is about to test that claim. Some will finally get to prove it. Some will find out the constraints were doing them a favour.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • DixonBaxi sets the EA SPORTS FC 27 brand identity free, turning one triangle into dozens of forms built to move, remix and belong to fans.
  • FC spent three years building something millions love, and DixonBaxi kept the shape at the centre of it rather than redrawing it.
  • Sources indicate that type does the loud work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DixonBaxi sets the EA SPORTS FC 27 brand identity free, turning one triangle into dozens of forms built to move, remix and belong to fans.

The triangle was already the mark. FC spent three years building something millions love, and DixonBaxi kept the shape at the centre of it rather than redrawing it. The studio set it loose instead. One triangle now arrives as a wireframe outline, a dotted halftone field, a pixelated edge, a solid green slab or a beam of light, and the identity holds together because the shape never changes, only the way it behaves. The line on the posters says it plainly: FC is not played, it is lived.

Sources indicate that type does the loud work. The grid sheet sets EVERYONE'S PLAYING in stacked condensed caps, with the FC27 lockup held to two columns and the tagline stretched across five, and the annotations name the voice: Cruyff Sans Condensed Medium for the calls to action, Cruyff Sans Regular for the small print. THE WORLD'S GAME runs the same way on the billboards, the heavy word GAME dropped below a tracked-out THE WORLD'S in the same condensed face.

The grid behind it all is the triangle itself. Lines flow across the posters the way crowds move, and the lockups sit inside the same diagonal geometry, so a headline, a phone screen and a stadium banner all read as one system. The palette stays close to the pitch: electric green leads, with hot pink, purple and blue in support, and black fields that let the colour shout.

The system proves itself on real objects. A green controller carries the triangle pattern across its shell, with the FC27 lockup set into the touchpad in pale gold. The Grounds, the open world where players meet, compete and chat beyond the pitch, gets its own mark: FC set inside a heavy triangle, with SCREEN, STADIUM and STREET as its three corners, and ten small variants beneath it in pink, purple, green and white.

The launch trailer pulled 5+ million views on day one, and the same triangles now run from campaign posters to the game itself, built for a community the studio counts at one billion fans. Make it your Club, your City, your Crew, your Home, your Block: the identity hands the shape to the fans and lets them finish it.

Industry News: Meet Laerke Ryom, Patricia Urquiola's pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Peter Vinther (unless stated otherwise).
  • Architect and designer Patricia Urquiola has chosen fellow multidisciplinary Laerke Ryom as her pick for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, in partnership with Kohler.
  • Ryom, who is based in Copenhagen, first came to many people’s attention as one of the co-founders of the design community Ukurant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Peter Vinther (unless stated otherwise).

Architect and designer Patricia Urquiola has chosen fellow multidisciplinary Laerke Ryom as her pick for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, Ryom discusses her innovative work and how it’s rooted in Danish design traditions.

Ryom, who is based in Copenhagen, first came to many people’s attention as one of the co-founders of the design community Ukurant.

Together with fellow founders Josefine Krabbe Munck, Kamma Rosa Schytte and Kasper Kyster, Ryom demonstrated her work as part of its first exhibition at Danish design week 3 Days of Design in 2020, and Ukurant swiftly became a recurring highlight of the design event.

Since graduating from the Royal Academy of Fine Art in Copenhagen’s master’s program in furniture and object in 2022, Ryom’s tactile designs have continued to evolve, and she has worked with a range of materials and products.

For her collection Blå, she made handwoven denim upholstery out of worn-out jeans, while the Buckle chair, made with furniture brand Fredericia, resembles a leather jacket.

“I find very interesting the way she moves naturally between furniture and textiles, starting from discarded materials and giving them a fresh logic through simple gestures,” Urquiola stated of why she chose Ryom.

Sources indicate that “There is something light in the way she works. Her work feels open and still very much in evolution.”.

This experimentation has become something of a signature for Ryom, whose latest exhibition, Raiments, was a sleek exploration of how upholstery could almost become a furniture piece in itself.

To the designer, her work now is in some ways a continuation of the projects she worked on during her time at the Royal Academy.

“During my studies, I was investigating different materials and different typologies, which I actually still think I’m kind of doing – I don’t see myself as limited to one material,” Ryom told Dezeen.

While she “really strongly identifies as a furniture designer”, Ryom has also designed smaller products, such as metal bowls for the Bread & Butter exhibition in Copenhagen and quilted lamps.

To her, function is always at the forefront, and Ryom believes that even details that appear to be purely decorative have a function if they tell a story.

“Even when I’m doing collectible things for galleries, I’m always thinking of the functionality of the pieces,” she explained.

Recent findings suggest that “Even if you can say, ‘[what’s functional] about doing a little skirt on a chair’, as on the Raiments chair, it tells a story; a story of the cover being loose, something that is its own thing, [separate] from the frame. For me, that’s still a function or a means to an end.”.

Her aim is to create pieces that straddle the line between collectible and functional design; something that is artistic and yet commercial enough to someday go into production.

“I want it to be something where the distance between the categories disappears, and they become a shared thing,” Ryom explained.

“That’s something I think a lot about, that the collectible design and the artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production.”.

The collectible design and artistic work I do should have a little sprinkle of something that you could see in production.

The idea of giving beauty to everyday objects, rather than creating pieces that are purely functional or purely aesthetic, is one that has deep roots in the Scandinavian design tradition.

While Ryom’s pieces might not be the pale-wood designs usually associated with Danish design – though she has worked in wood, using offcut wooden pieces to design furniture for Ukurant in 2023 – she sees herself as part of this tradition.

“Even if people don’t think that what I do looks like typical Danish design, I feel like it’s completely rooted and very fundamentally based on the principles of the Danish design tradition,” she explained.

“I view myself as someone who is not in opposition, but who is developing or following along [with it].”.

While her own pieces in the past have so far mostly been made in smaller quantities, Ryom sees positively on the current trend of significant brands, such as IKEA and Disney, working with younger designers and mass-producing their work.

She believes it helps to spread knowledge about designers to a public that isn’t always aware of the people behind the products.

“I think it’s an important thing because what we see, at least here in Denmark, is that the knowledge about designers today, for the general public, is crazy small for a nation that kind of brands itself as a design nation,” Ryom mentioned.

“Talking to my parents, even with them having a designer for a daughter, they’re still trying to figure out ‘what is it that you actually do’?

Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it.

Sources indicate that ryom herself, meanwhile, notes she sees a big difference between her current work and that of a few years ago. She thinks it comes from “starting to believe in yourself and your intuition, and getting more skilled in your craft”.

But, she also consciously works on developing her ideas and taking them from the initial inspiration stage to the final product.

“Inspiration is something that I stumble upon in my everyday life, but at the same time, it only becomes interesting when I sit down and work with it,” she said.

“Inspiration can only take you so far – at some point you need to get working on it, interpret it and experiment with it and investigate what the substance of the inspiration actually is.”.

Recent findings suggest that as someone who’s constantly exploring new materials and ways of designing, Ryom also highlights the importance of collaboration. She indicates that while she likes doing a lot of the work on her furniture herself, she has also gotten better at reaching out to experts to get input for some of her pieces, including her Enfold chair.

The steel chair is covered in a ruched leather upholstery, held in place by buttons, that creates a very tactile, sculptural seat.

“It did it all myself, but I reached out to a fashion designer who does a lot of leather bags, and I could talk to her and ask ‘how would you do the finishing here, or what kind of tool would you use there?'” she stated.“I really like figuring things out myself and doing it myself, but seeking the knowledge of those people who have really done the craft.”.

Being chosen by Urquiola meant a lot to Ryom, who really admires the Spanish designer.

“It was actually a little surreal, because she is someone that I look up to,” Ryom mentioned. “When you can say anyone in the world, I feel very, very honoured that she pointed at me – that’s a huge thing.”.

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

According to recent reports, picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

It has been revealed that the magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your strategy, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear rapidly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy® at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

According to recent reports, turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can initiative around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Standard or Everyday awards will NOT be bookable through Turkish.

Search for "Saver" fares in economy and note the exact flight numbers, dates, and times. Take a screenshot — you'll need these details when you move to the Turkish website.

Industry observers note that tip: United's calendar view lets you scan a full month for saver availability. Use it. Flexibility of even 1–2 days can be the difference between finding a seat and hitting a wall.

Industry observers note that go to turkishairlines.com and navigate to the Miles & Smiles award booking tool. Search the same route and dates you identified on United. Turkish's search engine pulls real-time Star Alliance availability, so what you see here is what you can book. If the saver seats from Step 1 appear, you're ready to move.

Crucial: If you don't yet have a Turkish Miles & Smiles account, create one now — it's free and takes just a few minutes.

Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Industry News: How Baseline Can Help You Ship Less JavaScript

📅 2026-08-07 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
